certification of train drivers, but we remain somewhat sceptical about the need to certify the on-board staff as well, as is the case with other means of transport.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the distinction between international transport and transport between member states and national transport dates back to 1956, to be precise, to article 70 of the treaty establishing the european coal and steel community, the first european transport regulation. it seems to me quite obvious that when the construction of the internal transport market began, cross-border transport should be entrusted with caution to the european institution, but it is equally obvious that later on the false distinction between international and internal transport was dropped for road transport, sea transport, air transport, internal transport and even, from 1 january this year, for rail freight transport. why, then, madam president-in-office, should this distinction continue to exist only for the last pre-modern enclave, that of passenger rail transport? why, mr vice-president of the commission, go to such great lengths to liberalise 5% of the rail passenger market by 2010, three years from now? why not let the beneficial effects of competition also help the remaining 95% of the railway market to regain that competitiveness vis-à-vis road and air without which we cannot overcome any of the problems we face? why should we allow only 5% of passengers to finally enjoy the obvious protections which apply to all consumers, particularly those with disabilities, and which we have already extended to all air passengers? does it not seem to you that ten years of transition for all, or even fifteen years for the new member states, is a sufficient period to allow even the most unstable of the national monopolies, which today defend their reserved internal market, to prepare themselves to face competition which cannot be destructive, because today the market is declining and only competition can help to expand a market for all. i mean, is it possible, gentlemen, that we are not finding the capacity to get out of a logic that was valid 50 years ago and that today honestly jeopardizes our whole strategy?

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the last few years. i am in favour of the third railway package. i was originally of the opinion that the state should never hand over the railway to private companies. but if the infrastructure remains in public hands and private companies are only able to transfer local, regional and crossborder transport services under very clear conditions, and in a way that is socially and environmentally compatible, then i think we must accept fair competition. however, if state monopolies were merely replaced by a few private monopolists, as is the case in some energy companies, then liberalisation would certainly not be effective. i would argue from my experience as a frequent rail user that the quality of the railway offer does not depend on the degree of privatisation but rather on the clear political will to give railway preference over road. the cost-effectiveness and attractiveness of the railway system as a whole are decisive, for example, also welcoming stations, well-coordinated timetables, reliability, comfort of the trains, etc. we have a positive example in the middle of europe: switzerland. the state does not shirk its responsibility there, even though 45% of the railways are not owned by the swiss federal railways. there are very clear guidelines and a political will on the part of those responsible. the railway is functioning and competitive with the road. a negative example is italy, where only large projects have been pursued and existing railway lines have been badly neglected for decades. perhaps these european impulses are now beginning to change the thinking in italy too.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the third railway package is a fundamental step towards the objective of a liberalised market and a common policy to protect passengers' rights and obligations at european level. the jarzembowski report is certainly the central body of the third package and i fully agree with the rapporteur's approach: it opens up not only international but also national rail transport to competition, it also requires the principle of reciprocity to be respected and thus prevents undue advantages for companies from countries which are closed to competition. the sterckx report, on the other hand, deals with the rights and obligations of passengers: i would also like to say that i agree with the rapporteur's approach, which rightly calls for the regulation to be extended to all rail passengers, both national and international. international passenger traffic represents only 5% of rail traffic, so what sense would it make to adopt a regulation applicable to such a small percentage of consumers? another argument in favour of extending the scope of application is suggested by the legislation in force for the air transport sector, where no distinction is made between international and national traffic in terms of passenger obligations and rights. many member states will have difficulty in reconciling their present situation with the provisions of this regulation, and we therefore believe that the proposed measures should be implemented gradually and, above all, be guided by the criterion of feasibility: for example, passengers with reduced mobility will see the progressive removal of architectural barriers and obstacles in the event of major renovation works, the construction of new stations or the purchase of new trains and coaches. the companies will be responsible for passengers and their baggage, and there will be minimum rights to compensation in the event of delay throughout the european union.
traffic on european roads has tripled in the last 30 years and, despite cars being four times safer than in 1970, road accidents cause more than 40 000 deaths a year, with a direct and indirect cost of €180 billion, 2% of eu gdp. the ambitious targets set by the european union for 2010 to halve the number of road accident victims cannot be achieved without taking into account the fundamental nature of education; the report therefore urges states to further strengthen and disseminate information policies and road safety awareness campaigns among road users of all ages. parliament also called on the member states to step up their efforts to raise awareness of the need for more seat belts in all vehicles, including buses, and proposed that information campaigns be launched to combat fatigue at the wheel, that safe barriers be set up for motorcyclists and that common minimum standards be established for the examination and certification of driving school instructors. the report also proposes that the health and safety rules at the workplace should also apply to motor vehicles used for mobile workplaces.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the resolution we are voting on tomorrow and the debate this evening place the european parliament in that worldwide movement which is appealing to the united nations general assembly to allow the adoption of a resolution for a universal moratorium, which is one of the first steps towards the general abolition of the death penalty in the legal systems of all countries. we would like the council of ministers, as has been said, to make a real effort to achieve this. the presidency is very busy and we hope that this will remain one of the priorities of the semester. a similar commitment has been made by the council of europe and the european commission. however, from what mrs ferrero-waldner said, i do not think she was very convinced that the first step should be a moratorium. i would like to emphasize this point and ask mrs ferrero-waldner: "without this step, would abolition be any closer?" i think not. the european union could use the wide-ranging relations it enjoys in its neighbourhood policy, association agreements and strategic partnership in its international relations, and i believe that european political parties could also work in international fora to ensure that their organisations work on the accession countries. i believe that the aim is to ban the death penalty from the legal systems of all states, which would also help to ensure that the united nations enjoys the prestige of an institution which safeguards universally recognized rights.
on behalf of the alde group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i have followed a statement and a note issued by the german presidency this morning. in this note, the text reads: 'the german presidency calls on the governments concerned to introduce a moratorium on the death penalty with immediate effect.' i read the note from the german presidency. that is exactly our position. i also thought i knew of a statement by president barroso in which he fully supported the italian initiative to put forward a proposal for a moratorium at the current un general assembly, which will certainly win out: in 1999 there was an absolute majority for a resolution which was not tabled. i do not understand, therefore, - or rather i understand all too well - how, in the face of the enthusiasm we are seeing around the world at this hour for an initiative which is our initiative - the initiative of the european parliament, the initiative of the chairmen of our groups, the initiative which was announced in strasbourg by graham watson and other colleagues in a very precise way - it is possible to hesitate, at a time when france is putting an incredible emphasis on abolition, by changing its constitution; at the same time as rwanda is doing so; the european union is not going to be able to do that. we have heard statements from all sides - from syria, from lebanon - supporting this position. i think that tomorrow the european parliament, as the council of europe has already done, will take the lead in this movement. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to remind you that 60 years ago there was an axis between rome and berlin. i was ten years old and i remember it well. today, thanks to the german presidency, the italian initiative and the very recent french initiatives, a new reality is emerging. i think it is historically significant that berlin and rome today, to some extent, are expressing themselves in a clear position, without hypocrisy and without fear of winning, because there are too many people here who are afraid of winning, not of losing.
on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, 'no one shall be sentenced to the death penalty or executed; no one shall be removed, expelled or extradited to a state where there is a serious risk that he or she will be subjected to the death penalty, torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.' this is what the charter of fundamental rights of the european union provides for and this is what makes me, and i believe, makes us proud to be part of the european union. it is the defence of human dignity, it is the understanding that no one can be master of another's life and that there must be no revenge but justice. and that should apply to all courts, including military courts. too many countries still have the death penalty and among them are large countries like china, but also the greatest military and democratic power, the united states of america, which has not yet been able to get out of its far west culture. i hope that the congress against the death penalty in paris, which we will be attending as a parliament, will be a further step, starting from the moratorium, towards the abolition of the death penalty in the world, together with poverty. i also hope that the people who will be marching in the streets of paris will be a warning to all those who, in europe too, are thinking of reintroducing the death penalty. it is the road that leads us anyway so that the un can fully approve the moratorium.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i speak on behalf of the new psi. the execution of saddam brought the debate on the death penalty back to the fore, a debate that is absolutely appropriate, although it should not be used for instrumental purposes and, above all, it should not be an argument to be raised in the alternative. this is first and foremost a battle of civilization and progress. we are not only faced with an indispensable guarantee for the individual, a demand for further strengthening of the sphere of inviolability of the individual, but we are faced with a historical and universal necessity, a point of arrival and global meeting for the civilization of the 21st century. it has been said, and i agree, that after the abolition of slavery in the last few centuries and the prohibition of torture, the right not to be killed as a result of a judicial measure must be another common denominator, a new and irreducible dimension of the human being that makes us all a community. today, this parliament is sending the first clear message in this direction.
mr president, i am pleased to speak because i come from tuscany, where the death penalty was abolished for the first time in history on 30 november 1786, and i am still moved to remember that in 1987, together with amnesty international and the movimento per la vita italiana, i obtained the commutation of the death penalty in the united states for paula cooper, a 16-year-old black girl who later came to thank me. i also like to recall that as an italian member of parliament i introduced and obtained the abolition of the death penalty by law in the military code of war, which is why i have given this matter a lot of thought. i interpret optimistically human history which, despite everything, is a tiring journey towards good, driven by the increasing emergence of a decisive value: the dignity of every human being. this dignity is so great that it is not to be welcomed and therefore determines the equality of all whatever the condition of human life. it is also indestructible: even the hands of a criminal cannot erase the traces on the face of the man who committed the crime. life and dignity are not at the disposal of anyone, not even individual states. this is the real reason why the death penalty should be abolished. all the other practical reasons, which i know well, can be objected to, but not this one. europe, which wants to build its identity not so much on competition and the market as on dignity and human rights, cannot remain silent. i don't want to talk about inconsistencies right now. the time will come when human dignity and the consequent right to life will extend their persuasive power also to other areas of human life, where today they are, unfortunately, obscured, even within our union, in the most emblematic areas of poverty and human marginalization, such as birth and death.

member of the commission. mr president, first of all i would like to thank all those who have spoken today for their very positive speeches, which show how fully aware the problem of climate change is among the members of the european parliament and, of course, this is also a reflection of public opinion which has become very aware. i would like to thank the german presidency and in particular mr sigmar gabriel for the cooperation we have had, for the way he has spoken and defended environmental issues and i hope that the german presidency will be fully effective and will respond to the expectations of european citizens and to the views expressed tonight. climate change is a global challenge and the european union's leadership is crucial in addressing it. today's debate has given us the opportunity to stress the importance of the decisions which are to be taken in the european union in the coming days and weeks: the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force. we must ensure the credibility of the european union in its global leadership role in tackling climate change and we must send the strongest possible message to our partners in both the developed and developing world. we must also stress the importance of the decisions to be taken in the next few years on the international climate change regime and i will perhaps refer to this later to ensure that even more efforts are made across the globe after the first commitment period under the kyoto protocol ends in 2012. the scientific and economic arguments for taking ambitious, global action to tackle climate change are clear and compelling. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the programme to include the following areas: this is precisely what the commission is seeking to do with the climate and energy package. the next few years will be crucial in shaping a global framework to ensure that irreversible and potentially catastrophic climate change is avoided. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption, and the council will be consulted on it. it is of great importance that you support the european union's strong commitment to decisive action, both internally and internationally. i should like to answer some of the observations that were made tonight. firstly, concerning targets, i must repeat that 15 months ago we were not discussing targets. the word "target" was not mentioned. in the european council conclusions, the council mentioned exploring reduction pathways in the range of 15 to 30% with developed countries. it did not occur to anyone to have a unilateral commitment for the european union. somebody mentioned that perhaps there's some confusion. i have to make it clear that we have a target, which is 30%, and this is the mandate we are asking the european council to give to the commission to negotiate with other developed countries. however, irrespective of this agreement and until such an agreement is reached, we have a unilateral commitment to reduce by 20% the reductions in the european union. to underline the magnitude of this commitment, i would point out that it is more than twice our total obligation. i heard that there is not enough ambition and that we have not exercised leadership by setting this target. no other country in the world is so ambitious not even california. governor schwarzenegger has received much praise. i have been asked why we do not have a similar target to that of governor schwarzenegger a 25% target for 2021, but using 2006 as a basis. therefore, if you do your calculations, his ambition is less than half of our 20% reduction. therefore, let me make it clear that we are ambitious, we have to exercise leadership in the world, we have to practice what we preach and our target is really ambitious. of course, in order to achieve what science tells us, to limit the average temperature increase on the planet to 2 degrees celsius, we need a 50% reduction by all the countries in the world by 2050. that goes for the developed countries and the developing countries a 60-80% reduction by the developed countries and a 30% reduction by 2020. someone mentioned flexibility: these targets of 20% and 30% are flexible. they are not for all the countries in the european union, but they will be adjusted according to the burden-sharing agreement that we had a few years ago regarding the achievement of our total target. it should be a similar system. nairobi was mentioned. of course, montreal was different from nairobi. in montreal we had a big achievement in the montreal action plan. according to this plan in nairobi we had certain priorities which were achieved. mrs doyle was right when she said they were not ambitious, but it was a step - a bigger or smaller step, but still a step - and the european union achieved all the priorities it had set, especially in terms of trying to help the least developed countries to get some of the investments with the usual cut-off and flexible mechanisms. mr wijkman said that we were not ambitious because we do not have a partnership with china or that we have a partnership that we do not finance. the truth is that we have a european union-china partnership and a european union-india initiative, and both have specific objectives which will be financed by european union funds and funds from various member states of the european union. of course they are very important, because, as you said, after 2020 china, india and the other fast developing countries will emit more than all the oecd countries. it is therefore absolutely necessary to bring them on board so that we can fight climate change together, but according to the common but differentiated principle of the united nations convention. i said how important it is to have the participation of china and india and the other fast developing countries. however, it is more important to have the developed countries. our first objective should be to consider how to bring on board developed countries, like the united states, which emits 25% of the world's emissions and has not ratified kyoto. public opinion in the united states is changing and we are encouraged by the signals we are getting there. however, more work is necessary. in particular, we must strengthen our emissions trading system, because a market-based instrument like this could be the best way to bring the united states on board. some states in the usa already have an emissions trading system. in the northeast there is an emissions trading system regarding power generation. california and some other western states will be introducing them, and we will cooperate with them in order to have a similar system in order to link the systems together. so the global emissions trading system can be born from the bottom up. in order to do that we need a strong emissions trading system in the european union, otherwise we cannot argue with them. that's why we need to have national allocation plans that really create scarcity in the market. if i had accepted all the proposed national allocation plans from the member states, the emissions trading system would have collapsed. you, the members of the european parliament, with whom we had a lot of discussions about the emissions trading system, should help to persuade those member states which have reservations about the national allocation plans. i am going to do my job and i shall assess the national allocation plans as is necessary in order to fight climate change. it is very important to determine what the basic elements are for a future regime. we have to set goals, the means by which we are going to achieve these goals and establish who will be participating in achieving these targets. i spoke about the participants both developed and developing countries. i must now mention the targets: 2°c is the target. it is essential to keep the commitment made by the european union. the means are: firstly, the use of the market a global emissions trading system is necessary? secondly, we need research, technology, development of technology and deployment of technology, as minister gabriel mentioned. therefore we need to make it financially interesting for the economic partners to deploy new technologies. we also need to transfer technology to developing countries and in order to do that we need finance, because without finance it will not be possible. we have the kyoto flexible mechanism the cdms, the joint implementation but we also need other funds. i am grateful to minister gabriel, because when i announced the adoption by the european union of the global energy efficiency and renewable energy fund, he immediately came forward with a significant contribution from germany. italy followed, and i hope other countries will do so, because this money is necessary in order to transfer technology to developing countries to enable those countries to be energy efficient and to make efforts in order to fight climate change. today i heard a lot about biofuels and second-generation biofuels. i said that today the commission adopted a very important piece of legislation. however, everybody looked at the cars and not at this piece of legislation. but it is very important! i would say that we would save more carbon dioxide with this directive than with the other one, without saying that cars are not important - they are very important, especially for the future. having a new car fleet in the european union is important for fighting climate change. today's adoption by the commission of the fuel quality directive is encouraging sustainable fuels for transport, biofuels, and especially encouraging second-generation biofuels, which are friendly to the environment. on cars, my proposal still stands. my proposal is there, as it was 15 days ago. i am very happy that today the president said that next week we shall be discussing it in the college. we need clean, competitive, affordable cars that will contribute to the fight against climate change. we must protect consumers, workers, the public at large and, of course, fight climate change, protect our planet and protect our countries. finally, on davos, it was very interesting because although there were very important issues to be discussed iraq, the middle east and doha a poll revealed that a majority of 57 percent of the the president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. i shall try to deal with just a few points. many colleagues have said: we have been talking about climate change for many years, but nothing is actually happening. i would ask that we do not underestimate what the commission has put forward in recent weeks and do not make it smaller than it is. i believe that the commission has for the first time developed a common strategy for securing energy supplies and protecting the climate. i would point out that in the past we have generally discussed both separately. we have a common strategy! and what were the main proposals that you criticised earlier? the first package dealt with the question of energy efficiency. not only is the european union able to save billions of euros by 2020100 in energy efficiency improvements, which we urgently need for consumers, for investment in research and development and for many other issues on our agenda. the 20% increase in energy efficiency means the avoidance of 780 million tonnes of co2. this is twice what we have tried to save in europe under the kyoto protocol. energy efficiency is often not as well suited to large-scale ideological and political discussions as is nuclear energy. energy efficiency - these are often many small issues that need to be controlled, monitored and pushed back again and again. but it offers the greatest opportunities, both for the security of energy supply and for climate protection. i think the commission's proposals in this respect are an excellent package. i would be glad if, in addition to all the big headings, we could at least give as much thought to the question of how we can actually implement the many individual programmes contained in this package in community policy as well as in the policies of the member states. secondly, of course, 120 grams of co2 emissions per kilometre in the automotive industry are part of the issue of greater energy efficiency. but to your question earlier, how do we make sure that the biofuel ratio actually counts in reality? we are all in favour of moving the european petroleum industry from the current 5.75% of biofuels to be blended to a much higher proportion. the commission proposes 10%, and some member states may even consider going beyond that. i think that 12.5% or 15% is not unattainable and that must be effectively ensured so that no mineral oil is placed on the market and at petrol stations in the european union that does not contain a certain proportion of biofuels. i believe that this is absolutely necessary if we are to become more independent of oil and gas imports in this area, to become more independent of international price increases and to make the most important contribution to the long-term reduction of co2 emissions from fuel consumption. the second major area is renewable energy. let us not pretend that it is a given in the european union that all member states will accept a common target - as proposed by the commission - of 20% of primary energy consumption in europe to be renewable energy. it's a long way to go. i would ask the european parliament to help us and the commission to make this objective a major goal at the spring summit of heads of state or government. i think it is one of the most important goals we have to achieve. unfortunately, mrs grossetête, who asked me to give her an answer on nuclear energy, is no longer in the chamber. perhaps you could give her the answer: if nuclear energy accounts for 15% of final energy consumption in europe, then it does not make much sense to concentrate on just that 15%. if we did that, 85% of the workforce would be unemployed. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not undermined by the fact that the community is not able to meet its own energy needs. i suspect that won't be the case any time soon. that is why the focus on renewable energy, as proposed by the commission, is the absolutely right way forward. of course, we will have to break this down into burden sharing, whereby each country in europe has to take a certain share and thus reach the 20% of primary energy consumption in 2020. let me close by mentioning two areas where we are far from having a real breakthrough. many of you have said that we need to make sure that we get emerging countries like china, india, brazil -- the big emitters of the future -- to get on board with at least voluntary, better yet binding commitments to reduce co2. that's right! but without the technological solutions we can offer these countries for their growth, they will not get on board! it is absolutely irrelevant whether the european union decides to go for 30, 20, 40 or 10%, the only chance of getting these countries on board is to make them offers for the use of technologies for their energy supply that guarantee their growth and at the same time do not damage the climate in the way that this used to happen in the industrial countries. we're a long way from that. despite the good initiative of the global energy efficiency and renewable energy fund, despite the willingness to transfer technology through cdm projects under the umbrella of the kyoto protocol, the offer is far from sufficient. i therefore recommend that you take part in the relevant international negotiations from time to time to see how widely the european union and the developing countries differ in their understanding of the situation. when we talk about climate change, our partners in the developing world usually interpret this as the old colonialists coming to impede their economic development. if we go to brazil, and we talk about how we can protect the rainforests -- also to not put as much co2 into the atmosphere -- or at least to maintain the natural absorption capacity of co2 in the forests -- then we get the answer from the official side: you still haven't gotten used to the fact that these are our rainforests. we are the ones who decide this, not the old colonial states of europe who want to make rules for us again. we are still that far from a common understanding of climate change, and it is very difficult to get closer to it. some colleagues have said that we must make concessions. i think they meant the european people's renunciation of wealth and so on. i don't think that's the case. and yet, we must be willing to give back to the industrialized countries some of the advantages we have had over our former colonies in the last few hundred years, some of the wealth we have accumulated on the basis of the poverty of the former colonial countries, in order to give them answers on how to advance their economic and social development without destroying the climate. that's the renunciation we're talking about. we are not renouncing our wealth, but we are renouncing the desire to take all the wealth we have accumulated in europe and other industrialized countries for ourselves. we will need to allocate some of this wealth to finance technology development and transfer as well as the necessary adaptation to climate change that is already taking place. this is the second demand of the developing countries to the industrialized countries. before they're willing to talk to us about limiting their carbon emissions as part of their growth, they want to see that we're willing to repair the damage that's already been done by climate change in these states and help them adapt to climate change. we now have a fund that is to be 300 million euros by 2012 - maybe a little bit more - to finance adaptation measures worldwide. who in this room actually believes that 300 million euros is really enough for global climate change adaptation? in my country, this is about the size of the budget of two mediumsized cities. it's not enough! these are the two questions that are being asked of us. they do not ask us: are you prepared to reduce by 20%, 30% or 40% in europe? they ask us: what are you doing to enable real technology transfers to our countries and thus achieve growth and climate protection at the same time? and second, what are you doing to finance the climate change adaptation measures that you are responsible for in our countries? these are the answers we need to give if we want to bring china, brazil, india -- the big emitters of the future -- on board. like commissioner dimas, i believe that america will join a treaty if it works. whether it's called kyoto or something else, we'll see. but the united states will participate in a functioning market, a functioning emissions trading system, a functioning climate change. as long as we do not provide answers to these questions, the united states simply cannot - under any government - participate in it with binding commitments. a second comment on the austrian colleague who said: 'good roar, lion!' or on mrs harms who said: 'enough of words, let me see action'. i think that the words have not changed enough, and if you need proof of that, look here in the chamber or at my house in the german bundestag. if we are convinced that climate protection is indeed a human challenge, why are we not succeeding in getting colleagues in national parliaments who are committed to health reform, the labour market, foreign policy and peace policy in parliamentary debates to also commit themselves to climate protection? why is it that we cannot keep the members who were in the chamber earlier for the vote here, to participate in the debate, to be annoyed by what the commission or the council says, to make their own proposals, to approve or reject, to criticise or to contribute to the debate? we have not yet reached the political public to the extent that we should, otherwise there would be a unified view of the different positions in the individual member states. let us be a little careful about saying that enough has been said. i think we have a long way to go before we convince those we need in the end to win majorities even for difficult decisions. it is not enough for environmental policy experts to be convinced; there are others, including those in our member states. i'm a little reluctant to tell other people what they have to do. we have enough to deal with in my home country, and i'm not the only one, i guess.

as the german presidency has rightly pointed out, a sound energy and environmental policy is no longer a matter of delay if we are to ensure that our citizens and the eu enjoy healthy and sustainable development over time. i therefore agree with my colleagues that this issue should be given the highest priority in the work of the coming months. it seems paradoxical, but precisely on the fiftieth anniversary of the european project, and at a time of political deadlock due to the failure of the constitution, the difficulties of enlargement and the alienation of part of the european population, there is an opportunity, with far more appropriate economic, technological and political instruments, to relaunch the process with concrete proposals, reviving and adapting to today's needs the idea that was at the origin of the european process: the pooling of efforts and intentions to achieve adequate energy independence and sustainability. as was the case 50 years ago, economic development will depend on it, as will the health of our citizens and the environment in which we live. today, moreover, the european union's role on the global stage has added to its potential to influence the political stability of the planet and to set an example for those young economies which, in the midst of economic development, are still unaware of the consequences of this.

the president of the council. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. it is, of course, quite another thing to move from the central challenges of energy or climate protection to a very important topic which has already been discussed by you in the european parliament and by the european union as a whole in the past - and not just once, but repeatedly - the issue of passenger data. as we all know, after the terrorist attacks of 11 september 2001, the united states enacted legislation requiring airlines operating flights to and from the united states to grant the us authorities electronic access to data from their automated reservation and check-in systems, the so-called passenger name records. if they don't, the us will threaten to strip the airlines of their landing rights. i would like to recall briefly the framework conditions. in may 2006, the european court of justice annulled the council decision on the agreement between the european community and the united states on the transfer of passenger data to the united states and the commission decision on the adequacy of data protection following an action brought by the european parliament. in essence, the european court of justice has justified its decision by the lack of competence of the european community to conclude such an agreement, since it does not fall within the scope of the first pillar. the commission did not comment on the substantive question of whether the level of data protection is adequate. as you know, the negotiations with the united states on a successor agreement were very difficult, but they were finally concluded with an interim agreement, which is now based on the third pillar and will last until 31 july this year. it is based on the us privacy commitment, which was already the basis of the previous agreement between the european community and the united states. the commission presented to the council at the beginning of january 2007 a recommendation to authorise the opening of negotiations on a new passenger name record agreement with the united states of america to replace the current interim agreement. the eu negotiating mandate for the presidency of the council, with the support of the commission, was discussed today in the coreper. it is expected that the council will take a decision on this in february 2007 and will set out negotiating directives. it is expected that the negotiations on a new passenger name record agreement will be extremely difficult, as the united states shows no interest in intensifying data protection. rather, they are seen as departing from the continuity of their data protection obligations. however, in the interest of the european union, the conclusion of an agreement is essential for the level of data protection to be ensured. in the absence of an agreement, there would be great pressure on airlines to continue to provide passenger data in order not to risk the withdrawal of landing rights in the usa. the german presidency, with the support of the commission, will work towards a legally secure and data protection-friendly regime that fully takes negotiating mandate to open this very difficult exercise. the commission is recommending to the council to strive for full respect of fundamental rights, notably the right to privacy. i have said on a number of occasions that the right to privacy is for me non-negotiable. it has to be respected, fully and completely. legal certainty is also an important element for air-carriers. it must be taken into account, as it has been from the very beginning. as i have already stressed in this parliament several times, the commission is committed to continuing to give due consideration to privacy on the avviato un dialogo esplorativo con le autorità americane per affrontare sia la questione generale della protezione dei dati, sia le questioni specifiche sollevate dall'uso dei dati swift da parte del caso, una soluzione europea che dovrebbe, a mio avviso, includere regole chiare e garanzie precise, che il ministero del tesoro americano dovrebbe garantire e inserire nei documenti. in altri termini, i due punti in equilibrio sono, come al solito, protezione legale per i dati personali che sono trasferiti, da un lato, e certezza giuridica per tutti i soggetti interessati, e, mi permetto di dire, certezza giuridica anche per le banche e, come la presidenza ha ben sottolineato, swift non è una banca. e' chiaro allora che quando parlo di garanzie da parte delle autorità americane, io intendo specificare in quali circostanze, per quale obiettivo e da parte di chi quei dati possono essere conosciuti e utilizzati. dico subito che la limitazione dell'obiettivo alle sole indagini per fatti di terrorismo, e quindi per la prevenzione del finanziamento del terrorismo, deve essere chiara e precisa, in modo da evitare il rischio, anche indiretto, che dati del genere possano essere utilizzati abusivamente, ad esempio per spionaggio economico. e' chiaro inoltre che appare necessaria un'ulteriore limitazione, e cioè quella di collegare l'uso di quei dati alla ricerca su persone specifiche che sono sospettate di attività di terrorismo. in altri termini, non una generica azione di trasferimento dei dati indipendentemente da un'individuazione di sospetti che meritano ulteriori approfondimenti. siete al corrente della lettera che ho scritto nel novembre scorso a tutti gli stati membri per chiedere informazioni sulle condizioni alle quali le loro banche utilizzano dati personali attraverso swift. soltanto sette stati membri hanno finora risposto all'invito a fornire chiarimenti. questo è un fatto non piacevole e io ovviamente chiederò ragione in alcuni casi: nel caso specifico dell'italia ad esempio, è stata chiesta una proroga per dare una risposta. in altri casi, semplicemente non vi è stata alcuna risposta. dalle sette risposte che ci sono invece pervenute – sebbene non se ne possano trarre conclusioni generali perché è troppo esiguo il numero degli stati che hanno risposto – emerge che le banche utilizzano normalmente i dati personali per il solo obiettivo di eseguire ordini di pagamento e che esse non sono state informate, in quei casi, del fatto che dati personali vengono trasferiti al ministero del tesoro degli stati uniti da swift. quindi la risposta generale fornita è semplicemente "noi non siamo a conoscenza del fatto che qualcuno, cioè swift, trasmette dati dopo averli ricevuti da noi". e' emerso, invece – ma questo lo sapevate già – che in molti casi le banche centrali erano informate proprio dal ministero del tesoro statunitense del trasferimento da swift europa a swift stati uniti e da swift stati uniti al ministero del tesoro statunitense. voi sapete che sono in corso delle azioni e delle ulteriori indagini da parte delle autorità nazionali di protezione dei dati, intese a far luce sulla questione e capire se oltre al caso belga, che è ormai noto, vi sono altri casi specifici in cui le autorità nazionali di protezione dati possono aprire un fascicolo e quindi una procedura. e' evidente che, appena avrò informazioni al riguardo, ve le comunicherò come ho fatto in passato. c'è una domanda specifica che riguarda la possibilità di applicare ai dati swift il sistema denominato automated targeting system (sistema di individuazione personale). sulla base delle spiegazioni tecniche fornitemi, risulterebbe impossibile o altamente improbabile che il sistema in oggetto sia stato utilizzato per trattare i dati swift, per la semplice ragione che esso è inserito nel department of homeland security relativo alla protezione dei confini e quindi al movimento delle persone passeggeri. non a caso il parlamento europeo aveva posto una questione sull'applicazione di tale meccanismo ai dati pnr. i dati swift sono in un settore totalmente diverso perché ricadono nella sfera di applicazione di una diversa amministrazione, che è quella del tesoro. nell'interrogazione presentata si chiede altresì se la commissione è al corrente di altri esempi di autorità americane che richiedono dati da soggetti privati in questo settore. io non ne sono al corrente e quindi non posso rispondere a questa domanda. e' indubbio tuttavia che, se la lotta al finanziamento del terrorismo è uno strumento indispensabile per prevenire il terrorismo, non è possibile che tale lotta pregiudichi o riduca un diritto fondamentale, come la protezione dei dati finanziari personali dei clienti. come sapete, una delle violazione riscontrate dalle autorità belghe e dal comitato europeo dei garanti della privacy è proprio la mancata informazione preventiva ai clienti, il che coincide con quanto hanno detto le banche, anche loro non informate di questo movimento. in conclusione, presidente, onorevoli deputati, credo che la necessità di lavorare ad uno strumento europeo risponda a due motivazioni. in primo luogo, non possiamo ridurre o mortificare la nostra collaborazione euroatlantica in materia di lotta al terrorismo: sarebbe un errore grave che ritengo l'unione europea debba evitare. in secondo virtù di uno strumento europeo, analogamente a quanto cerchiamo di fare con il pnr – anche se le due materie sono molto diverse, ma il principio è lo stesso – a trovare una soluzione europea che impedisca differenze di trattamento tra stato e stato dell'unione europea verso gli stati uniti, credo che sarà possibile rafforzare il potere negoziale dell'unione europea, dimostrando nel contempo che il nostro obiettivo è rafforzare il legame euroatlantico e non indebolirlo.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, this legislative proposal on the statute for a european private company is very important. it is essential not only to remove barriers to trade but also to develop the factor of production at community level. to this end, it is undoubtedly necessary to create unitary legal entities to overcome the current legal uncertainty. it should not be forgotten, however, that the reform of company law, in addition to the objective of market transparency and the protection of savers, will have a direct impact on the future of the european social model. if it is a legitimate objective to allow full mobility for companies to take advantage of the benefits of the single market, this must be done by identifying the rights of workers who have the same qualities of transnationality. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european parliament is able to exercise its right of initiative in the matter of the internal market. this is a significant correction for a more attentive attention to the aspects inherent in that strengthening of social europe, which must have the participation of workers as one of its fundamental pillars. we therefore support this important proposal and thank mr lehne for his work, warning the commission that, while it is a legitimate aim to allow full mobility for businesses to take advantage of the benefits of the single market, this must be done without market considerations being at the expense of social equity.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i congratulate mr varela suanzes-carpegna and thank him for his question, which has given us the opportunity to deal with this subject. i have been a rapporteur in this parliament on the reform of procurement, supplies and services, in this case directives 17 and 18. although time is very short, i think it is worth remembering the terms of the problem. in directive 18, the general procurement directive, as i heard from some of the speeches this morning, parliament has given great consideration to environmental problems, the modernised system of electronic procurement, the social sector, the question of thresholds and i believe that we have legislation which is certainly exceptional, but which in any case does not concern the subject of this morning's debate. the problem is entirely different: the commission is currently reviewing an international negotiation which puts the eu countries and therefore eu companies at a disadvantage compared to others. what's the matter? in 1994 and in subsequent years, a number of other types of international activities were envisaged by means of plurilateral agreements. the united states, china and other countries actually enjoy privileges which european union companies do not enjoy. today this system is being reviewed, but we must establish the procedure for its revision, because the united states of america alone - i remind myself and my colleagues - is producing almost 200 billion dollars a year, a sum which, however, remains within the united states. the point is that while everyone can come to work in europe, our small and mediumsized enterprises cannot go to work in the rest of the world. the government procurement agreement (gpa) agreements are, amongst others, agreements which provide for the exclusion of european companies from the international system. what choice is there, then, today? the commission, as far as i understand it, believes that by abolishing the privileges of others, we can once again compete on a level playing field. it's not like that. i believe that it is necessary to protect european small and mediumsized enterprises by granting them the same privileges within the european union, and therefore vis-à-vis the european union, as small and mediumsized enterprises in the united states and other countries of the world enjoy today. i therefore not only thank my colleague, mr varela suanzes-carpegna, but i also believe that the position taken by france at this moment in the council is certainly to be favoured and facilitated in relation to the position of the european commission.

new technologies. it is not possible to contradict the hierarchy by calling energy recovery recovery, which is instead disposal. this is a direct contradiction of the hierarchy and risks creating undue competition with renewable energies. i would like to make it clear that there is no ideological objection to incineration and energy recovery, but i also agree with mrs brepoels that it is mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union must also provide itself with new instruments to limit the production of waste by promoting reuse, recycling and recovery in order to reduce its negative impact on the environment. without concrete recycling targets at european level, member states that have not developed recycling techniques will try to achieve the targets of reducing landfills by favouring incinerators and ignoring the more virtuous steps. the five-tier hierarchy alone will not prevent this, so we must aim to recycle at least 50% of biodegradable waste, promote separate collection and recycling systems and ensure that reusable or recyclable material is not disposed of in landfills and incinerators. the amendments tabled by mr jackson, which allow municipal waste incinerators to be classified as recovery plants rather than disposal plants, in fact undermine the application of the five priority levels and open the way to private business in incinerators. if we really want europe to become the recycling society of the future, we must first focus on prevention by reducing waste production and then prioritising reuse and recycling.

the agenda includes the report by mrs fiona hall, on behalf of the committee on industry, research and energy, 'towards a european radio spectrum policy' (2006/2212 (ini)) (a6-0467/2006)
member of the commission. madam president, i have to compliment the european parliament, in particular the rapporteur, mrs hall, for realising the importance of the choices europe is about to make with regard to radio spectrum policy. this is an area where political decisions have a direct impact on the quality of jobs and growth in the european economy. services dependent on radio spectrum represent around 2 to 3% of europe’s gdp. there have been studies for the world bank and for the oecd which clearly link the development of electronic communication services to economic growth. an econometric study made for the commission tentatively associated better spectrum break relation with 0.1% of extra gdp growth per year. this would quickly cumulate to deliver real benefits. the urgency of the matter can be summed up in the word ‘convergence’. practically all communications are quickly becoming digital and there is an increasing number of infrastructures competing to carry services. the old categories are disappearing and we need to respond with a regulation that permits the spectrum users to choose the mix of services and technologies that they prefer and that in many cases permits them to buy and sell spectrum rights to each other. the reasons for regulation are still strong. we have to manage interference. we need to ensure that the rights to use spectrum are clearly defined and we need to ensure a level playing field. the report that we are debating tonight is in most aspects in line with this policy vision and i want to thank the rapporteur for her efforts. one area of divergence concerns including spectrum for terrestrial broadcasting distribution in the planned reforms. we are not questioning the importance of the television companies’ public service function, nor their contribution to cultural and linguistic diversity. we should, however, think very carefully before we privilege one specific form of broadcasting distribution without regard to the costs to our society in terms of opportunity. a case in point: the report quite rightly highlights wireless broadband as a tool for rural development and for breaching the digital divide. this requires tough choices about the balance between broadcasting and other services. there are necessary decisions to be made to safeguard the resources and functioning of public service broadcasting, but we should not use spectrum policy as a substitute for real debate. the amendment gives a more balanced approach by mentioning the need to secure stability and security for media services and the importance of a level playing field for new entrants and new technologies. i have one final point to make: on the basis of the full analysis, the choice of the national regulators is to award spectrum to broadcasters. these users must also have the same obligation as any other users to be good stewards of a public resource and use it as effectively as possible. we think that our reform proposal would help to implement this principle.
member of the commission. madam president, i presume an answer would be expected from the commission, but i promise i shall keep it short. i share the appreciation of parliament regarding the vital role played by public service television and other media for democracy, diversity and for the encouragement for a public debate. it is necessary that future regulations continue to ensure that this programming can be distributed to the citizens in accordance with the public service obligations assumed by those broadcasters. however, assuming that these goals can be satisfied and keeping in mind the reality of convergence, we should carefully assess the need for the spectrum required to offer a public broadcasting service and to ensure its efficient use. in consequence, we need to provide broadcasters with the means and the flexibility to continue to develop their offer to the benefit of our society. we have listened carefully and your comments will be taken into account during the revision of the telecommunication regulation, which will be proposed by the second half of 2007.

on behalf of the pse group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank amalia sartori for her excellent work. it is a fortunate coincidence that we are approving the timetable just after 8 march, as president záborská said. on 8 march, international women's day, celebrated in many countries around the world but not all. last year we had reports of police charges in turkey; this year we have heard that young women in tehran who were preparing to celebrate the 8th of march were arrested. like labour day, international women's day also grew out of the socialist movement and became international. march 8, 1908, had been the day of bread and roses. fifteen thousand women in new york had marched to demand bread, which meant wages and jobs, but also roses, which meant the right to vote, free time, children's rights, dignity and respect. two years later, in copenhagen, the socialist women's international will propose an international day to be permanently fixed in the calendar, in memory of new york. a hundred years later, if we look at the six areas of action in the table, we find a remarkable coincidence between them and the demands of the women who marched under the slogan "bread and roses". they demanded bread, meaning work and wages, we demand equal economic independence; we are not asking for a vote, we are asking for a balanced presence in the places of representation. they asked for respect for minors, we ask for child services; they asked for roses, that is, quality of life, we ask for the eradication of all forms of violence to give quality and dignity to life. but then, we were not talking about eliminating gender stereotypes. today i think one of the reasons why we still need to ask for "bread and roses" is because of the persistence of gender stereotypes in everyday life. i think that the fight against stereotypes should be given priority. achieving this objective will make it easier, or perhaps only less difficult, to promote equality between men and women in all areas.

the european parliament has been a party to the treaty on the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons since the end of the cold war in 1970, and has played a decisive role in limiting the spread of nuclear weapons and in reducing their number. the treaty has historically been of fundamental importance for the prevention of nuclear proliferation and disarmament and was therefore extended indefinitely and unconditionally in 1995. as the presidency of the council stated, the treaty is based on three principles: disarmament, non-proliferation and peaceful use of nuclear weapons. it is on the basis of these three principles, modelled on the international situation today, that the treaty in question must be given a new impetus, and this in view of the fact that the balance achieved, with the application by more than 180 nations, is now in danger. the international community today faces new threats to its security. the principle that the treaty is the single, indispensable multilateral instrument for maintaining and strengthening international peace, security and stability must be strongly reaffirmed, as it establishes the legal framework for preventing the further proliferation of nuclear weapons. the european security strategy and the european strategy on weapons of mass destruction stress the importance of nuclear non-proliferation, disarmament and the treaty itself, to which all member states are signatories. i think it is essential that the european parliament has a clear idea of its position for the future. the european union must continue to commit itself to the implementation of the treaty, presenting itself united at the vienna meeting which will prepare the 2010 review conference. that is why a united vote by the european parliament would be essential, as a strong signal to the council and the commission, so that they can have the necessary strength in vienna to play an active role in strengthening the current non-proliferation regime. in order to achieve the objectives set out in the treaty, the european union must contribute to a structured and balanced review of its functioning by the review conference. this must include the implementation of the commitments made by states and the identification of areas and means through which further progress can be achieved, as well as further development of the verification system ensuring the exclusively peaceful use of nuclear energy by non-armed and recognised states. the principle that all possible cooperation in the development of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes must be strengthened on the basis of the treaty must be reaffirmed, and it is in this field that the european union can make a decisive contribution as the leading research and production body. the international situation requires us to unite our efforts in the field of nonproliferation, disarmament and the peaceful use of atomic energy. finally, i hope that europe will have a unified strategy also for the fight against terrorist organisations which might have access to such weapons.

the president of the council. the commission has already made a number of proposals. i am pleased to be here today to speak about euro-mediterranean relations and to be present at the debate on the report of the committee on international trade on the establishment of the euro-mediterranean free trade area. the report by mr arif contains many interesting statements on eu-mediterranean relations. the eu has an interest in a safe, politically stable and economically developed mediterranean area. historical and geographical factors play a role, but so do current developments such as the growing threat of terrorism and the close economic interconnections. almost every day we are confronted with the fact that the regions of north africa and the middle east have not yet found political and economic stability. the commission's draft resolution clearly identifies the main problems underlying this. the middle east conflict leaves traces in political, economic and social life that have a lasting impact on the region. the rapid growth of the population in the southern mediterranean countries and the resulting economic slowdown are leaving more and more people without access to education and jobs. young people in particular see no prospects for life in their home countries. they try to emigrate to europe and/or become easy prey for the supposedly 'simple solutions' that radical thinking offers them. the governments of some mediterranean countries are reluctant to make the necessary political reforms and are denying their populations political participation. but the draft resolution also recognises that the barcelona process has made considerable progress in this region by, quote, creating political, economic, social and cultural links between the northern and southern mediterranean. the barcelona process has not been able to resolve the middle east conflict, but that is not its task either. but it has another added value which should not be underestimated: as one of the few forums, it regularly brings israel and its arab neighbours to the same table! under the roof of barcelona, there is a chance for practical exchange and cooperation, even in times of political differences. it is up to the participating countries themselves to take advantage of this opportunity. let me give you two examples. despite the controversy over the election result in the palestinian territories, there was constructive participation by palestinian and israeli representatives in the meeting of senior euromed officials and the euromed committee in march 2006. the second example: at the special meeting of the euromed senior officials and the euromed committee on 22 february 2006 on the occasion of the 'cartoon debate', there were constructive proposals from both the eu and the arab group. the presence of both the israeli and the arab delegations was also noteworthy. the barcelona process is a tool which we must not abandon, even if the ambitious objectives set out in the barcelona declaration in 1995 - the creation of a common area of peace and stability, the creation of a common prosperity zone, the development of close partnership in the social, cultural and interpersonal spheres - have not been achieved. despite its shortcomings, it can help to transform the mediterranean region from a 'sea of confrontation' into a 'sea of cooperation', as former german foreign minister fischer once put it. the barcelona process not only brings together government representatives and academic elites on a regular basis, but also brings together the people and civil societies on both sides of the mediterranean. the 'anna lindh foundation for intercultural dialogue' is contributing to this and this commitment is to be intensified in the future. an important body of euro-mediterranean cooperation is the 'euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly (empa) ' which was established in 2003 and which is expected to have a growing influence on the promotion of democratic structures and human rights in all euro-med countries. the summit on the occasion of the 10th anniversary of the barcelona process in november 2005 showed that, despite differences in views on the scope and the concrete form of the cooperation, the will of the eu and the mediterranean countries to cooperate closely continues to exist. the work programme adopted by the summit for the next five years sets out concrete objectives in all areas of the barcelona process, such as political, economic and cultural cooperation and migration. the conditions for further cooperation are therefore in place. i am not going to go into detail. there is no stability without economic progress. we all know that, and the euromed framework is no exception. this is why the euro-med foreign ministers, at their summit in tampere at the end of november 2006, reaffirmed that the creation of a euro-med free trade area by 2010 remains the common objective of all euro-med partners. is this adherence to a goal agreed on over ten years ago reasonable or just stubborn? first of all, i think that 2010 has become a symbol of the importance that the euromed partners attach to a free trade area. in addition, much has been done in the economic sphere to make a free trade area seem feasible: the bilateral free trade areas of the association agreements, which are currently in force between the eu and almost all the mediterranean countries with the exception of syria, are being implemented satisfactorily. the aim is to gradually integrate the mediterranean region into the european economy. the german presidency will do all it can to support the european commission in gaining momentum and making further progress in the ongoing negotiations. i would mention in particular the following areas: the gradual liberalization of services and the right of establishment; the progressive liberalisation of trade in agricultural products, processed agricultural products and fishery products; the creation of a dispute settlement mechanism and the convergence of legislation, with particular emphasis on the approximation of technical legislation. the aim is to provide the mediterranean countries with easier access to the eu's internal market, as the eu is their most important trading partner, accounting for over 50% of their trade. this development is of course linked to the progress made in the implementation of the above mentioned association agreements. other challenges will follow, such as the competitiveness of the mediterranean partners' businesses. the integration process has also gained a major impetus among the mediterranean countries themselves with the agadir agreement, which has been in force since 2004 and aims to create a free trade area between the mediterranean countries. the eu promotes this south-south cooperation by, for example, providing financial support to the secretariat. we hope that other countries will soon join the agadir agreement, along with egypt, jordan, morocco and tunisia. liberalisation and economic reforms do not go without effect on the socioeconomic situation of a country. the impact of changes in this area depends above all on the controlled and targeted implementation of the necessary structural changes. the eu is actively supporting the mediterranean countries in this process. for example, in the context of the barcelona process, it has for years been providing substantial funds for restructuring and modernisation in the employment and training sectors and for modernising transport infrastructure. the regional eu funding programmes such as euromed market, anima, euromed innovation help to improve the framework conditions for investment and entrepreneurial initiatives, thus strengthening the private sector. in addition, the european investment bank's mediterranean facility (femip) is a well-equipped and proven support instrument, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises. femip also supports environmental, infrastructure and training projects. as you know, the big hurdle for emerging market economies is convincing investors that they expect a stable, profitable environment. this is particularly important because foreign direct investment is urgently needed. this is a subject on which the mediterranean countries need our special support. you've asked for it repeatedly. i am therefore particularly pleased that an ad hoc working group on investment will be set up during the german presidency on 23 april this year. the euromed partners will work together to identify the main problems and to seek ways and means of improving investment flows in the mediterranean. i am not going to go into detail. in conclusion, i would like to stress that i share your view that uncontrolled economic growth is not the only way forward, but that social and environmental aspects must also be taken into account. this is of course also true of eu-mediterranean relations. the german presidency will therefore hold attractive conferences on both topics with high-level participation. the european council will be holding a meeting in brussels on the basis of the conclusions of the european council in brussels on the future of the european union. the common area of security and prosperity that the barcelona process aims at cannot be achieved in a sustainable way without effective social dialogue and new jobs. rather, there is a growing risk that high unemployment, especially among young people, will threaten social stability and worsen the prospects for social and economic development in the southern neighbouring countries. secondly, a conference on energy efficiency and renewable energies will also be held in berlin on 19 april 2007. a forward-looking energy policy is essential for sustainable economic development and the conservation of resources. ministers from the eu's southern and eastern neighbours, as well as representatives of industry and not slacken in our efforts to achieve this goal. we all - governments, parliaments and other political leaders - are called upon to do this and can certainly achieve a great deal if we join forces. member of the commission. mr president, any discussion of european-mediterranean relations is first and foremost a discussion of a shared political challenge. today, the mediterranean region and europe form a strategic and economic area under construction. at a time when we are rediscovering our shared cultural and political heritage, we are cementing our future economic collaboration, because we want once again to play a key role in creating an area of stability, peace and prosperity. the vast euro-mediterranean area is the home to two interdependent entities: the 27-member european union, and the mediterranean region with its more than 250 million inhabitants. we are interdependent politically as partners trying to bring peace to the middle east and elsewhere in the mediterranean, and working to promote pluralism and democracy. we are interdependent economically: euro-med trade relations are healthy and growing. today, mediterranean countries’ exports to the eu 27 have grown by 10% per year on average between 2000 and 2006. imports from the eu 27 have also increased, but at a slower pace of 4%. the eu trade surplus has been reduced substantially and in 2006 trade was basically balanced. however, we are interdependent in other ways: environmentally, sharing more than 46 000 kilometres of mediterranean coastline, and jointly confronting challenges linked to climate change, water and the depollution of the sea. we are interdependent with respect to energy, too, thanks to the flows of oil and gas resources that originate in, and transit, the mediterranean. we are also interdependent demographically, given the need for dialogue with the countries of north africa on how to handle legal and illegal migration. finally, we are interdependent culturally because of the urgently required in-depth dialogue between cultures and religions.in response to this interdependence, the eu has set up the neighbourhood policy and the barcelona process: complementary and coherent frameworks for policy and cooperation. within these frameworks, we have association agreements and neighbourhood action plans which have been concluded with almost all countries in the region. the most recent agreement with egypt was adopted at the eu-egypt association council on 6 march. the euro-mediterranean free trade area, as has been mentioned, is gradually taking shape and will act as an interface between an increasingly globalised world and europe’s open, inclusive regionalism. we are building on our liberalised trade in goods to liberalise trade in services and business establishment in a way that encourages much-needed regional economic integration. active euro-mediterranean institutions have been set up such as the euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly. the year 2007 will certainly be an important one in our relations with a region that is undergoing major change, which has great expectations of europe and for which a close relationship with the union is a major priority. the year 2007 will be the first year of operation of the european neighbourhood and partnership instrument. our work with our partners is animated by the conviction that, if changes are to last, they must come from within society. in the context of the neighbourhood policy, the gradual implementation of political and economic reforms is opening the road to a rapprochement between europe and the mediterranean countries. if we are to assist our neighbours in implementing challenging reform programmes, we must have something appealing to offer to them. we have already offered to strengthen our trade relations. we could also work to relax formalities related to the granting of visas. the proposals contained in the commission’s communication require significant political will, as well as economic and financial commitments on an equivalent scale. the european parliament’s contribution will be vital to ensure that europe maintains a i would like to turn now. i should like to congratulate the rapporteur and the members who have contributed to making this motion for a resolution relevant and complete. the resolution refers to the mixed results of the barcelona process as regards trade liberalisation and economic integration, while highlighting the complexity of the task and the socioeconomic constraints, both structural and linked to the current international context, which characterised this neighbouring region of the eu. indeed, the mixed results in terms of prosperity derived from the establishment of an fta are not always attributable to the process itself or to its weaknesses, but are often due to a number of structural constraints inherent in this region, which have somehow prevented the process of economic integration realising its full potential. however, despite these constraints, there has been an increase of trade following the liberalisation under the barcelona process: exports from mediterranean partners to the eu have doubled since 1995; eu exports have increased by 60% and the bilateral trade deficit of the mediterranean countries has decreased from 20% to 10% in the same period. the creation of a euro-med fta remains an objective both of barcelona and of our neighbourhood policy. in both contexts, various initiatives have been developed to deepen and support liberalisation in the fields of both further tariff liberalisation and the elimination of non-tariff measures. new negotiations in the areas of agriculture, services and investments have been launched since the marrakesh trade ministerial last year, and our european neighbourhood policy action plans set up priority actions, particularly as regards the elimination of regulatory and non-tariff barriers. from the beginning, the barcelona process has foreseen accompanying and mitigating measures to the euro-med fta. these include: asymmetry in tariff dismantling; a gradual approach concerning liberalisation – for example, the agriculture sector is starting only now once a reasonable period followed industrial liberalisation; and last but not least, the provision of significant aid in support of economic and structural reforms and of sustainable rural development, earlier through meda, currently through the new enp instrument. our priority remains to enhance sustainable development and competitiveness in the mediterranean region through the elimination of obstacles to trade and by promoting regional integration, investments, regulatory convergence towards the eu internal market rules, research and innovation and the reinforcement of infrastructure and networks in the region. in a nutshell, this means working towards the shared prosperity which is the objective of the barcelona process and our neighbourhood policy. we will make every effort to ensure that this vision becomes a reality. honourable members, at the heart of our relations with our mediterranean partner countries is our very deep and strong desire to promote security, growth and stability in the region. however, there is also the abiding conviction that we are taking part in an even more ambitious project: constructing a region and affirming our common goals and values. the european commission is counting on the european parliament to rise to these great challenges with the help of the euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly and i look forward to our continued working together.
