member of the commission. mr president, i warmly welcome this report and wish to thank parliament for its positive reception of the commission’s communication of 27 april 2005 on a methodology to check fundamental rights compliance in the commission’s own legislative proposals. let me briefly recall why the commission adopted this communication on a methodology for compliance with fundamental rights, the first product of the commissioners’ group on fundamental rights, anti-discrimination and equal opportunities. we, the union’s institutions, must at all times show that we cherish fundamental rights, not only in words but in actions and above all in our own legislative action. this is crucial for the union to be credible and legitimate in the eyes of its citizens. the charter, which the institutions subscribed to in 2000, must encourage us to enhance respect for individual freedom in all its facets. this includes classic civil liberties to be upheld, precisely in our current efforts to combat terrorism. it also includes economic and social rights and, last but not least, the new generation rights such as data protection, good administration and bio-ethical guarantees. but, briefly, it must become clear to our citizens that the european union locks a true fundamental rights culture into its own policy-making. it is therefore a matter of great satisfaction and encouragement for the commission to see that our communication of 2005 has found such a prominent echo in your resolution of today and that this parliament makes the same commitment on its part to include internal rules for monitoring fundamental rights. taking rights seriously must be a common leitmotif for all institutions throughout the eu’s legislative process. i also wish to thank parliament for some constructive practical suggestions which the voggenhuber report offers to the commission in order to develop further our human rights compliance methodology. as you know, we have scheduled a review of our methodology to be launched later this year, and the commission will present parliament with the results of this review. the commission is very keen to share its experience with parliament in that respect. in the context of this review, the commission will of course pay utmost attention to your suggestions. for instance, we have noted that we should refer not only to the charter as a point of reference, but also to european and international human rights conventions, and that parliament emphasises the commission’s right to withdraw its proposal where changes are made in the legislative process which would violate a fundamental right. we are also open to giving even greater visibility to fundamental rights in our impact assessments. finally, a major theme of the planned review will be how to involve the newly-established fundamental rights agency when preparing new policy initiatives which are sensitive to fundamental rights. as regards the call for a new annual report from the commission on fundamental rights in the eu, we think that it could be useful to have a yearly general discussion on this issue. this could take place in the we should avoid any duplication of it. but, with that caveat, i would like to say how much we commend this report on its content and how seriously we take it.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank all the colleagues who have contributed to the drafting of this report. we believe that this is the first time that a comprehensive study has been devoted to the islands, taking account of the specific features of the islands in all areas of community competence: although cohesion policy 2007-13 pays particular attention to structurally disadvantaged areas, no specific measures are foreseen for island regions. parliament has repeatedly highlighted this gap and, although the context of europe's islands is heterogeneous - there are 121 of them, with a population of around 15 million - they share a number of difficulties which constitute a competitive disadvantage: higher prices due to additional transport costs and low competition; difficulty in accessing the single market; need to import raw materials; higher energy costs; infrastructure deficiencies; immigration; limited diversification of economic activities and vulnerability to environmental risks. it is no coincidence that the average gdp per head in the islands is 72% of the eu average. it is therefore necessary to recognise their specific features in the implementation of community policies, starting with state aid. we therefore believe that more flexibility is needed to balance the additional costs and, as far as energy is concerned, to compensate for fluctuations in fuel prices. particular attention should be paid, in the context of the operational programmes of the structural funds, to the implementation of infrastructure works, especially in the framework of the european maritime policy, in order to fully integrate the islands into the internal market and the lisbon strategy. on the other hand, islands have an advantage in terms of energy production: wind, sun, and sea. they have a unique potential value, which is why the commission must give priority to projects for renewable energy and energy security. tourism is also a resource to be developed. a community policy for the promotion of island tourism, a quality and origin mark and a thorough analysis in favour of sustainable tourism are needed. we are proposing, among other things, that 2010 be the european year of the islands. the report also deals with the problem of illegal immigration, which we consider to be a human tragedy and an intolerable burden for the mediterranean islands, which the european union must take on. we welcome the creation of rapid border intervention teams and call for the establishment of a european coast guard. it is urgent that the european union allocate the necessary resources to ensure rapid and timely action in this area. there are other proposals which deserve further consideration, such as the financial instruments jaspers (joint assistance for projects in european regions) and jeremie (joint european resources for micro, small and medium-sized essential to review the regulatory framework to take full account of the specificities of the islands and to update the statistical indicators accordingly: to take islands into account in the context on behalf of the its group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, how can we not take account of the structural disadvantages of the islands of our europe? it was essential that this should be an objective in the community state aid regulation. the own-initiative report on the islands of the union and their undeniable limitations, presented by my very esteemed colleague mr musotto, is a milestone in the recognition of the importance of islands in the regional development frameworks of europe. it is the first time in this parliament that i have had the opportunity to analyse and comment on such a valuable and worthwhile report. it is to be shared because it is complete in the aspects considered and very balanced in the method, as well as being absolutely shared in its substance and aims. i shall be glad to vote for it and i hope that it will receive the highest possible approval from all my colleagues. can the union not consider how statistically unassailable it is that some 15 million citizens live on islands and that over 90% of this population have incomes below the european average? the undeniable structural deficits, a direct consequence of insularity, are the main cause of this status, and for too long the union has practically ignored it. the excellent musotto report, in addition to describing in its recitals the reasons and motives for the lack of development and clearly outlining the specific resources of the islands, also focuses on the measures, and indeed the instruments, analyses and statistics, which the union can use to take account of the structural handicaps of the islands in the allocation of the structural funds and aid to lessfavoured areas. this guideline is an act owed to island communities, recognising their role in european civilization and their role today as a major environmental and economic resource for the union. if the islands are supported within the undeniable development limitation which is still the obstacle to their development due to their insularity, and if this is taken into account in the guidelines for the structural funds, the union will make a substantial contribution to removing inequalities, even discrimination, which are not only unjustifiable by virtue of the acquis communautaire but are contrary to the recognised objective of a fair and compatible development of europe's regions.

member of the commission. mr president, it has been a most interesting debate. let me start by congratulating the rapporteur, mr musotto, on his report – which i did not do in my opening remarks –and for bringing this issue before us today in the first ever report dedicated to islands. he has made history! much has been said this morning about state aids, and i should like to respond to that first. again, operating aid – aid aimed at reducing a firms current expenses – is normally prohibited. it is prohibited in the treaty and it is prohibited by the regional aid guidelines, because of its highly distortive effect. that being said, it can be granted exceptionally in the poorest regions that are lagging behind in terms of regional development. the regions that can benefit from operating aid are, as you are aware, the 87(3)(a) regions, which are the outermost and sparsely populated regions, provided that a number of conditions are fulfilled. in the poorest regions and, again, the 87(3)(a) regions, operating aid can be authorised only on a case-by-case basis, provided it is limited in time, degressive, proportionate, and designed to tackle specific structural handicaps. in reply to mrs sudre, as you are aware, the commission accords a particular status to the outermost regions, given their remoteness and specific constraints on integrating into the internal market. for islands other than outermost regions, a generalised approach based on the characteristics of these regions seems rather difficult. enormous differences exist between island regions in europe, and you are an example of that. they are characterised by a large diversity, and in terms of regional development and their gdp per capita, a significant number of large islands are rather wealthy, as some of you rightly pointed out. granting operating aid to an island that has a gdp per capita among the highest in the eu would completely distort competition in the relevant markets without any justification in terms of regional development. thus, the commission cannot accord the status of assisted area to all european islands, given their extreme diversity. in response to mr arnaoutakis, i note that subsidising fuel and energy costs constitutes operating aid. such aid can only be authorised if the general conditions – which i have just touched upon – are fulfilled. it must not prop up structurally loss-making activities, particularly those that are very damaging, for example, to our environmental or climate change objectives. furthermore, regional operating aid is certainly not the best instrument to tackle the local problems of islands. as i mentioned in my opening remarks, the islands’ main problems can be tackled more effectively with horizontal instruments. for example, local services that are not economically viable can be supported through services of general economic interest. work and investment for all kinds of infrastructure can be financed. they do not have an aid element and, in the case of very small islands in particular, the de minimis aid and the eur 200 000 threshold can be sufficient, as i mentioned. as regards mrs attwooll’s comment about the market investor principle, i believe that we can apply a more refined economic approach to assess situations of market failure in islands and proposed investments. however, as i have mentioned already, making the rules more predictable and more transparent and reducing the administrative burden of state aid notification are objectives of the state aid reform. i understand the specific concerns of smaller businesses, who have to try to pick their way through the state aid maze, and we agree upon this. that is why i have followed up on the suggestion made by some of you that the commission should provide user-friendly guidance explaining our rules clearly and simply. my services have now almost completed a full update of a vade mecum offering a concise overview of the basic eu rules on state aid. the vade mecum does not aim to provide an exhaustive description of the rules. instead, it focuses on the issues that are most relevant for people involved in regional development. i hope to have this vade mecum on line on the dg competition europe website very shortly, in a couple of weeks time, and i would be happy to provide copies to interested members. i would now like to turn to four wider issues raised by some members. mr smith mentioned the need for statistics. the commission is working well with eurostat on a regular basis. this may we will publish the fourth cohesion report, which will include more statistics. mr smith also mentioned access to the transmission network for renewable energy. it is indeed vital and that is why the commission takes the view that full structural unbundling of energy markets is the best solution to the problems of concentration and foreclosure of new entrants we have experienced in these markets. several members suggested the need for a specific unit on islands in dg regional policy. i will certainly take good note of this, but, as you are aware, it is my colleague, mrs hübner, who is taking the decisions here and not me. i am sure she will examine your idea carefully. finally, we will look carefully at your proposal for designating 2010 as the year of islands, but i assure you that the commission will continue to pursue the best interests of islands in 2007, 2008 and 2009, so do not think that we are neglecting this important issue. on the contrary.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place at 12 noon. the commission shall be assisted by the committee of the regions.

the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a fire. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there has been very careful work in my committee, of which i was rapporteur, and which has been unanimously voted in committee. the envi committee is obviously concerned about the protection of the environment, but in this particular case we have concentrated on the question of how the environment can be protected also through the rule of the market. i want to say this because the key point of the report i have presented is precisely this: for those who produce, sell or buy organic food, it must be clear, with absolute certainty and without any margin for error, that this food is indeed organic and not contaminated by, for example, gmos. i believe that this 'zero threshold' of contamination is indispensable from the outset and that no further action is required. the seller of a product - i am thinking, for example, of a high-end automobile - cannot tolerate the fact that the product contains even a single bolt that does not belong to that automobile. this is the key point of the statement made by my committee, which we would like to see clearly reflected in the final text.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am speaking as an italian, and i would like to point out that italy is the fourth largest producer of organic products in the world and the first in the european union. we therefore support the amendments to the regulation which the report makes: the changes relating to the scope, flexibility for member states, controls and free movement of organic products in the european union. as regards labelling, we believe that an organic product must be absolutely guaranteed and that therefore at no stage of the production process there should be accidental contamination by gmos. the rules in force allow for an accidental contamination threshold of 0.9 for organic products, which is unfortunately the same as that for conventional agricultural products. in conclusion, in order to avoid a collapse in consumption due to a crisis of confidence in foods that are selected and purchased precisely because of their characteristics and their naturalness in the production method, a threshold for accidental contamination by gmos for organic products should be defined.
i believe that the measure under consideration can be greatly improved by parliament during the vote in the chamber tomorrow. a measure such as the present one, which sets a contamination threshold of 0.9% for organic products, the same as for conventional products, does not help organic producers, much less consumers. the figures provided by the commissioner also show that this is a measure which could cause serious damage to the organic sector. in fact, if the same threshold is applied to organic products as to conventional products, this creates confusion among consumers, who may no longer be inclined towards organic products, and this is also detrimental to the agricultural production system, which has experienced a great deal of growth in this sector in recent years. i therefore believe that parliament must return to the zero tolerance threshold in order to give these products more and more value, ensuring that they are consumed more and more and that consumers are protected more and more. an organic product with a 0.9% threshold is pointless, and consumers have no interest in buying and spending more for a product that no longer offers the necessary guarantees and is not free from contamination.
on behalf of the its group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i reject the attempt to deny the clear indication of the country of origin on the labelling of products in favour of an eu trade mark which would only serve to hamper traceability. the commission is more concerned with homologating than harmonizing. organic products enjoy a favourable advertising position on the market, thanks to the 'bio' label, and a substantial turnover compared to other products, despite higher retail costs. the labels used so far have produced satisfactory results in terms of differentiating supply and demand. this would be undermined if a common eu trade mark undermined consumer awareness. the regulation must guarantee the independence of certification bodies, particularly as regards relations with operators from third countries. we need an accreditation system based on strict and transparent standards, which is not what the commission wants. in conclusion, the idea of imposing an eu organic logo on products from third countries, without the necessary specification of the regional and national origin of the products, is to be rejected.

the commission's vice-president mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there is now a strong community acquis in the field of maritime safety, but much remains to be done. the commission wanted to complete the building with a new package of measures to strengthen the prevention of accidents and to take better account of their consequences. and in submitting seven proposals, the commission has taken utmost account of the resolutions on enhancing maritime safety adopted by parliament after the prestige accident. we're responding to it. in this way, european maritime administrations can be exemplary. no ship will be able to evade control in european ports. the control of the controllers, namely the classification societies, will be much more rigorous. a clear chain of decision will allow for the reception instead of refuge of ships in distress. operators will be better able to meet their responsibilities towards their passengers or third parties. finally, the systematic return of experiments by accident will become possible. i am glad that the european parliament shares the ambitious approach proposed by the commission. your rapporteurs have done a remarkable job. the commission remains committed to the simultaneous examination of the seven proposals and to the preservation of the 'package' approach, in order to ensure the effectiveness and consistency of the proposed measures. for technical reasons, you wanted to examine two of these seven proposals in advance. by putting forward a proposal on the responsibility of flag states, the commission intends to fill a gap in the european security system. it is the responsibility of national administrations to ensure that ships flying their flag comply with safety standards. clearly, the situation in europe needs to be improved. it is not normal for member states to be included in the grey, or even black, list drawn up by the paris memorandum. it is not normal that there should be such a wide variation in the detention rates of ships flying the european flag, from 0.9% to 24.14% of extreme cases for the period 2003-2005 according to the figures of the paris memorandum. let's get this straight. it is not a question of imposing a new layer of bureaucratic requirements on operators or national administrations or of adopting new safety rules, but of ensuring that the rules already in force are actually applied. the commission proposal simply seeks to incorporate into community law the rules of the international maritime organisation, which state that flag states implement international conventions, and to make compulsory a measure which is only optional, namely the imo audit scheme. we want to ensure that our maritime administrations have the best quality and thereby influence the quality of our ships. this will help to avoid possible unfair competition between european shipping companies. i'm going to move on to the second proposal. the aim is to give ship owners greater responsibility by strengthening the liability regime. the commission suggests that a minimum set of rules be established which are common to all member states in this area - civil liability and insurance - and that rules be drawn up which actually prevent accidents and repair damage. some may object that there are international conventions on the same subject. to which i would reply that these conventions are imperfect, and from two points of view. firstly, not all of them have entered into force, and in fact they are delaying their entry into force. secondly, even if these conventions were to become fully operational in the future throughout europe, there will still be cases which they will not cover. and then, especially in the background, these conventions have a flaw. they enshrine a principle which urgently needs to be modernized: the limitation of responsibilities. more specifically, these conventions define the threshold beyond which the shipowner loses his right to limit his liability. and the problem is that this threshold is set at a level that is virtually uncrossable, the unpardonable sin. a threshold which cannot be exceeded is a preferential treatment for shipowners to the detriment of victims where the damage suffered exceeds the compensation ceiling provided for in those same conventions. it is also a favourable treatment for the bad ship owners at the expense of the good ones. the owners of ships which are alleged to have committed serious misconduct - on the scale of misconduct, one degree below inexcusable misconduct - causing major pollution, should no longer be able to benefit from this privilege of limitation of liability. our proposal is in line with this. it is therefore both an immediate alternative response to the difficulties of implementing international conventions and a first step towards the modernisation of all these texts. i am not going to go into the details of the commission's proposals, but i would like to say that i am very pleased that the commission has taken the initiative of putting forward a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks arising from exposure to asbestos. i shall be able to answer mrs vicenzi and mr savary, whom i would like to thank very warmly for their excellent work.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the commissioner for his words on this report. the process of this important directive is finally coming to a close and i would first of all like to thank all those who have devoted themselves over the past few months to an exciting and, i believe, very useful debate, starting with the shadow rapporteurs and all the officials without whom it would not have been possible to deal with such complex issues. this directive has been the subject of much discussion, sometimes knowingly and sometimes inappropriately and without knowing the substance of the matter, also because these are very complex issues. i think it's important to clarify what we're talking about. this is a directive against organised crime and i would stress, finally, against organised crime in its traditional form and in the form it has recently acquired, namely a directive against the damage that crime does to europe through counterfeiting of goods and the infringement of intellectual property. many colleagues have asked me in recent months why we need to harmonize. i would like to say that organized crime has long been an illegal activity that operates globally, knows no borders and can rely on immense resources. on the contrary, the law is fragmented in different and sometimes contradictory legal systems, and is therefore weaker. it has been estimated that the volume of counterfeit goods has increased by 1,600% in the last ten years and i think europe must do something about it, because we are talking about a huge market and very concrete and material things, namely toys, clothes, shoes, food, cosmetics, chemicals, foodstuffs with false names, glasses, compact discs, dvds and other goods, that is, all the goods that european citizens consume every day. as has been said, this phenomenon produces enormous damage. it is harmful to european industries, because obviously counterfeiting alters all the most basic rules of the market and competition, and it is harmful to workers, because obviously those who produce counterfeit goods do so in total and utter disregard of the laws protecting the rights of producers and because counterfeiting of markets on the grounds of recession and unemployment. it has been said that in the last ten years in europe this phenomenon has led to 125,000 new unemployed. the result is damage to the economy through tax evasion and damage to consumers because we in this parliament spend many hours writing regulations to protect european citizens, but not effectively fighting counterfeiting, and we have no tools to enforce these regulations. i think that the counterfeiting of brand names of generic medicines, which are often marketed in developing countries, is a particularly serious form of counterfeiting and i am very pleased that the executive secretary of the world health organisation's anti-counterfeiting task force has spoken positively about the report, because it specifically mentions the health risks and sets a high degree of seriousness for counterfeiting of medicines. so i think we have to move on. i think that the text of the directive is also very innovative compared to the commission's text and that we have reached a positive compromise. i think it is important to have clarified and limited the scope of the directive, for example by excluding patents for which the civil code remains the most appropriate instrument for settling disputes. although this is a very controversial text, i think we must not stop there and that we cannot escape the reality of these arguments. the harmonization of the criminal law is a step forward in the construction of the european single market, which is certainly favoured by rules, but also by measures such as these which prevent the rules from being constantly disregarded. so acting at this level helps and strengthens the identity of a political europe, but above all it strengthens the idea of a europe which is useful to the european citizens. we are coming to this vote in parliament with the comfort of a very broad vote in support of the directive by the legal affairs committee. i therefore hope that a large majority will support this compromise, because at this time powerful interests and lobbies want the european parliament to do nothing, but i believe that it would be damaging to the image and political harm if, faced with a crime as devastating as counterfeiting, the european parliament were to raise its hands and say that europe cannot do anything against this crime. in the past parliament has been at the forefront of the construction of the single market and of political europe, and i am convinced that it will be at the forefront of this too.
i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr zingaretti, for his cooperation and for having tried to mediate in some way on this directive which imposes criminal law on infringement, without a framework of reference for the rules defining infringement itself, and indeed by unifying trademark, patent and copyright infringements. by conflating counterfeiting and counterfeiting with intellectual property infringements, the fight against criminal counterfeiting risks being rendered less effective. it would have been more useful to limit the application of the directive to copyright infringements involving the commercial production of counterfeit multimedia products, which is the domain of organised crime. on the contrary, improper expansion of copyright can pose serious risks to the privacy of consumers of multimedia products. in addition, the directive abandons the concept of commercial scale in copyright, risking the criminal prosecution of private and non-profit-making use of users using the internet for peer-to-peer, video streaming and so on. the directive requires states to take criminal action even without a complaint from the party concerned and gives private parties a direct role in investigations, which goes beyond technical assistance to the authorities and ends up becoming a role of impulse and direction. finally, the directive lacks economic and social analysis. the tightening of sanctions in italy has had no effect. that is why our group proposes that the directive be rejected.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. i thank you for a debate with many valuable and important comments and suggestions. i would like to comment on a few points raised in the debate. the commission considers that the restriction of the scope of the directive to the area of community competence alone is an essential point in order to cover cases under both community and national law. if this were not the case, the implementation of the directive could face considerable difficulties, since community law and national law are closely intertwined. there is a risk that citizens will not understand which law actually applies, which means that legal certainty could be compromised. the commission also considers that all types of intellectual property rights deserve criminal protection. the commission therefore advocates the inclusion of patents. however, this should not impede the implementation of the directive politically. the commission can accept that patents are excluded from the scope of the directive. the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal to include a new provision on the protection of intellectual property rights in the directive. with the exception of the definition of legal person, the commission has omitted definitions because they are unnecessary or because they could create legal uncertainty. the commission therefore prefers to leave the member states free to decide in accordance with their respective laws and in the light of the measures already taken by them.

the commission's vice-president madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking mrs karin roth, who has just shown that the german presidency is very committed to this problem of maritime safety, and i thank her very much for that. in march i presented to you two of the seven proposals in the third legislative package on maritime safety. the debate and vote that followed clearly showed the broad support of parliament. i am confident that the same will be true today of the other five proposals. three of them are part of the preventive part of the package and i will first refer to the amendment of the directive on classification societies. by granting community licences to these companies, we indirectly control almost 90% of the world tonnage. this is how essential the quality of the work of these bodies is. the commission has therefore proposed the establishment of an independent structure responsible for certifying quality control systems. secondly, we are introducing a gradual and proportionate financial sanctions regime. it is a more flexible system than the current system, which only provides for the withdrawal of authorization. this will make it easier for the commission to require the correction of any malfunctions. finally, the certificates accompanying the equipment installed on board ships should be mutually recognised by the approved bodies. this mutual recognition, based on equivalent standards and the highest technical standards, will have two positive effects. it will remove unnecessary barriers to free movement in the internal market and reduce the costs for marine equipment manufacturers of multiple certification procedures. the savings made can be used to the benefit of safety research. beyond the necessary formal simplification of the port state control directive, the commission wants to promote a more efficient use of resources. on the one hand, we want to replace the individual objective of each member state to control 25% of vessels with a collective objective for the whole of europe. in short, we want to control all the ships. on the other hand, we want to inspect ships with a high risk profile more frequently. today, too many substandard ships are still out of control. the new system will avoid this, while rewarding quality vessels with fewer inspections. substandard vessels that transit european waters without calling at a port pose a particular risk. that is why we have wanted to strengthen inspections in the anchorages off the coast. finally, the strengthening of the provisions on denial of access, in particular through the introduction of permanent ban measures, is a strong measure. it is unacceptable that ships are not only detained but also repeatedly banned. the union must make it very clear that it will not accept repeat offenders in its waters. the third text, which strengthens our preventive arsenal, amends the directive on traffic monitoring. the legal framework for places of refuge needs to be clarified in order to improve the efficiency and speed of decision-making in maritime accidents. this requires being prepared to deal with any type of situation involving any type of ship. the crucial point in this respect is the independence of decision-making, a condition for speed and, therefore, a condition for a dangerous situation not to turn into an environmental disaster affecting several states. the aim is also to consolidate the safeseanet network as a europe-wide system for exchanging information on the monitoring of ship traffic and movements of dangerous or polluting cargoes. a final element of the proposal is to gradually equip fishing vessels over 15 metres in length with automatic identification systems to reduce the risk of collision with commercial vessels. many tragedies will be avoided. that is all for the first three proposals of a preventive nature. the last two proposals are aimed at better dealing with the consequences of maritime accidents. the commission proposes that technical investigations be carried out systematically after a maritime accident. it is not a substitute for judicial investigations, but an effective tool for the european union, based on international rules, which will make it possible to better understand the causes of accidents. here again, the question of the independence of the investigating offices is central. the idea is also to promote cooperation between administrations, particularly where several states are affected by the same accident. the european maritime safety agency, which is already working on a common investigation methodology, must help us to set up a framework for systematic community cooperation. the last proposal concerns the compensation of accident victims. the aim is to incorporate into community law the provisions of the 2002 athens convention on the rights of passengers and to extend them to national traffic and inland waterway transport. all european passengers will thus be able to benefit from the protective regime established by the convention, regardless of the mode of transport used and the journey made. i insist on this point. how can it be that a passenger travelling between two ports in the same country is not treated in the same way as another travelling internationally? that is my opening remarks, ladies and gentlemen. i shall then express the commission's position on the reports by mrs vlasto and by mr sterckx, mr kohlíček, mr costa and mr grandes pascual. i would like to thank them in advance for the excellent work they have done. i would like to conclude, madam president, by saying that if we are to avoid further oil spills, we must now be able to secure the entire chain of maritime traffic and, in this respect, none of these proposals is useless. these seven proposals are necessary if we are to have a really effective system, a system which really allows europe to be an example to the world in the field of maritime safety.
the rapporteur. i believe that the european union is regaining some of the trust of european citizens, partly because it is pursuing a strategy of consumer protection, which in our case means a strategy of protecting travellers, that is, consumers when they travel. this has already happened in the field of civil aviation and i hope it is happening in the railway sector too. i think that is the way the rules of procedure, on which i had the honour of being rapporteur, should be read. it is a regulation which takes some important small steps towards harmonizing the protection of passengers and their baggage. to this end, it seeks to make compulsory, or at least to extend, the application of the athens convention, which already governs this field as regards the definition of rules and liability, and the imposition of compulsory insurance for all those who transport people, identifying forms of immediate response in the event of an accident with timely and satisfactory compensation. the regulation in question goes a few steps further than the athens convention. i do not want to dwell on the technical aspects at this stage, but i would like to stress that the scope of these protections is being extended. the athens convention could only deal with international transport. however, the baltic and the mediterranean are basins in which many transports have the character of inland transport. moreover, following the enlargement of the union to bulgaria and romania, the major european inland waterways must now be treated in the same way. that is why i have supported and continue to support - and i hope that parliament, the council and the commission will do the same - the extension of the coverage of passenger protection to domestic transport. as far as internal transport is concerned, the few obstacles that have been put up have virtually disappeared since the last accident, which occurred in early april with the sea diamond near the island of santorini. we cannot imagine that the two missing persons are not protected, which they would be if they had disappeared in the atlantic or indian ocean. it is clear that this discrimination is not possible. as i see some residual difficulty in accepting the extension of protection to inland waters, i hope we will not have to wait for an accident on some river before deciding to extend coverage to inland transport. it seems to me that we cannot imagine protecting the people who travel on a large riverboat any differently from those who travel on a small ship in the seas we protect. moreover, if we consider the technical aspect of some ships that now make river and sea routes, it would be quite ridiculous that they should be covered only when they are at sea and not on rivers. i therefore believe that the regulation we are adopting is a two-pronged approach, in that it also takes account of this aspect of maritime safety, thereby making it easier for those who travel by sea to do so. i would point out that people with reduced mobility are better protected, that anyone who has an accident is compensated immediately, that there are also limits to the liability of the carrier, because if he adopts the athens convention he has no unlimited liability, and so on. there are a thousand other aspects, but the fundamental one is that we treat all european citizens equally when they are travelling, whether on international routes, on national routes, on inland waterways or even outside european waters when they are covered by european provisions. in view of this, i hope that we can move forward in this direction, and thus gain the attention and recognition of the european citizens who can look to this part of the union's activity which continues to provide useful and important answers to all citizens and which, in some way, also makes up for other shortcomings in a more general debate that we are currently holding.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i am not saying anything new when i stress that the issue of maritime safety in the territorial waters of the european union is unfortunately a constant and sometimes dramatic issue. only three months ago the 45th accident in half a century occurred in the straits of messina, one of the most crucial points of shipping in the mediterranean. the accident, which involved a ferry and a hydrofoil, has again caused deaths and injuries. this massacre might have been avoided if the sophisticated ground-based radar system, which is supposed to monitor maritime traffic, had been fully operational. the only system which is now monitoring traffic in the straits of messina is the ais, the automatic satellite vessel identification system, which is compulsory for vessels over 300 tonnes. in this connection, the committee on fisheries, with a view to improving the safety of fishermen and their vessels - i would remind you that many serious maritime accidents are caused by commercial vessels not seeing fishing vessels - approved in its opinion an amendment which calls for the mandatory use of the ais system for all new fishing vessels. as regards existing vessels, provision should be made for financing, particularly for small vessels, since most of the vessels operating in the mediterranean are owned by small businesses which are already in serious economic difficulties and have had to make immense sacrifices in order to adapt to the policy of fishing with the so-called 'blue boxes'. madam president, commissioner, hoping for the development of maritime transport means therefore guaranteeing the safety of everyone and everywhere, of passengers and workers on board, in inland waters and not, but also means increasing controls and tightening penalties for infringers. the vote in this house can therefore be a concrete proof of europe's will to move in this direction.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, maritime safety, which is the subject of five directives which parliament is called upon to adopt, forms the package of measures which is praiseworthy in that it aims at better prevention and more efficient response to maritime accidents and at managing their environmental impact. in my view, it is good to incorporate the 2002 athens convention into community law, thereby making the liability of carriers and the insurance cover of passengers and their baggage objective. the right guarantees are given to users and a kind of safety cycle is also set in motion, which stimulates greater monitoring of navigation and equipment and safety procedures, precisely because the various maritime transport operators are involved. as regards the sterckx report in particular, i think it would be appropriate to develop the european system for the exchange of information and the use of the automatic identification system for fishing vessels, provided that there is then concrete support from 90% of the union for the instrumental adaptation of fleets, especially for the benefit of small operators. i do not, however, approve of the desire to deprive the national states of their freedom of action in the field of emergency management and the procedures for receiving ships in distress. i do, however, agree with the text of the amendment which states that a state cannot waive its obligation to assist ships in distress. i also agree with what mr vlasto and the commission are suggesting about further strengthening the inspection regime for ships and the associated risk profiles. in conclusion, i welcome all the steps towards a continental policy on the sea and safety in terms of human, environmental and economic resources, all those which promote the improvement and harmonization of the performance of maritime administrations, and the promotion of registration under the union flag.
member of the commission. the question has nothing to do with the issue we are discussing, but i am pleased to hear your questions and to have the possibility of answering them. first, i want to clarify that the commission is not even dreaming of increasing or harmonising the corporate tax rate – that is very far from our intention. what we have in mind, and what we have already tabled as a general proposal – not even a legislative proposal – is the harmonisation of the tax base only, i.e. the calculation of the tax base, which is now different in each and every member state. we have 27 different ways of calculating the tax base, which results in enormous compliance costs and administrative burdens for companies. the lack of consolidation and of transparency makes it very difficult, or senseless, to compare the corporate tax rate of ireland, which is 12.5 %, with the corporate tax rate of france, which is over 30 %, because we cannot compare the two tax bases. we have no intention of harmonising the tax rates, only the method of calculation of the tax base, and certainly we have no power to force things. if the present legislative proposal, according to our time schedule, receives unanimity in early 2008, then of course ireland, and all the other member states, should comply. if there is no consensus – and i think that at least at the beginning there will be no consensus – then what we can do is to present a new proposal, not for all the 27 member states but only for those who want to join. that is what we call enhanced cooperation. enhanced cooperation is optional. only those member states that agree with the purpose of the exercise would participate, and ireland, according to the best of my knowledge, will not be among the countries that will champion participation. however, i believe that after a while, when the positive experiences are well known, then even those member states that are reluctant for the time being and that will not join at the beginning of the enhanced cooperation can join later, because one of the conditions of enhanced cooperation is to leave the door open for other member states who may wish to join in at a later stage.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr vice-president of the commission, i am sorry that the transport live night show is not the council's favourite, since it is to the council in particular that i would have liked to address myself. i think that what i am going to say to my colleagues and to the vice-president of the commission is well known and i think it is also shared, and we know that we have some problems with the council. parliament welcomed with great interest and understanding the commission's proposal to revise the rules which seek to deal with the problem of security against any attack on airports, aircraft and the aviation system. the commission has approached this matter with great openness, bearing in mind that we are about to carry out an important task, namely to build a single safety system, which reduces the inconvenience to passengers and allows for the extension of safety and better organization to this end. i think i can say that we have also made some improvements, trying to define the limits within which we can allow people with weapons on board and trying to solve the technical problems of the difference between conventional and postal freight, to identify the ways of organizing inspections at airports and to consider many other technicalities. however, we have come up against a problem in which i still cannot understand the logic of the council's opposition. the theme is very simple: security is both a private and a public problem. each of us, when we travel, has an interest in traveling safely. however, where security can be affected by terrorist attacks, it is clearly in the collective interest to defend against such attacks. in the united states, for example, this is considered a matter of public concern and is entirely the responsibility of the taxpayer. in this connection, we reiterate the idea which we have put forward - and which we are perhaps still insisting on - that the principle should be accepted that the costs of security should be borne by the citizen who travels and by the states which defend themselves, including in infrastructure and aircraft, all the more so as we were merely asking for this principle to be accepted, leaving it to each member state to decide how to combine the two sources. as a second principle, we asked that the costs borne by the citizen for security be transparent and clearly defined, and as a third principle we asked for a guarantee that any surcharge paid for security was actually used for security. we have only asked for these three principles to be accepted, renouncing the interinstitutional agreement signed in 2001, according to which the commission would have had to submit much more detailed proposals to deal with the problem of security financing, which would then of course also have been accepted by the council. we have not had an answer on this point and have not been able to reach a conclusion. i hope that tomorrow, if the house cannot repeat the unanimous vote in committee, it can at least find a large majority that shows not the strength but the good will of parliament to find a real solution to the problem for all european citizens. i would stress that unfortunately security is an issue we will have to live with. hiding behind the scenes and pretending that the problem of its financing does not exist is not an answer to the times, the problem and our expectations. we are therefore in favour of a more technically advanced organization in the field of security, but we ask that this problem be solved at least in principle. if we can achieve this as soon as possible, i believe we will have done what is in the best interests of our citizens.

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this debate on relations between the european union and the swiss confederation offers us an interesting and opportune opportunity to reflect briefly on what we can learn from the ancient democracy of the small but historically important swiss federal republic. the swiss federal tax system, if it were well known to the taxpayers of the member states of the european union, would be - as it is objectively - a model to be imitated, especially in the protection of economic freedom. i would remind the taxpayers of the member states that swiss legislation is based on important principles, such as the principle of legal equality, the principle of economic freedom and, above all, the principle of the guarantee of property. the principle of legal equality requires that taxation be proportionate to economic capacity. the principle of economic freedom provides that the collection of certain taxes on trade, which would be prohibited in the context of commercial policy, is prohibited by constitutional rules. finally, the important principle of the guarantee of property, enshrined in article 26 of the federal constitution, prohibits the tax burden when it takes the form of confiscation, so that the guarantee of property constitutes a limit to taxation. this is what the member states must learn, which, like the italian state, still oppress the taxpayer with tax legislation and a tax burden that in italy exceeds 40%. we must learn from this great historical experience the principles of economic freedom contained in the swiss constitution. we padanians are lucky to be neighbours of these free men of switzerland. finally, we should also think of the principle of freedom of religion, which prevents non-religious people from being required to pay taxes for religious services, and the fundamental right to express one's will directly by means of a referendum on taxes. it is time to end the tax dictatorship of the states over the taxpayers! the people's vote on taxes!

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, today the process of the owninitiative report on housing and regional policy, for which i am the rapporteur, comes to an end. the report has in fact already begun with the work of the urban intergroup, chaired by mr jean marie beaupuy, of which i am vice-chairman. this work has made a major step forward with the european charter on housing, proposed and drawn up by mr hutchinson and approved in this very intergroup. i would first of all like to thank my colleagues, and especially the shadow rapporteurs, for their significant and important contribution. i am grateful to the coordinators and officials who have actively contributed to the drafting of the report, providing useful and useful corrective information to the document under consideration. it is only thanks to the understanding shown by all and the right attitude of collaboration that it has been possible to arrive today at a text which i find balanced but at the same time innovative and on which i hope there will be a broad consensus. the work with the european commission, the german presidency of the council of ministers and the european investment bank has been very fruitful indeed. we have established a very effective relationship with the trade associations and non-governmental organisations that have approached my office. a heartfelt thank you goes to the rapporteurs for opinions of the committee of the regions, mr flo clucas, and of the economic and social committee, mr angelo grasso, for their great commitment and for the excellent texts produced. i would also like to thank those who worked with me on the drafting of the report, namely the official from the group, mr anu ahopelto, the official from the regi committee, mrs agneszka kunat, and my assistant, mr valentino izzo. before going into the substance of the text, i think it is necessary to clarify the methodology used. the aim which i set myself when i began work on this own-initiative report was to raise the debate on housing policy to the level of a european issue, while being aware of the difficulties which exist. the treaty, as is well known, does not confer specific powers on the union in this area. however, article 7 of the edf regulation for the 2007-2013 programming period provides, in a limited number of cases and in any case only in the new member states, for the possibility of providing community funds to support projects for the renovation of buildings. it should also be noted that a large number of european policies - energy, environment, transport, security, cultural and social - have a strong, albeit indirect, impact on the quality of housing. the housing problem cannot therefore be regarded as a problem in itself. the approach i have taken to the own-initiative report is therefore a global one, considering housing choices within a more general policy of sustainable urban development, strongly linked to the sectoral and horizontal policies i have just mentioned. the report was therefore built around two main dimensions: the social dimension, which concerns the link between housing conditions, urban decay and social exclusion, and the environmental dimension, which concerns problems ranging from energy waste to the insecurity of buildings, from the quality of common areas to the protection of water and seismic risks. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a step in the right direction. horizontal, i.e. between the various european sectoral policies; the commission has also proposed a number of measures to improve the quality of housing in the eu. some of the most important issues. right to the house: if parliament, as i hope, were to vote in favour of this own-initiative report, it would for the first time recognise the right to adequate and affordable housing as a fundamental right. quality of housing: the text approved by the regi committee on 20 march deals with improving the quality of buildings. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the appropriate resources: budgetary constraints have reduced the level of public resources available for urban investment, while processes of administrative decentralisation and regionalisation in many countries have increased the powers of cities. it is therefore necessary to provide local authorities with adequate financial instruments and to ensure that the right to housing can be effectively and fully enjoyed and that appropriate housing policies, and more generally urban development, can be derived from it. the house is calling for the right to housing benefit to be strengthened and, in particular, for facilities to be made available to young people.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank mr janowski and mr andria for the excellent work they have done. in particular, i appreciated the commitment to a more adequate housing policy. it is worth remembering that housing is a real emergency, especially in large european cities, where the cost of housing is very high and forces households to spend more than 50% of their salary on the mortgage or rent of the house. the house will be voting in favour of the report. i hope that we will move towards a project to redevelop the public housing which is often in very poor condition and, more generally, towards a strategy to rebuild the disadvantaged urban areas of the major european cities.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, europe's continuing commitment to the ever-increasing opening up of markets must not prevent europe from asserting its own interests in the global world. the lisbon strategy is an ambitious and shared objective and it makes it possible to meet the challenge that the competitors of the european union have set us. it is important to bear in mind, however, that the great game of trade and development is often played with unequal rules, and this lack of reciprocity, although justified by the delay in many countries in reaching their development milestones, is detrimental to our production systems, with serious social consequences. we must not forget that the european union is a major player in the world economy. our policy is to open the market, gradually reduce customs duties and create a level playing field. in this context, the policies of innovation, opening up markets, supporting the conversion of mature and no longer competitive production sectors must be integrated with the instruments for the protection of intellectual property and, more generally, with trade protection, as indicated in the green paper and as mr caspary's report pointedly reiterates.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, europe has always defended the strictness of the rules of the wto and has applied a close control on any practices which might cause distortions in the internal and international markets, often by itself and at the expense of its own immediate economic interests. for these rules to make sense, the eu must strongly insist that they be applied by other members, in particular by direct competitors. it is also important that these standards are periodically adapted to the constant evolution of business practices and the production system, as in recent cases of relocation, in order to safeguard both the quality and quantity of work in the union, as well as the respect of social and environmental standards in non-european countries. in this connection, the procedures under way for the creation of the european quality label and for the protection of intellectual property must be encouraged and accelerated, so that the competitiveness of our enterprises, especially the smaller ones, and the quality of our production can be safeguarded both within and outside our frontiers. as a member of the committee on development i feel obliged to remind you that flexibility and gradual progress are necessary for those developing countries which are committed to ensuring the basic needs of their populations before they are fully open to the market: equal access to clean water, to education, to efficient sanitation systems, for example, are essential prerequisites for further sustainable economic development.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is clear to everyone in this house and in the economic and productive world of the european union that ever greater cfp can promote a freer and at the same time fairer and more controlled development of the market. if the european union is to remain the world's leading economic power and the area of greater freedom and less social inequality, it must not only encourage the development of the capacity of developing countries to promote external trade in the face of their unfortunately severe loss of competitiveness on world markets, but also increase aid for trade, in the knowledge that liberalisation and aid are not mutually contradictory initiatives. in this context, the significant sum of eur 2 billion is still not enough, the concept of cap itself needs to be clarified by adopting the conclusions of the world trade organisation's task force on aid on financiable interventions and by integrating development and trade policies as much as possible, as provided for in the integrated framework, also in terms of poverty reduction.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in the european context it is difficult to imagine strong economic growth and the creation of jobs and wealth without an efficient and modern transport network. the trans-european transport network plays a decisive role in enabling the free movement of persons and goods within the territory of the european union and is one of the decisive factors for achieving the objectives of economic and employment development of the european union identified by the lisbon agenda, all the more so in a europe which has deepened two dimensions with enlargement: the central eastern and the southern. for this reason, the european union has set as one of its objectives for the tens the elimination of bottlenecks in the rail network and the adaptation of priority routes in order to absorb new flows generated by enlargement, especially in border areas, and to improve the accessibility of peripheral regions. in this way, the tens can be a reference point for community legislation aimed at promoting economic and social development and territorial cohesion for the countries of the union. as we all know, the funding for the tens has been considerably reduced compared with the initial forecasts: the 2007-13 programming set the funding for the tens at eur 8 billion, a sharp reduction from the eur 20 billion initially requested by the commission, while doubling the available funds over the period 2000-2006. we have accepted this penalty and have moved forward with the forces that have been made available to us, pursuing throughout the long negotiations four fundamental objectives: (1) simplification, to make the procedure easier; 2) cross-compliance, in order to favour modes of transport with a lower environmental impact; (3) selectivity and concentration, to encourage the concentration of resources on projects with high community added value; (4) proportionality, in order to diversify the maximum amount of community resources available depending on the type of project to be financed. i have mentioned only some of the objectives we have achieved in order to establish a precise identification of financial commitments: the increase of co-financing rates to 20% for priority projects and 30% for the cross-border section. a clear increase in community financial support for projects aimed at eliminating bottlenecks in the networks of the most disadvantaged regions, as the commission intends to do in the context of the revision of the tens. the use of up to 85% of budgetary resources for priority projects, a clearer definition of bottlenecks to overcome natural barriers, a new link for the european rail management traffic system, which can now benefit from co-financing rates of 50%. new and innovative parameters for the 'loan guarantee instruments' issued by the european bank and new measures to provide risk capital participation, with the possibility of involving the private investment sector. i would like to clarify the question of comitology by giving details of the compromise reached: the agreed procedure follows article 5 and not article 5a, which would have been the optimum for parliament, but would have caused further delays in the work, preventing the allocation of community funds by 2007, with very serious consequences for the implementation of the programme. even if article 5 applies, parliament is expected to be heavily involved. all proposals will be sent to both the committee on the rules of procedure and parliament in parallel, thus allowing parliament to make its own assessments well in advance, before the proposals are adopted. this fully meets the need to keep both the committee on budgets and the committee on transport constantly informed. in addition, commissioner barrot, in his letter of last november, gave a personal commitment to keep the chairmen of the two parliamentary committees concerned informed of any changes. the letter was included in the final text of the regulation, as a guarantee of the commission's commitment to parliament. i personally strongly believe that the question of comitology must be studied and analysed in order to avoid future deadlock situations. this compromise is an isolated case, prompted by the need to speed up the procedure in order to avoid blocking the allocation of community funds for the tens. in the light of this clarification, mr president, i would ask all the honourable members in the house to vote against the amendments tabled. since agreement has been reached on the text as a whole, to vote in favour of these amendments would mean to abandon this agreement, to reopen the negotiations with the council and to frustrate all the efforts made during the negotiations, which were launched with the very intention of unlocking the funds for the tens in a speedy manner. i would like to conclude by thanking all my colleagues and especially the shadow rapporteurs of the other groups who have contributed to the report.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to report to the house on the work of the committee, which has discussed mr donnici's credentials in depth and has reached a large majority in favour of the report. i am defending the committee, which i have the great honour of chairing, and i am responding to those who make petty insinuations - which obviously do not do honour to this parliament either, since the committee has a flourishing number of lawyers in it - that it would not be calm and objective. we have people and lawyers like lehne, medina, wallis, frassoni, just to mention the coordinators, and also many other personalities throughout the committee. we have always discussed this at a high level, with great depth and with great sincerity. we have been increasingly studying the role of this parliament, which is a giant in many ways and in its role in europe, but which is a dwarf sometimes when you try to force it into a bureaucratic corner. the question we're discussing is part of this big question: the fact is that mr occhetto's resignation is contrary to the european act and mr donnici cannot be given a positive assessment. the rules governing the european electoral procedure are a matter of community competence and therefore the reference to national provisions laid down by the european act of 1976 is only supplementary. the national provisions must, however, be in conformity with the fundamental principles of community law, its primary rules and the spirit of the letter of the 1976 act. for these reasons, the national legislative and administrative authorities, as well as the judicial authorities, cannot fail to take account of the community's legal framework in electoral matters. the compatibility of mr occhetto's resignation must first be assessed in the light of article 4 of the 1976 act, which states that members of parliament cannot be bound by instructions in receiving mandatory mandates and that the freedom and independence of members is the fundamental pillar of the freedom of the citizen. this is laid down in the 1976 act, but the new statute for members of the european parliament which i am now quoting, although it enters into force in the next parliamentary term, is at present a legislative act of primary law in the community system, adopted by the european parliament with the approval of the council and published in the official journal. it is quite clear that mr occhetto's decision to withdraw from the election is the result of an expression of will that was conditioned and vitiated by an agreement concluded with the other party on the list of civil society, di pietro-occhetto, before the 2004 european elections were declared, and that this decision must be considered incompatible with the letter and spirit of the 1976 act, in particular article 6. it could not in any circumstances be validly revoked, as it has been revoked. in giving reasons for its decision to the contrary, the council of state - and i repeat this in this italian-speaking chamber - made no mention of or took account of the principles of community law mentioned above, thereby disregarding not only the spirit and the letter of the act but also articles 4 and 6 of the text. in accordance with settled case-law of the court of justice of the european communities, the infringement of community law by the authorities of a member state, even if committed by a court of last instance, by a judgment which has been entered in the register, does not prevent the court of justice from being able to find that the national supreme court has infringed community law. but it does not relieve the state, in this case italy to which the said court belongs, of its financial responsibility, as established. i think that this clearly shows the situation in which we find ourselves. i want to say two things quickly which belong to italian law. the act of waiver may validly have as its object rights which are present and in that case it is fully operative in terms of the explanation and effectiveness of the waiver which mr occhetto made in respect of mr chiesa. the waiver is also valid for future rights, but of course this waiver can be revoked before the event is determined, before the waiver holder is in a position to effectively waive. the resignation of mr occhetto following the announcement of the election results did not alter the ranking of the candidates on the di pietro-occhetto list. the final point, mr president, is that it is a basic principle of law to recognize that a waiver can only take effect when the necessary conditions for the exercise of the right have been met. for this very reason, in the decision of 3 july 2006, which is used to demonstrate a contradiction with what we have done - precisely because of that decision of the legal affairs committee - we gave a favourable opinion on the election of occhetto, because at the time the proclamation was in accordance with the european act, because we recognised his resignation as invalid, irrelevant and null and void. and donnici's exceptions were irrelevant then. that is why there is no contradiction. we decided this last year, and today we can confirm that same decision because it is consistent, it was deliberated by a legal committee which is of course not partisan, but it is in the interests of this parliament to promote and guarantee its autonomy.
