vice-president of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i congratulate the rapporteur, mr newton dunn, on this report. i think that the importance of developing all the means at our disposal in the fight against organised crime is clear to everyone, and i do not think anyone can doubt it. i shall confine myself to giving a few brief indications of some recent progress which the european union has made in this field and some initiatives which the european commission will be taking in the very near future. firstly, i particularly agree with the rapporteur, precisely because it is a matter of improving our knowledge of the phenomenon of organised crime. we do not have a clear picture of the scale of the crime phenomenon and the flows of organised crime. the development of europol's activities in this field is particularly noteworthy. europol, as you know, this year, starting in 2007, will publish and propose to supplement its traditional crime intelligence report on the state of crime in europe with an annual threat assessment. the europol report will therefore be a proactive report and not just a knowledge report; the commission will therefore be able to indicate, year by year, the sectors in which the threat of organised crime has increased and, as we hope, those in which the threat will also have decreased. unfortunately, we are seeing a growing increase in all the major areas of organized crime. another important achievement, the rapporteur was now referring to, is european action in the field of crime statistics. we have not yet had a statistical picture. you will recall that in a communication adopted last year i proposed a system of crime statistics at european level. we have already set up a group of experts and i am pleased to say that eurostat has already published the first european crime statistics. we're starting to see some real results. in the field of prevention, which is extremely important, we have decided to concentrate, for example, on the fight against corruption, which is often linked to organized crime networks. we have decided to establish a european network of national experts in constant contact, precisely for the purpose of preventing corruption. i have considered including in the programme for next year, 2008, an initiative which will explore the links between corruption, money laundering and therefore organised crime networks. this is an area where europe needs to do more. there is also a great deal of action on human trafficking; there is an action plan, already adopted and in the process of being developed, for concrete implementation. as you probably know, we have also been promoting a european day every year, specifically against human trafficking, which will be a concrete sign of a development, of a european awareness which has so far been insufficient. we also thought we should focus on witness protection, which is essential if we are to fight organised crime. i shall be putting a working document with some concrete proposals before the end of july this year, that is to say within the next two months, at the disposal of this parliament. this working document will be the result of an analysis we have made with the police, with the judicial authorities of the member states, on how witnesses in the fight against organised crime should be protected, because if witnesses are not protected, a fundamental element in the fight against organised crime is lost. on police and judicial cooperation, coordination must be strengthened, in particular between europol and eurojust. a multidisciplinary approach is certainly essential and we have done a lot for europol. i have proposed a new statute for europol to increase its powers, extend its mandate and give europol more flexibility. unfortunately, organised crime has a very high degree of adaptability and so europol must also be extremely more flexible. i hope that the council will accept our proposal for community funding for europol. this would have the immediate advantage of democratic control by the european parliament over the use of europol's budget, which would then be subject to a democratic parliamentary supervisory authority in a more transparent manner. as you know, the council is still somewhat reluctant to accept this proposal of mine. on the operational side, europol is gaining strength. where's the weak spot? the weak point is that the member states do not provide europol with the necessary operational information that europol needs to coordinate its activities. you probably know that the central information system of europol is fed 70% by only five member states and 30% by all the others. this shows what europol could be if all member states contributed better. this is something they will have to do now because all three europol protocols have entered into force and so cooperation will be better. eurojust also needs to do more. i will certainly be presenting a proposal on eurojust this autumn, i think between october and november, and it will be a proposal to strengthen eurojust's powers of initiative. the point at the heart of my initiative will be the association of eurojust, i would say the normal, systematic association with the joint investigation teams. these joint investigation teams are a fundamental tool in the fight against crime and eurojust is called upon to participate in the joint investigation teams in an insufficient, non-organic and sometimes episodic way. that's not right! eurojust must be a regular player in the joint investigation teams in order to increase its capacity. of course, all this great work we are doing must always strike a balance between the security requirements which are, as i am personally convinced, a fundamental right of the citizen. citizens have a right to security, but alongside security there are other rights, also fundamental rights, and so i believe that the issue of data protection in the area of police cooperation - a matter which has not yet received a positive response in the council, despite my proposal a year and a half ago - will finally have to find an organic answer, namely a european legislative initiative on data protection in the so-called third pillar. this will also serve to give the citizen a tangible sign that alongside strong action against organised crime, we strongly respect other fundamental rights such as the right to the processing of personal data. in all these areas, i hope that the council will decide in june to incorporate the provisions of the prüm treaty into european legislation, that is to say, to move from what has been a simple enhanced cooperation between some member states to a provision which is organically integrated into the context of community legislation. if the council, i hope, gives the green light to this proposal, we shall have taken a step forward. finally, i would like to mention two themes. firstly, the practical implementation of the new fundamental rights agency, which was inaugurated in march, which will be an important instrument for ensuring respect for fundamental rights, also at the request of parliament and the commission, in the field of cooperation and police investigations. and the big theme is fighting organized cybercrime. as you know, yesterday i presented a communication on so-called cyber crime, which deals with various sectors of organised cyber crime, from paedophilia to cyber attacks on banking systems. i believe that this cybercrime issue is one of the new frontiers on which this parliament will obviously be able to work.

the improvement and simplification of the exchange of information, to the improvement of investigation methods, to the strengthening of the coordination of investigative and repressive activities. i the necessary synergies between national police authorities and to launching a genuine european policy in this field. in recent years, criminal associations have increasingly taken the form of a real enterprise, finding in the economic and financial markets the preferred place for the laundering of illicit proceeds, and the damage that this entails for the national and community economies is easily imaginable. we must also combat organised crime on the economic side and systematically attack the financial resources, movable and immovable property lawfully acquired. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem. i also hope, and i take note of the commissioner's communication, that the united nations convention on transnational organized crime and the two protocols on human trafficking and the smuggling of migrants will be ratified and applied as soon as possible. i am sure that on the basis of these indications concrete proposals will be made by the commission in the near future and i take note of this with great pleasure tonight and i wish the commissioner good work, who has not only shown himself to be sensitive to these issues but has also put into practice some of the initiatives he has outlined tonight.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat organised crime, and it is therefore important that the commission should be able to take action to combat it. exactly on may 23rd, 15 years ago, a very serious event happened in the history of italy, in the history of europe: an important judge like giovanni falcone was murdered by the mafia in a terrifying way, blowing up the highway in the stretch from the airport to the city of palermo. that judge, his wife, and three other officers in the escort died with him. and 1992 was a terrible year, because after falcone, another judge was murdered by organized crime, by the mafia, like paolo borsellino. both of them understood the importance of implementing international police and judicial cooperation and therefore understood the need to fight criminal organisations at a higher level, at an international level, aiming above all at intercepting the capital of criminal and mafia organisations. falcone and borsellino were the latest victims of a series of massacres in republican italy that began with the portella della ginestra massacre on may 1, 1947. so much has changed in recent years, criminal organizations have become transnational and this changeover was already completed at the end of the 1980s, when the liberal dogma was affirmed in the policy of the international monetary fund and the world bank. the globalisation of the economy and finance has been achieved by deregulating financial and trade markets, privatising services and strengthening tax havens. what has been established is what a leading research institute, the transnational institute in amsterdam, has called the globalfix, that is, the global compromise between the theoretically legal economy and the criminal economy. international trafficking in arms, drugs and money laundering. the criminal vocation of liberal globalisation has in some ways been established. if we look at the world bank and the international monetary fund, we find that the underground economy has quadrupled since the 1980s. in 2001, the value of the underground trade was between $6.5 and $9 trillion a year, or between 20 and 25 percent of the world's gross domestic product. we are talking about a horrifying figure that could help to reduce poverty on a global scale. important developments have taken place in this context. first of all, the collapse of the soviet union, which meant that many state assets were transferred in cash and directly to cartels and criminal organizations. it is no coincidence that the russian mafia is very strong today, both economically and politically. a lot of this money is in many swiss accounts, in the cayman islands, in the islands that mr matsakis was talking about, in the strait of gibraltar. and the other big phenomenon that took hold in the 1990s was the american and british push for deregulation of financial and international markets. the globalisation of financial markets has the seeds of a reorganisation of criminal powers. the other big event that expanded the profits of organized crime was the resumption of war activities. war and its intertwining with liberal globalization has led to a frightening increase in profits for international mafias, starting with the increase in profits from drugs. in the andean region of colombia, the logic of the war on drugs has led to an exponential growth in coca production and its transformation of coca plants into cocaine. the war in the balkans has turned that territory into a free zone where dirty capital is now recycled and heroin refined for the european market. and think of what happened in afghanistan! in 2001, before the military occupation, opium production was 74 tons per year. in 2006, the source is the us state department, opium production rose to over 6000 tons, a growth strongly linked to the military occupation. today, afghanistan produces 93% of the world's total opium. how much is the production of drugs worth in the global market today? the un, which unfortunately is not very credible on this subject, says that 1% of the world's gdp is derived from drug trafficking; the us state department says it's 2.5% and the european monitoring centre for drugs says that between 2 and 5% of the world's gdp is generated by international drug trafficking. and that's just a figure, because to that we add human trafficking, arms, waste, counterfeiting of products and all these profits are immediately recycled and put on the legal market. we must intervene on capital, assets and financial transactions, and that is why we believe that the confiscation of assets of the mafia, of transnational organized crime, is a central point in the fight we must wage against the mafia. pio la torre understood this and proposed a law to the italian parliament in which he said that action should be taken mainly on capital. that is why i support the report by mr newton dunn, because it deals with this point, where it is emphasized that we must intervene by attacking the capital of criminal and mafia organizations. a section of my group will not support this report, perhaps for understandable reasons, because it considers it to be lacking in safeguards, particularly on the processing of personal data. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. i think that the fight against organised crime is a priority, but it is not just a matter for the police. we must intervene in the cultural field, we must build a real social anti-mafia, which will take charge of the large pockets of social discomfort, unemployment and we must also intervene in the political field. in recent years, the mafia, transnational criminal organizations have infiltrated public administration and politics. it is not by chance, and i conclude on this, that the president of my region, for example, is being investigated for links with organised crime and the mafia. i would like to end by supporting the paragraph in the newton dunn report which calls for monitoring the activities of these administrations which are infiltrated by organised crime, by the mafia.

as we speak, it may have been done already. so, access to this information through the health portal will be made available to all citizens very soon, if it is not already available. the commission will support the creation of a european register on multiple sclerosis, which will mostly be based on the existing registers in some member states and expanded to include the other member states. more importantly – because we have to be practical as well –funds to support this initiative will be provided under the seventh framework programme. on other issues, of course, many pieces of legislation are already in place, such as the issue of discrimination and access to work. however, based on the outcome of the conference which will take place in the future, which i mentioned in my opening speech, and on the discussion with the stakeholders, we will see if there is also a need for new legislative initiatives and consider what steps have to be taken. we will then, of course, be ready to proceed with new initiatives. overall, as you know, we are dealing with inequality; it is a difficult issue. it was a priority of the uk presidency and has been taken over by the commission and the other presidencies as well. but we have to live within the realities – the existing legal and treaty realities of the european union, the issue of competences, how much the commission can oblige member states in certain areas of health. most is done through guidelines and recommendations. even under the proposed constitution as it stands, provision of health care remains the sole competence of the member states. so, we try to encourage, coordinate with and support the member states, and we will raise this issue with them whenever possible but, at the end of the day, this specific area of health care provision is the responsibility of the member states. that does not mean that we will not continue encouraging them to proceed, to follow the code that has been mentioned and to take other steps, but i believe that, through our health service initiatives (we will be presenting a proposal before the end of the year), we will be able to tackle some of these aspects and, of course, i will be happy to continue discussing these with you.
in writing. it is not easy to intervene in a debate on a disease that affects over 400,000 people in europe, with a new case every 4 hours. it is also not easy because ms, whose origins are still largely unknown, particularly affects young people, my peers, who, without warning, see their ambitions and dreams for the future and their daily life settings fall apart. but today there is a concrete and possible hope, linked to the great, encouraging, scientific research that day by day and laboriously takes new steps to identify the causes, mechanisms and remedies of the neurological collapse that is the consequence of multiple sclerosis. at this stage it is our main task to encourage, support and encourage research, including financial support, which must finally be free from conditions and from limitations and fears, often prejudiced and instrumental. at the same time, all the commitments made by the european commission in a 2003 resolution, in particular on the development of the 'code of best practice', must be respected. i also believe that it is the duty of the community institutions to promote and support the activities of all associations, such as aism in my country, which, with dedication and professionalism, carry out commendable work and provide effective help to people affected by multiple sclerosis and their families.

the agenda includes the report by mr dimitrios papadimoulis, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on the prohibition of the export and safe storage of metallic mercury (com (2006) 0636 c6-0363/2006 2006/0206 cod)) (a6-0227/2007).
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too would like to thank the rapporteur and the many colleagues who have been involved as shadow rapporteurs for their efforts and work on this very complex subject. but i want to be clear that no one is unaware of complexity. the differences between the various types of funds are obvious: the allocation, capitalisation, defined contribution and defined benefit funds, funds which are in fact company funds and funds managed through the accumulation of the resources of the contributions in the company's balance sheets. it is therefore difficult to find solutions that do not take account of this extreme articulation. however, it is also true that we should all have been more consistent in this matter. i am referring in particular to the council, which in my view is becoming a swamp that absorbs and suffocates all the efforts made by parliament to make balanced and coherent progress on social matters. this is the case, for example, with the working time directive and the directives adopted by parliament on the regulation of temporary employment agencies. we have made some progress where possible, even if we have to accept the inevitable logic of compromise, if not the guillotine, but we have not made any progress towards transferability. once again the matter is postponed. at this point we hope that the timid but positive steps taken to ensure that certain preconditions regarding minimum thresholds are met will not be overturned either, such as the conditions for the maturation of pension rights for workers in the second pillar, the conditions for the refund of contributions paid for workers leaving before the conditions for the acquisition of rights have matured and the conditions for the treatment of workers leaving who leave their contributions in the fund, since there is essentially a delay in the performance of the benefits, but there are already acquired rights relating to the equity of the latter. on these points, in some cases the minimum thresholds identified in the report are still critical or are being questioned. in future, much more will have to be done to address these problems, including ensuring that workers involved in mobility processes can at least be assured that they will not be discriminated against or penalized. however, i believe that any solution that falls below the thresholds would be so bad that a traumatic solution would be preferred by a vote against it in parliament. we hope that at least the compromise reached within these thresholds can be maintained in the relationship with the council.
on behalf of the its group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the right to free movement between the member states of the union in respect of supplementary pensions must not be restricted. neither the pension schemes of each state nor the conditions of acquisition may call into question the transferability of acquired rights. the european population is living longer on average and, as mrs oomen-ruijten rightly pointed out, supplementary pensions are becoming increasingly important throughout the union, particularly if we want to guarantee the living standards of the elderly population in the context of a european social model which, although it can be improved, remains a system that does not appear on any other continent. it is therefore essential to further improve the mechanisms for acquiring supplementary pensions and their transferability, without imagining anything less than what seems barely sufficient. in particular, it seems appropriate to extend the scope of application to all complementary collective schemes. i would personally have liked to see the principles of the report applied to invalidity and survivors' pensions. as regards the period of contribution required, i agree to the minimum period of five years for the right to acquire and to the other conditions laid down in the amendments governing that right. the conditions for the treatment of supplementary pension rights acquired by outgoing workers appear to be balanced, while i believe that further steps should be taken to improve the transferability of rights. in conclusion, we are living in a time when the states are trying to combine flexibility and labour mobility, which i think are excessive, with incentives to make social security more accessible. in this context, the concerns of young people about their future retirement and the very difficulty of maintaining a decent standard of living in old age should not only be repeatedly proclaimed but should be seriously addressed by the institutions, especially since it is shown that defined contribution pension schemes offer less guarantees of pensions commensurate with the cost of living. as the rapporteur and many colleagues have also said, labour mobility should be better rewarded, also and above all in terms of supplementary pension guarantees.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the money paid by workers for supplementary pensions is workers' money. the money paid by employers to their employees to make them better off in retirement is also workers' money. there should therefore be no problem in adopting a directive on the transferability of rights which are already workers' rights. mr mann, you say that this directive, as the commission has courageously put it, entails considerable costs for insurance funds and must therefore be rejected. i say that the higher the cost to pension funds, the greater the benefits to workers and the greater the number of workers who will join voluntary pension funds. in conclusion, i regret to say that once again the council is acting as a brake on the european union. since the agreement of all 27 eu member states is required, a negative vote in the council is sufficient to block a proposal. i wonder why we are still complaining that france and the netherlands voted against the constitution. we all want europe to move forward, but when it comes to actually meeting the expectations of the citizens towards us, we always take the worst position for the citizens and for the workers. it is clear that this is not the way forward.

the president of the council. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has not yet adopted a decision on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens. i would like to thank you very warmly, on behalf of the council presidency, for your contributions, your encouragement, but also for the initiatives taken so far on this very important subject and also for the admonitions expressed in some of your contributions. let me make two points. firstly, respect for human rights and international humanitarian law in the recipient countries must be in place in all cases before authorization can be granted. i made it clear that we are committed to human rights at various levels around the world. this has been a subject of discussion in this parliament on several occasions. the right to life, the prohibition of slavery, the right to political and social participation, equality before the law, freedom of speech and assembly and the prohibition of discrimination continue to be violated in too many countries of the world. it is therefore our duty to ensure that these violations of fundamental values are not encouraged by the supply of arms. secondly, there are the embargoes. the united nations security council, the oecd and the european union have imposed embargoes on a number of countries, and this draft european parliament resolution calls in particular for the embargo against sudan to be respected. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the arms trade agreement is implemented. it is not by chance that this criterion is placed at the very beginning of the code of conduct of the european union. i can assure you that as your presidency, we will continue to work for an effective arms trade treaty. the central role played by the european parliament in this debate is also a great help and support. i hope that we can continue to do so in this cooperative way in the presidencies that follow.
member of the commission. mr president, i thank parliament for its support, for its initiative and for its motion for a resolution. as i mentioned before, the commission, as part of wider eu efforts, strongly supports the opening of negotiations on a legally binding arms trade treaty, within the un framework – this is important to highlight. an international instrument promoting high standards of responsibility is clearly desirable and, for this enterprise to be successful, we need to build the broadest possible consensus and encourage all states to support this initiative. we would wish it to be a legally binding, separate and self-standing initiative that would cover all conventional arms transfers, set out the principles defining illegal transfers, include monitoring and be broadly based. we know that it will not be easy to persuade all suppliers worldwide, and it will therefore be very important for all the major arms producers to avoid having a situation such as we had with the icc or with the mine ban treaty. we will, therefore, seek the broadest possible consensus.

political stability, and – most importantly – advancing the development level of their country which remains one of the poorest in the world. for the international community, helping the transition of myanmar/burma towards a more open and more developed society – led by a legitimate and civilian government – should remain the paramount goal. the military leadership’s erratic governance continues, in economic terms and in the political sphere. the military continues to employ practices of forced labour, while civil society faces repression, uncertainty and operational difficulties. the ‘88 students’ – the then leaders of the 1988 uprising – continue to exploit the minimal space for civil society as much as they can, while the national league for democracy is marginalised and while the member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the green paper has created a good opportunity to discuss the need to improve labour law to meet the challenges of the 21st century. it has generated a huge amount of reactions from a wide range of stakeholders. these responses contain useful information on national legal systems and on the new challenges of the european labour market brought about by increased cross-border mobility and the wider scope of international business activities across the eu. the quality of the response to the green paper was astonishing. i believe it is the result of consultations and discussions between governments and some national parliaments, as well as the social partners and other stakeholders at both eu and national level. some of the issues raised during these public consultations have already been the subject of european parliament debates and resolutions. i congratulate the rapporteur, the political groups and the members of the european parliament for their contribution in the form of this own-initiative report. the report seeks to identify how the debate launched in the context of the green paper can be put into practice in the form of concrete measures that would gain wider support. in doing so, it fully recognises the competence of the member states in the field of labour law and their labour relations and the traditions and practices of collective bargaining. the debate highlighted the importance of labour law as a tool for addressing labour management issues in a rapidly changing world with high capital and technology mobility. labour law and collective bargaining are closely interlinked. labour law is the basis on which the social partners at all levels can negotiate compromise agreements on employment, lifelong learning opportunities, flexible working time arrangements and the organisation of labour markets, which would allow for easy transitions between jobs and from one type of contract to another. it is perhaps no surprise that the reactions of the social partners to the green paper also showed sharply contrasting views on how to proceed. sharp disagreements emerged in parliament's debate on this report, as well as in parallel debates at eu and national level, on the following points: the status of the standard contract for an indefinite period of full-time employment compared to new flexible forms of work and the emphasis on measures addressing labour market segmentation; the approach to be taken to non-standard employment contracts, some of which lack adequate guarantees of employment security; the cases are mainly those of multilateral employment relationships; very often flexibility is required without adequate employment protection and without a real chance of achieving genuine security in a more stable employment relationship; the focus of the green paper on individual employment relations raised doubts as to whether sufficient attention had been paid to the collective dimension of labour law and the contribution of social dialogue; it was argued that the commission should have confined this debate to the social partners at eu level and not opened it to a public debate involving eu institutions, member state governments and social partners at both eu and national level; there were also objections to the contribution that the eu can make to supporting labour law reform and the development of minimum social standards applicable to all forms of employment contracts. i believe that the report in principle supports: the view of flexibility and security as two mutually reinforcing factors contributing to productivity and quality of jobs; adopting a life-cycle approach to the development of employment security; providing basic protection to all workers, regardless of the type of contract they have signed; helping workers to change jobs quickly and sustainably; ensuring that efforts to modernise labour law are consistent with the improvement of legislation approach and with the reduction of excessive administrative burdens, in particular as regards compliance with legal requirements for small enterprises; proper enforcement of eu labour legislation and raising awareness among employers and workers of the minimum eu rules in force, in particular to combat undeclared work. we consider the principles of non-discrimination, equality between women and men, flexibility of working hours to reconcile work and family life, and opportunities for education and retraining to be the basic pillars of employment security, necessary for a smooth transition from one job to another and from one type of employment contract to another. the report recognises the difficulty of distinguishing between the categories of workers and self-employed today. there is concern that increased crossborder mobility may affect the consistent application of the community acquis. i agree with the positive interest of parliament in finding ways of tackling this problem, while respecting the right of member states to determine whether it is an employment relationship. i believe that the report also rightly emphasises the usefulness of the dialogue between the international labour organisation and the eu in this regard. we need to draw on the expertise of the ilo and learn from its efforts to establish basic labour standards in which flexibility and security can be successfully combined. the commission has the task of trying to assess the main themes and alternatives of this policy, which have emerged in a number of the replies received. this includes those recently presented in the european parliament's own-initiative report. ladies and gentlemen, i look forward to a debate on this highly sensitive and complex subject and hope that this debate will provide further impetus and result in the successful adoption of the report presented.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament is proving itself. the work done so far in the committee on employment and the economic and social committee has been of a good standard. it has broken out of the narrow band of ideological clashes and oppositions and has brought attention back to the real purpose of the green paper on employment policies and to the real possibility of designing innovation. globalization and demography are just two of the major challenges. sustainable development also requires changes in the organisation of work and the use of time. the most careful reflection shows that there is no such thing as time away from work, but time for personal life as well as family life; that it is wrong to identify the new frontier of social conflict between insider and outsider; that the relationship between flexibility and safety is ambiguous and involves the needs of employers and the needs of the people who work; the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the information provided by the member states.
on behalf of the alde group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, in congratulating myself on the work done, not only by the rapporteur but, i believe, by all the groups as a whole, which produced the text in question, voted by the committee on employment, i would like to try to clarify a point. i do not think that the text we have voted for is dominated by conservative and disappointing reflections. i believe that this text will help to break down all ideological resistance and barriers to the forms of flexibility in the employment relationship which today often not only exist but are a necessity in order to enable the european business system to respond to the competitive challenges which are posed to it in a more global sense. however, to protect these requirements, it is necessary to ensure that these forms of contract are genuinely concluded. a more flexible contract which is part-time, fixed-term, with temporary employment agencies responds to a need for flexibility in responding just in time to spikes in demand and production supply requirements, which exist in the competition of the labour market. it cannot be the wrong instrument for introducing forms of discrimination on the basis of costs and protections, which would turn the flexible contract into a kind of raft or shortcut for social dumping which has nothing to do with the requirements of competitiveness and which turns the challenge to competition into a challenge to cost competition only. i therefore believe that, while we affirm the need to accept the existence of these forms of contract and not to oppose them from an ideological point of view, we must also raise the level of specific protection and guarantee associated with these forms of flexible work. the rest is as follows: the primacy of collective regulation over individual derogations; in writing. the latest serious and most recent case of counterfeiting of a consumer good - a toothpaste containing an antifreeze, sold on the european market and produced in china - brings to the fore the problem of combating the 'multinational counterfeit'. it is in this large asian country, where de facto slavery is permitted for workers without any security, that the majority of the industry is concentrated in the counterfeiting of medicines, cosmetics and foodstuffs, as well as toys and clothing containing carcinogenic chemicals which are strictly prohibited in the european union. unfortunately, this phenomenon - which until a few years ago was limited to high-end products (creams, perfumes, watches and luxury bags) - is now spreading to products that are available to an increasing number of users, with a consequent high risk to consumer health. today more than ever it is necessary for the political and industrial west to take a firm stand against the powerful and wealthy china. on the one hand, we must strengthen the coordination of member states' inspection activities on imported products and, on the other hand, we must persuade the chinese government to apply extensive and very strict on-the-spot checks in order to protect the european industry from unfair competition, also due to counterfeiting and piracy.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in november 2006 the european commission adopted a working document, a first progress report on the strategy for simplifying the regulatory environment, followed by a further communication in october 2005. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the working document was approved by the legal affairs committee, which took stock of the progress made in implementing the simplification programme, which was launched in 2005, as i said. in particular, 43 refusal decisions are announced and i would like to give parliament this news, these figures: the commission has adopted 12 codifications, 8 repeals and 46 other substantial simplification measures, to which must be added 500 new legislative initiatives contained in another programme specifically modulated and dedicated to codifications, while 200 are already announced for 2007. i would therefore like to make a few comments on this point, which are the substance of my report, and of course very brief, to give parliament a real and concrete picture of the situation and the in-depth reflection of the legal affairs committee as a whole. i would like to make three strong points to the commission - and i think it is important to say and emphasize this - that: 1. to systematically include simplification initiatives in a specific part of the legislative and work programme in order to identify them specifically; 2. indicate at the same place the priority it intends to give to individual simplification initiatives; 3. avoid the proliferation of documents containing lists of simplification initiatives in order to have as precise a reference framework as possible. the commission must therefore - and i must stress this again - be consistent with itself and with the aims of the simplification it has highlighted and initiated. in particular, it is worth noting the desirability of recasting finally becoming the ordinary legislative technique. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. in this way, the entire text of the legislation is always available, even if it has been amended from time to time, with the new parts and the parts which have remained unchanged clearly indicated. this is a very important piece of legislation for parliament. the result would be the much-needed greater legibility and transparency of community legislation. the commission working document ultimately proposes to use the initial summaries of its proposals to explain better the objectives of simplification. however, the initiative may also prove counterproductive, and while a summary may be justified by a discursive text such as a communication, it is not so for a normative text, which in its initial summary may also find uncertainties and therefore we must be very careful and very precise about this. finally, the report highlights the strong signal given by the amendment of parliament's rules of procedure with regard to the improvement and introduction of the procedure provided for by the codification of article 80 and of a new ad hoc procedure for reconsiderations, article 80a. these are the questions which parliament must consider, i hope unitedly and as a whole without amendments, so that this can become an important point for the approval of parliament itself tomorrow.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great pleasure to see such an important report completed and fulfilled today. i would like to thank all the colleagues, the shadow rapporteurs, the groups and the officials who made this possible. the desire to reduce the harmful effects of alcohol consumption has become a priority in health and social policies worldwide in recent years, and the european union is also doing its part. the european commission has given us a text containing some very good ideas, and we have tried to develop them and add to them. the study of the damage caused by alcohol abuse has brought out a most dismal and disturbing picture: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union's energy policy. healthcare costs in europe amount to €17 billion, with €5 billion spent on treatment and prevention. it should be stressed that the problem arises from the abuse of alcoholic substances, while alcohol consumption cannot be demonized in itself, it is part of the culture, history and traditions of many european states and the quality of certain alcoholic products in many cases are the flagship of the producing countries. the employment aspect must not be forgotten either. it is estimated that more than one million people in europe are involved in the production and processing of alcohol. the european commission, which i thank, has presented a communication focusing on certain priorities, and we have welcomed it by seeking to broaden the scope of action through a number of key points: research into the phenomenon of youth consumption; dissemination of information, assistance and prevention at a cross-cutting level; strengthening public information campaigns, educating the community on the risks of irresponsible alcohol consumption; the commission will also be taking account of the phenomena of violence, especially domestic violence, linked to alcohol consumption. in particular, actions identified to counter the damage caused by abuse are: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be given the opportunity to discuss the matter with the council of ministers, and that the council should be given the opportunity to adopt a decision on the matter. another innovative aspect of the report, which was welcomed by the commission, is the idea of spreading a responsible and conscious approach to alcohol consumption through the so-called short intervention. gps, through their direct, daily contact with patients, can become a valuable tool in identifying the existence of alcohol-related problems even before the patient himself is aware of them: a simple questionnaire called audit, which is already being used on an experimental basis in some european cities, can help with this ad personam intervention. other measures include the promotion of measures to reduce road accidents caused by alcohol abuse, such as increased checks on drunk driving, the spread of tests to determine the alcohol content in the blood, the promotion of alternative driving programmes, the so-called shift driver, the lowering of blood alcohol limits and the tightening of penalties for drunk driving. the report proposes, and in this it seems to have the support of all the groups in the european parliament, a blood alcohol limit as close as possible to zero for newly-patented people, in order to give practical utility to the strategy beyond the mere appeal of principle and the caution expressed by the commission in its text, although many of the measures that could be taken to combat the damage of alcohol abuse fall within the competence of individual states, especially those concerning safety and health. the european union can seek to stimulate, encourage, promote and suggest the adoption of some of these measures. one of the points on which there was no agreement was certainly the issue of labelling the risks and dangers of excessive alcohol consumption. i personally think it is appropriate to ask the commission to carry out a thorough study to define the various information and communication systems, including labelling. in conclusion, the strategy, as amended by parliament, will bring substantial added value compared to individual national policies, especially as it will have the power to direct the action of the member states towards common objectives. in the text of the report i have tried above all to treat the subject with the necessary balance and common sense, avoiding demonizing moderate alcohol consumption, even in keeping with the millenary tradition of good drinking, but trying to suggest useful measures to reduce the negative phenomena, which unfortunately are now more and more frequent in the european and world context. i would like to thank everyone for their support and cooperation.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by congratulating mr foglietta on his excellent report, which deals very effectively with a dramatic and topical subject, namely the abuse of alcohol, particularly by minors. it has already been said, and this is certainly not a question of criminalizing the consumption of alcohol, which, when taken in moderation, can also be beneficial to health. it is a matter of strongly denouncing the spread of alcohol consumption by the very young. alcohol is often consumed with drugs or alcohol itself, which eventually becomes a drug in its own right. alcohol abuse is now a social emergency among young people because it causes very serious physical and psychological damage, to which unfortunately must be added the increasing number of road casualties caused by drunk drivers. unfortunately, italy has the highest number of car accidents in europe, and half of the victims are young people under the age of 30. most of the time they die on the weekends, in the evening, at night, many coming home from a party, from the disco where they've had too much alcohol. i would like to conclude, mr president, by saying that this report is a good one, an excellent one, and that we share its line in that it has been able to reconcile the prevention of the phenomenon with appropriate interventions in terms of education and communication and with zero tolerance for those who do not respect the rules.
author of the book. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the fact that we have postponed this debate from july to september, and that we are doing so in the circumstances in which we are doing so, with the council absent from the issues we wish to raise, is a clear indication of how unprepared europe is in fact to deal with the problem of terrorism in a comprehensive and forceful manner and how this parliament is unfortunately still too weak politically. there used to be terrorist groups in the various countries of the union, internal problems, europe was already largely united and even then there was talk of a common strategy which never came into being. we have arrived at 2001 which has shown how terrorism is global, and it is not a pyramidal organization but of cells connected to each other mainly through the internet and the best computer systems, rooted all over the world and able to strike as they want and when they want. however, there is no eu policy to control the internet and to give certain rules of security to citizens, who do not understand what measures the union has taken and what it intends to take in the short term. first of all, to hold accountable the providers who host sites that foment, support and justify terrorist acts, for example by compulsory blocking of sites that are directly or indirectly linked to people who preach, incite and justify violence. switzerland has done this for a long time, but europe is still wavering and thinking in vain. there is no common position on monitoring false places of worship, false imams, who, as recently happened in the netherlands and italy, have used places of worship to sow hatred, to plan attacks inciting violence against the west, democracy, human rights, including those of women, and even to carry out terrorist attacks in our cities. it is no longer enough, mr president, to talk about a common strategy against terrorism; what is needed is the strength and courage to take decisions, to act with the aim, on the one hand, of preventing future attacks and, on the other, of rendering harmless the terrorist cells that are nesting and proselytizing, using our values of freedom, freedom of worship and freedom of expression, to act precisely against freedom. the arrests in denmark of people suspected of planning an attack with explosives in the last few hours are proof that this is no time to let down our guard and that the anti-terrorism laws passed by denmark are working, but they also sound an alarm for the whole union: we cannot rely solely on the effectiveness of national laws and the efficiency of the investigative forces in individual countries, we need more coordination. political correctness is too often concealed by the inability or unwillingness to make decisions. democracy, freedom and the right of individuals to live in peace and freedom are at stake! freedom is guaranteed by the rules! we must do what is politically right to safeguard not only our own peoples but those throughout the world who have their rights respected and who are aware of their duties. every delay makes us accomplices! let us come out of this debate with a common commitment to immediate achievement and not with supposed positions of right or left, but strong and united. this will be the best tribute to the memory of the lives that since 9/11 have been taken by barbarism around the world. for each of us, terrorism is and always will be a crime against humanity.
author of the book. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we often say that the fight against terrorism is a priority and new legislative political initiatives are called for. i think we should first assess the choices made over the years by asking ourselves a few questions. firstly, is terrorism stronger or weaker as a result of our legislative initiatives? the second: we have made a decisive member of the commission. madam president, i appreciated the exchange of views on the report, which testify the commitment of parliament to the cause of human rights. inspired by the debate, i would like to convey the commission’s comments on the recommendations for increased transparency of the dialogue and involvement of the european parliament and of civil society organisations in all aspects of dialogue and consultation a point a number of interventions have referred to. while some of the report’s recommendations are already becoming part of normal practice, such as those concerning briefings and debriefings, the three institutions should carefully consider the different suggestions and find solutions, while taking into account the eu legal framework and the arrangements between parliament and the commission, which are foreseen in the framework agreement of may 2005. in doing so, we should be pragmatic. on one hand, this means not hiding behind regulations and ‘business-as-usual’ excuses, and, on the other hand, carefully evaluating the political opportunity and the consequences of increased transparency on the effectiveness of the dialogue and the readiness of third countries to engage in the dialogue in the first place. the impact on the actual dialogue and on relations with third countries should be carefully weighed, to avoid depriving the european union of an effective instrument. in all cases, i am confident that we will be able to find the appropriate arrangements to both satisfy the need for information and to preserve and increase the effectiveness of the instrument. on the issue raised on including human rights in trade and sectoral agreements, the commission considers that there is no need to replicate the human rights clause contained in the association agreement, partnership and cooperation agreement or sectoral agreements. the absence of such a clause in sectoral agreements does not prevent us from carrying out human rights consultations with the country in question or to use any other of the instruments of the european union human rights toolbox. on the subject of cooperation programmes for democracy and human rights, the commission would like to remind parliament that the new instrument, the european initiative for democracy and human rights, foresees specific funds for projects in difficult countries such as cuba and burma/myanmar, mentioned in this debate. on the issue of the universality of human rights, let me emphasise that the european union subscribes to the principle of the universality, indivisibility, interdependency and interrelation of all human rights. according to this principle, proclaimed by the world conference on human rights in vienna, human rights are dealt with globally in a fair and equal manner on the same footing and with the same emphasis. of course, this does not exclude the fact that, in a session, a particular set of rights receives more attention because of events on the ground or because of the readiness of our dialogue partners to address certain issues instead of others. the commission is particularly pleased to see that the report devotes several recommendations to women’s rights and to their inclusion in dialogues. we should also not forget other sets of rights and groups that deserve attention. on the question of electoral observer missions, the commission agrees that political dialogue, and in particular human rights dialogue, offers the opportunity to plead with partner countries for the follow-up to eu electoral observer missions’ recommendations. in that context, the commission has also advocated the continuous engagement of the european union head of missions. this follow-up should focus on actions by the political and electoral authorities concerned and on an active role for civil society and democracy promotion, including electoral reform. the commission is not convinced of the need to put in place a specific and separate post-electoral protocol mechanism for that purpose. the commission takes the view that assistance, dialogue instruments and monitoring mechanisms exist, in order to ensure post-electoral strategies and democracy support, and these mechanisms should continue to be used. with regard to the specific question by mr van orden, i will convey his concern and question to commissioner ferrero-waldner, who do doubt will provide you with an answer. to conclude, let me state that i have taken note of the many other specific comments made on particular situations. i assure you that such comments will be forwarded to commissioner ferrero-waldner, who will certainly give them due consideration.

acting president of the council. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the european union continues to face significant challenges in responding to the changing situation in the area of migration. the comprehensive approach to migration adopted by the european council in december 2005 remains the essential framework for defining responses to these challenges. in adopting the comprehensive approach, the european council stressed the need for a balanced, comprehensive and coherent approach covering policies to combat illegal immigration and, in cooperation with third states, to enhance the benefits of legal immigration. the implementation of the global approach has been a key priority of successive presidencies. the overall approach to migration has not remained static, but has been refined and developed by the european council in the light of developments and progress in its implementation, and is integrated into the overall migration policy of the european union. at its meeting on 21 and 22 june, the european council endorsed conclusions on enlargement and the strengthening of the global approach. these conclusions provide in particular for the application of the global approach to the border regions to the east and south-east of the union and for the development of partnerships between the european union and third countries in the field of so-called circular migration and mobility. the importance of implementing the global approach was underlined by events during the summer and, in particular, by the incidents at the southern maritime borders of the union. continuing to apply the comprehensive approach, the measures to be taken should encompass both measures to combat illegal immigration and to develop opportunities for legal immigration. the council has made efforts to pursue these two inseparable objectives. at its june meeting the council discussed the situation at the southern mediterranean borders. the council reaffirmed the importance of the role to be played by frontex and decided to carry out further work in the light of suggestions made by malta. this work was carried out and led to the adoption of council conclusions on strengthening the management of the union's southern maritime borders at the council meeting on 18 september. some of these conclusions imply urgent action which is oriented towards existing measures and possibilities. member states are encouraged to provide support on a bilateral basis to member states facing particular pressure in terms of illegal immigration due to their geographical situation and the degree of cooperation with neighbouring third countries. this cooperation will focus, for example, on return operations, reception conditions, responsibilities for asylum seekers, refugees and minors. the conclusions also stress the need to strengthen cooperation in this area with third countries of origin and transit, in particular with regard to the management of their own borders, the commitment to assume their responsibilities in search and rescue operations, the fight against trafficking and smuggling of human beings and the creation of an effective framework for returns. the need for close cooperation with international organisations such as unhcr and iom is emphasised. another important element is the intention to strengthen frontex's activities, in particular by creating longer-term joint operations and extending activities within the framework of the european patrol network. as regards longer-term measures, the council invited the commission to submit to it a report on possible additional measures, including an in-depth analysis of certain proposals submitted by malta, a study of the relevant parts of the law of the sea and to consider the establishment of specialised teams on asylum in the context of the ongoing debate on the commission's green paper on the common european asylum system. frontex plays an increasingly important role in the effectiveness of member states' control of the external borders of the union. frontex, as you know, only started its operational activities in october 2005, but in the relatively short time since then it has developed its operational capabilities and implemented important initiatives to strengthen the security of the external borders of the european union, focusing in particular on the fight against illegal immigration. several joint operations coordinated by frontex have been carried out and others are under way in the atlantic and the mediterranean. of particular importance was the launch in may of this year of the european patrol network which, in the long term, will integrate the future european surveillance system. another significant development was the adoption by the council in july of this year and the entry into force on 20 august of the regulation on the mechanism for the creation of rapid border intervention teams, the so-called rabbit. the regulation allows for the provision of rapid operational assistance for a limited period of time to a member state which requests it in the face of an urgent and exceptional pressure situation, in particular due to the arrival of a large number of third-country nationals at external border crossing points in order to enter the european union illegally. frontex is currently in the process of implementing this regulation. the availability of appropriate equipment is of paramount importance for the effectiveness of the activities coordinated by frontex. frontex, in accordance with the frontex regulation, has set up a centralised register of available technical equipment, called crate. this register already contains an extensive list of helicopters, aircraft, vessels and other equipment that member states are willing to make available for the purposes of activities coordinated by frontex. in terms of legislative measures to combat illegal immigration, the competent council bodies have already started to examine the proposal for a parliament and council directive laying down sanctions against employers of illegally staying third-country nationals. this proposal, which aims to combat illegal work as a factor of attraction for illegal immigration, was presented by the commission in may 2007. in the context of the co-decision procedure and with a view to reaching an agreement quickly, the council also attaches high priority to the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on common rules and procedures in member states for returning illegally staying third-country nationals, which is currently being examined by the competent council bodies. in the context of readmission policy, it should be noted that following the entry into force in june of the readmission agreement with russia, the decision on the signing of the readmission agreement with ukraine has already been adopted and a number of readmission agreements have been signed with the western balkan states and moldova. all these agreements will be concluded after the european parliament has delivered its opinion. a few words about the action programme on legal immigration. as is well known, the council and the portuguese presidency also give priority to the promotion of legal immigration. a high-level conference on legal immigration was organised in lisbon on 13 and 14 september by the presidency and brought together ministers, senior officials and academics, as well as representatives of this parliament and the commission. this conference addressed issues related to legal immigration, such as channels of legal immigration and management of migration flows, integration and the lisbon agenda, and migration and development. the results of this conference will provide a very important guide for our work in the months ahead. the council will also shortly begin work on the proposals for a framework directive on the rights of migrants legally residing in a member state to pursue an economic activity and creating a single residence permit and a directive on the conditions of entry and residence of highly qualified workers which we hope the commission will present in the coming weeks. these two proposals, together with others to be presented over the next few years, follow on from the action plan on legal immigration presented by the commission in january 2006. the council has already started to examine the proposal for a council directive amending directive 2003/109 in order to extend its scope to beneficiaries of international protection. the proposal is designed to extend the possibility of obtaining long-term resident status to beneficiaries of international protection. the council is awaiting parliament's opinion in order to adopt the draft instrument as soon as possible. on external relations in the area of migration, i would like to inform you that the council has actively pursued the implementation of the comprehensive approach to migration also defined by the european council in its conclusions of december 2005 and 2006. attention was also drawn to the conclusions on enlargement and strengthening the global approach to migration adopted by the council in june. in december 2006, the european council invited the commission to make proposals on how to apply the comprehensive approach to the regions bordering the eastern and south-eastern borders of the european union, to propose ways to integrate legal immigration opportunities into the union's external policies in order to develop a balanced partnership with third countries adapted to the specific labour market needs of the member states, and to suggest ways and means to facilitate circular and temporary migration, and to make detailed proposals on how best to organise and provide information on the various forms of legal movement between the european union and third countries. the commission submitted two communications in response to these calls and the presidency, following the adoption of these commission communications, submitted draft conclusions to the council to take forward work on the actions envisaged by the commission. the euromed ministerial meeting on migration will be held in november this year. the conference aims to develop initiatives and actions to implement migration-related issues. in addition, special attention was also given to africa by continuing and intensifying the dialogue on migration-related issues initiated in 2005 with african countries. priority was also given to the follow-up to the ministerial conferences on migration and development held in rabat in july 2006 and tripoli in november 2006. the ministerial conferences, the first at regional level and the second at continental level, identified a number of areas where cooperation between the countries of origin, transit and destination of migrants could be strengthened. the council is actively working on this matter with a view to translating into concrete action the joint programmes agreed in rabat and tripoli.
