response to these reports. this was the most appropriate course to follow in the spirit of the principle of subsidiarity. as you know, in many areas investigated by the commission, the european union has no power of action on its own. i am thinking here in particular of the supervision of the intelligence services. this is a fact to which the previous presidencies of the council and the high representative xavier solana have drawn the attention of your parliament and the parliamentary committee. they may, of course, regret that this is the case, but the fact is that the treaties in force limit the scope of the council's action in these areas. however, i can assure you that the portuguese presidency will continue to cooperate actively and constructively. i would remind the house of the full and transparent cooperation of the portuguese government, both during the investigations carried out by the temporary committee of parliament, which concluded its work in february of this year, and in the framework of the initiatives of the secretary-general of the council of europe, under article 52 of the european convention on human rights, concerning the alleged cia flights and illegal detention centres in europe. as is well known, although the council does not take a position as such on the reports by mr claudio fava and mr dick marty, under the auspices of this parliament and the council of europe respectively, this does not mean that it ignores them. in fact, the council has been an active and positive defender of human rights and international law in the european union's foreign policy. we have consistently argued that the protection of the fundamental values of international law requires a serious and in-depth dialogue on human rights in the context of the fight against terrorism. in this context, the union has stressed that human rights, the rights of refugees and international humanitarian law must be respected and must be preserved. the council will continue to monitor closely developments in the fight against terrorism in the field of human rights and will take appropriate measures to protect them. the union remains firmly committed to the total prohibition of torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment or punishment. we are guided by this objective and we constantly raise our concerns about this problem with third countries. the union and its member states have been pointing out that the existence of possible secret detention centres where detainees are held in a legal vacuum is not in line with international humanitarian law. the union guidelines on torture clearly stipulate that states must ban secret places of detention by ensuring that all persons deprived of their liberty are held in officially recognised places of detention and that their whereabouts are known. the eu directives on torture also require that no one be forced to return to a country where he or she is at risk of being subjected to torture or ill-treatment. it is common knowledge that the matters in question, which concern airport control, surveillance and information services, are essentially the responsibility and control of the member states. it is true that sitcen periodically analyses information provided by states, but it has no operational jurisdiction over so-called 'intelligence' activities. it should be noted that the member states of the union were equally confronted with the complexity which, for this purpose, characterises the system for sorting and processing applications for authorisation to fly over, land and inspect 'on the ground'. this is a new challenge for all of us. for our part, the portuguese government has not only carried out this sometimes difficult and very time-consuming collection of information, but has also set up a working group to evaluate the many procedures and to propose improvements, the importance of which was duly recognised by the final report adopted by this parliament in february. it should be noted that we attach particular importance to the work carried out by the secretary general of the council of europe and we take note of the reports by mr dick marty. the questionnaire and recommendations made by the secretary-general of the council of europe in the context of article 52 of the european convention on human rights have also enabled, both in portugal and, i believe, in the other member states, an unprecedented assessment of the national legal frameworks, safeguards and control mechanisms as a whole, including the analysis of the procedures for the screening, verification and control of applications for permission to fly over and land aircraft on national territory. in the case of portugal, it has certainly allowed improvements to be made at institutional, technical and operational level. as regards the recommendations of the secretary-general of the council of europe on safeguards for control, the dominant view of its members was that the initiatives under way should not involve unnecessary legislative duplication or the conferral of new powers on the council of europe. on the other hand, there seems to be a consensus that there is room for more effective implementation and more scrupulous monitoring of existing mechanisms. i believe that the more rigorously and calmly these investigations are carried out, the more effective their conclusions will be. although it is always advisable to be rigorous, not to confuse facts with allegations and to seek some restraint in language given the importance of the values involved and the good name of european democracies, the truth is that all these initiatives have scope and meaning. they must therefore be pursued, especially at a time when it has become imperative to analyse in a serious and uncomplicated way the new dilemmas, for example, security versus freedoms, posed by the terrorist threats. on the other hand, there is a growing need for an international law response to the difficult questions raised by the fight against an unprecedented threat. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the consolidation of the area of freedom, security and justice, on the basis of the hague programme and the action plan, is one of the main priorities of the 18-month joint programme of the german, portuguese and slovenian presidencies. the fight against terrorism is one of the major challenges in this context, and the three presidencies set themselves the objective of intensifying cooperation in this area and continuing to implement the european union's counter-terrorism strategy. as you know, the new european union counter-terrorism coordinator, mr gilles de kerchove, has recently been appointed and will be at the disposal of this house, as his predecessors were, for any clarification he may require. i would also like to take this opportunity to stress that the issue of respect for human rights in the fight against terrorism has been particularly covered in the context of the transatlantic dialogue, as happened, moreover, at the last summit between the european union and the united states last april, recalling, moreover, the conclusions of the european council of 11 december 2006. portugal, as the presidency of the european union, has shown its commitment to the continuation and deepening of this dialogue, which it considers to be key for both sides.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too thank the council representative. the commission, and i myself, have accompanied and supported the work of the temporary committee of this european parliament on the well-known matter and the serious allegations and facts which have been pointed out. it is clear that the seriousness of these events, and the mere fact that these activities have taken place, requires cooperation between all the institutions, between the commission, parliament and the council. and it is clear that we are reiterating once again - and i am happy to do so - that the fight against terrorism must be conducted in full respect for fundamental rights and the rule of law, which are the two conditions for a functioning democracy. i believe that in this spirit the illegal transfers of prisoners, the hypothesis that there have been more or less secret places of detention, are certainly facts which, if proven in the appropriate forms, would certainly constitute a serious violation of the rules of international law and of the fundamental rights of persons. everyone knows that the members of the european union are all bound to respect the great principles of the convention on human rights, in particular articles 5 and 6. it is clear that we want thorough investigations into these events to be carried out in the member states and it is clear that these investigations must be carried out by the competent judicial authorities. one point must be clear, but it has been made clear many times, both by the rapporteur mr fava and by the report of the council of europe. a parliamentary report may provide some information, but parliament certainly has neither the power nor the duty to undertake a judicial inquiry. and when, of course, sources are cited as evidence that remain unknown, it is obvious that the rule of law, the very rule of law that we must respect, requires investigations to be carried out by free and independent judges, who, on the other hand, have the duty to reveal the sources on the basis of which an accusation is made. it is clear that to accuse a member state or to accuse a person without revealing the sources of this accusation is a principle which may be included in a report of a parliament, but which cannot be included in a judicial inquiry. that is why i hope that the judicial investigations will continue, as is happening in some member states, including my own country. but it is clear that the report needs to be followed up, and i can therefore list the initiatives which i believe will help to follow up this report. i wrote to the governments of poland and romania on 23 july last, asking them - recalling the obligation of a full and thorough investigation - for detailed information on how the investigations had been initiated and what the outcome of the investigations was. i hope that both governments will respond to me and of course i will inform you of the answers of both governments, precisely because i believe that it is first and foremost in the transparent interest of the truth that an accusation against you has all the instruments of the system to explain that the accusation is not true, to prove that it is not true, or to entrust the investigation to independent magistrates. it is the interest of the accused that requires, in my view, a very clear answer. the second point: i have prepared a questionnaire for all the member states. i spoke about this in the last plenary session, which was devoted to terrorism. i have prepared a questionnaire in which we ask each member state what measures it has taken to combat terrorism, what results it has achieved in terms of the effectiveness of national laws and in particular what level of protection of the fundamental rights of individuals is in national legislation. my intention is to analyse the responses and then prepare a report for the council and parliament on the effectiveness of the member states' counter-terrorism measures and their adequacy and compatibility with the principles of respect for fundamental rights. the third point concerns air traffic. i had a commitment with the libe committee and it was a commitment to look at a very important legal aspect which is currently lacking: what are the boundaries between the definition of civil aircraft and state aircraft, i.e. aircraft exempt from those ordinary civil aircraft controls? the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to take them up. this communication will be adopted by the college before the end of this year, so very soon, and we will of course make a proposal to define this concept of state aircraft better, which often lends itself to interpretations which obviously escape the controls which are, on the contrary, necessary. but there is another initiative that is specifically about air traffic. in the framework of a general solution introducing common rules for all member states for all types of aeroplane entering the european common space without flight plans. you are certainly aware that from 1 january 2009 the rules for the application of the so-called single european sky will introduce common requirements for flight plans for all the member states and that within this framework we will therefore harmonise the rules on the flight plan of every aircraft that in any case crosses or enters european airspace. this will bring enormous benefits because it will eliminate the differences in treatment of over-flight and landing in the member states which we have now, to some extent, observed. the other issue is the ratification of the extradition agreement between europe and the united states. if there were, as there should already be, a european agreement which we have signed but which has not yet been ratified, the rules on the extradition of prisoners to and from the united states - and we are talking about prisoners under investigation or suspected of terrorism - would be much clearer. this agreement has yet to be ratified by some member states, fortunately a few. i have repeated a formal appeal to all the ministers of justice to have this european extradition agreement with the united states ratified as soon as possible. again, the issue of control of the intelligence services. this is a theme raised in both reports, but it is a sensitive one. i believe that the national response is what counts here first, but i believe that some common needs can be highlighted. the first requirement is to strengthen parliamentary control in the member states. there are member states which have adopted or are adopting national laws which greatly strengthen the power of national parliaments to scrutinise the activities of the services in each country. that, in my view, is the way forward, because as you will understand, i do not see a common european law regulating the secret services in the future, but i think that a discussion on this subject is particularly useful. in conclusion, mr president, i think this is a subject on which we must continue to debate, taking the rule of law as a principle, respect for fundamental rights, of course, but also the right not to be heard and not to be accused, unless on the basis of evidence which has been properly and procedurally gathered.
i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in the negotiations, but that it should be involved in the negotiations. it is a pity, because at least on issues such as terrorism and human rights, this house should be able to overcome its internal divisions and produce a common position. if we have not succeeded, it is because the fava report unfortunately started with a preconceived idea: the united states is guilty! so we have wasted a year not in seeking the truth, but in seeking the evidence of this guilt, omitting and even concealing any element that would contradict this thesis. i will give one concrete example and i dare say it is outrageous: we also went to poland to interview a journalist who a year earlier had been one of the first to report on the existence of cia prisons in poland. when we saw him, unfortunately, and i regret to say this ironically, he changed his mind: he no longer had those certainties: he told us he wasn't going to write that article today! the report contains no indication of his having reconsidered his position, but it is full of testimonies from journalists who agree with the rapporteur's position. we have wasted a useless year, spending taxpayers' money and finding nothing new compared to what we already knew from newspapers and official and unofficial american sources. and if it hadn't been for president bush revealing the existence of the cia prisons, we wouldn't even have this certainty. you, commissioner frattini, tell us that you wrote a letter to poland and romania asking for an explanation and that you have not received a reply. it's always rude not to answer, but it doesn't surprise me, because the complaints are not proven. you yourself, in your letter, speak of probable information, not concrete facts. and both countries have already told the highest levels that they have investigated and that in their opinion there are no cia prisons. it may be true or not, everyone can think what they want, but we cannot, as you yourself have said, commissioner frattini, accuse until there is evidence. the fact is that the fava and marty reports are too full of phrases like "it's very likely", "it can't be ruled out", from which then certain conclusions are drawn. and don't tell me to justify the lack of evidence that we're not a court and that ours is a political document. but then it is no longer political when it is asked to consider whether or not there are extremes to invoke article 7 of the treaty on union. i have to say that i am not in favour of the commission's proposal. let us stop producing biased interpretations of the past, let us stop investigating this subject on which we have found nothing! let us leave it to the judges - as commissioner frattini said - and to the journalists who have the means to do it and can do it better than us. let us concentrate on the future, on the policy, on the propositional part which is the only acceptable part of the fava report. the united states has certainly made mistakes, in some cases it has violated human rights, but it is very easy not to make mistakes when you do nothing to fight terrorism. terrorism is a new phenomenon, our laws did not cover it, today the law must adapt. we are trying to establish rules of conduct to prevent further human rights violations, to prevent the mistakes of the past from being repeated and to adapt our instruments to a new kind of global threat. the commission should therefore try to make an overall assessment of the measures taken by the member states. i am not sure that the commissioner has been able to give us a clear answer to this question. much remains to be done to tackle the problem of terrorism in a global, strong and coordinated way. i'm thinking about the internet or crime prevention and prosecution measures, to avoid a paradoxical situation whereby while governments work separately at the national level, terrorists instead act globally via the internet and their cells rooted pretty much everywhere. our future depends on our ability to defeat terrorism. let's unite to win this battle too.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, other members will repeat this in the debate that follows, but i think it is appropriate to stress - also in view of the next summit - that a european citizen is anyone who has the nationality of a member state in accordance with national law. it is therefore the case for anyone who enjoys the rights conferred by that status, first and foremost the right to vote and to be elected as a member of the european parliament. for whom have we been working for years when we talk about the right to freedom of movement, to education, to health, to work, to dignity, if not for the citizens who democratically elected us? i think it is equally important to maintain mutual respect between the member states: the european parliament has been a major player in the debate on the future of the european union. linguistically, it has already been violated countless times. the lamassoure-severin proposal is now designed to eliminate this equality of political weight. if that is the basic approach, then let us not be too surprised that it is so difficult to reach an agreement to define a future together. the european summit will therefore reflect in depth on the concepts of european citizenship and democratic legitimacy.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the report on the composition of the seats in parliament contains obvious contradictions, reinforced by the letter that the rapporteurs sent yesterday, as if to justify their position, on such politically sensitive matters, and it distorts the legal concept of citizenship as it has always been codified. the principle proposed in the report goes beyond national states and the treaties. from a legal point of view, european citizenship is the legal status of those and only those who are nationals of a member state and who therefore enjoy all the rights and obligations attaching to that status. and it is citizenship, not residency, that should be the text. this proposal also distorts the approach set out in the draft of the next treaty, which clearly states that the concept of citizenship has nothing to do with residence. the european parliament has missed a great opportunity to demonstrate to the other institutions that it is capable of finding solutions within itself based on recognised and shared legal principles. i ask the rapporteurs why the possibility of using the criterion of the number of nationals of member states instead of the resident population as a criterion for allocating seats has not even been considered. perhaps to give some an advantage over others? in writing. as rapporteur on the fight against fraud in the eu, i welcome the important agreement with philip morris to combat cigarette smuggling at customs. customs fraud is one of the main sources of damage to the community's financial interests, and cigarettes are one of the most vulnerable sectors. recent olaf operations - such as operation diabolo (135 million cigarettes seized, estimated value of eur 220 million) - have shown that customs fraud can and must be tackled: it is important to strengthen the operational capacity of the european authorities. the agreement with philip morris can serve as an example not only in the tobacco sector but also in other areas of the fight against counterfeiting. the proceeds of the compensation owed by philip morris, some eur 1 billion, should be used to strengthen the fight against counterfeiting in the eu.

of the capital requirements directive and ongoing work on the solvency ii directive, we must remain vigilant, particularly in the light of the rapid evolution of innovation in financial products. the recent financial turmoil has thus made more urgent some of the issues already on the council's agenda and has made clear the need for the european union to look together with its international partners for ways to enhance transparency, improve valuation processes, continue to strengthen risk management and improve the functioning of the market, in particular with regard to complex financial products. the ecofin council of 9 october agreed on a detailed work programme to be developed by the relevant bodies at eu level, in close cooperation with the main international partners, by the end of 2008. at the same ecofin council meeting in october, conclusions were also adopted on strengthening financial stability mechanisms in the european union. those conclusions are available on the council's website. this is the visible result of more than a year of preparation. in particular, the council adopted a set of common principles guiding cooperation between national authorities in the field of financial stability. in addition, it was agreed to extend the memorandum of understanding on cooperation and exchange of information signed in 2005 between banking supervisory authorities, central banks and ministries of finance to include three new elements. first, the common principles formally adopted at the meeting. second, the common analytical framework for assessing the potential systemic implications of a possible crisis. thirdly, common practical guidelines on the procedures to be followed in potential crises, crisis situations, cross-border. a work programme was also drawn up setting out the timetable for this and other actions to be developed with a view to enhancing the effectiveness of financial stability mechanisms in the european union. all this work is obviously aimed at protecting consumers and investors who depend on the smooth functioning of financial markets. let me conclude by stressing that i believe the council, together with the european parliament and the commission, subscribes to the objective of ensuring effective levels of prudential supervision and regulation with a view to ensuring financial stability, global competitiveness and the protection of consumer interests.

on behalf of the uen group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the issue raised by mr cappato's report is extremely sensitive and requires careful consideration by the european parliament to avoid proposing, even with good intentions, wrong and disastrous solutions. i would like to emphasize two points: first, the growing production of opium and opium products in afghanistan is likely to undermine the reconstruction of the country and the already difficult establishment of the rule of law in that unfortunate region. secondly, the growing opium production - which has increased by 30% this year - has not been matched by an adequate strategy to combat drugs. for these reasons i find the proposal in the report totally unacceptable and i would stress that: 1. the necessary quantities of morphine are already being produced in afghanistan under specific licences and under the control of the united nations agency and the afghan government's ministry of drug control; 2. the international narcotics control board, an international drug control body, argues that there is already a worldwide surplus of opiate products for medical use; 3. large-scale legal production of morphine would result in further production of the drug which would eventually cross demand from the world drug market and be cheaply marketed and accessible to all. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat drug abuse, and i am sure that the commission will take them into account in its proposals for action. in a country like afghanistan, in the conditions in which it finds itself today, the solution proposed by this report could be seen as a sign of surrender and defeat and could also undermine the commitment that the international community, the european union, the united nations, the reconstruction agencies are promoting in afghanistan through programmes to diversify opium plantations into agricultural production supported by financial incentives. i would just like to conclude by saying that the international narcotics control board has agreed to the accession of the afghan government, which has rejected the proposal to legalise the illegal cultivation of opium and has reiterated its commitment to comply with the obligations of the treaty.

ombudsman. madam president, i would like to thank the honourable members for this opportunity to address parliament on my annual report for 2006. i also wish to thank the rapporteur, ms sbarbati, and the committee on petitions, for their excellent report. my report records progress in handling complaints, promoting good administration and providing knowledge about the ombudsman’s role. i received 3 830 complaints in 2006. that means that the total number of complaints has stabilised at around the level reached following the 53% increase in 2004. i am delighted to inform you that the proportion of complaints falling within the mandate has gone up. this suggests that citizens are beginning to have a better knowledge both of my mandate and of that of my national and regional colleagues in the european network of ombudsmen, which is thus commensurately strengthened to the benefit of all concerned. the total number of inquiries dealt with in 2006 was 586. of these, 66% concerned the commission. given that the commission is the eu institution with which citizens have most reason to have material contact, it is normal that it should be the principal target of inquiries. during 2006, 250 decisions closing inquiries were made. in 95 cases, the inquiry revealed no maladministration. such a finding is not always negative for the complainant, who at least has the benefit of a full explanation from the institution concerned. even when maladministration is not found, i may identify opportunities to improve the quality of administration provided by the institutions. if so, i point them out in a further remark. many of my inquiries result in a win-win outcome that satisfies both the complainant and the institution complained against. during 2006, 64 cases were settled by the institution concerned to the satisfaction of the complainant. whenever i find maladministration, i try to achieve a friendly solution, if possible. three friendly solutions were achieved in 2006 and a further 27 proposals for such a solution were under consideration by the institution concerned at the end of the year. when a friendly solution is not possible, i close the case with a critical remark, or make a draft recommendation. a critical remark is appropriate if it is no longer possible for the institution concerned to eliminate the instance of maladministration. i wish to emphasise that the criticism is intended to be constructive, so as to help avoid similar maladministration in the future. in 2006, i closed 41 inquiries in this way. to better monitor the impact of my criticism and advice, i have this year launched a study of the follow-up to all critical remarks made in 2006, as well as to the 38 cases involving a further remark made during the same year. the results of these studies should provide further encouragement to the institutions concerned to improve their practices and develop a culture of service to citizens. in cases where it is still possible to eliminate the instance of maladministration, i normally make a draft recommendation to the institution, which must respond with a detailed opinion. during 2006, 13 draft recommendations were made. if an institution fails to respond satisfactorily to a draft recommendation, i may send a special report to the european parliament. two special reports were made in 2006. the first concerned the council’s responsibility for the choice of languages used in its presidency websites. the second called on the commission to deal properly with an infringement complaint concerning sports betting services. i am pleased to report that the commission reacted promptly and positively to that report. a new feature of the annual report which i wish to highlight, with an eye to supporting and encouraging good administration, concerns what i call ‘star cases’ of good practice by institutions, revealed through my inquiries. i would now like to mention some other activities that i have undertaken during 2006 with a view to ensuring the best possible service to citizens. firstly, i signed a memorandum of understanding with the european data protection supervisor (edps). our agreement aims to ensure the consistent treatment of complaints that raise issues of data protection and to avoid unnecessary duplication. the agreement allows me to benefit from the expertise of the edps by consulting him in cases where the text of the data protection regulation and existing case-law leave room for divergent views. this has already proved to be a useful mechanism for me when dealing with cases in which it is necessary to reconcile the legal right of access to documents with the right to privacy. i also signed an agreement with the spanish government to enable citizens to complain to the european ombudsman in any of the co-official languages in spain. i thus aligned my practice with the conclusions reached in june 2005 by the council, which provide for the use of those languages to facilitate spanish citizens’ communication with the eu institutions. honourable members, i am grateful for the support for the work of the european ombudsman expressed in ms sbarbati’s report, and i would like to inform parliament that, as requested in her report, i am already engaged in preparing the ground for a memorandum of understanding with the european investment bank. given that the implementation of eu law is largely the responsibility of member states’ administrations, i will continue to develop cooperation through the european network of ombudsmen. i am happy to inform you that the sixth meeting of the network took place last week in this very building. at the conclusion of that successful meeting, we adopted by consensus a statement that aims to make the eu dimension of the work of national and regional ombudsmen better known, and to clarify the service they provide to people who complain about matters that fall within the scope of eu law. the voluntary cooperation among ombudsmen that is now crystallised in the statement can, i believe, make an important and growing contribution to the european union’s ability to deliver concrete results, by ensuring that citizens can enjoy their rights as an everyday reality and that problems are solved in ways that are close to the citizen. the european ombudsman was established to help bring the union closer to citizens and to give the eu administration a ‘human face’. a fundamental aspect of our institution is that the ombudsman is an individual who communicates personally with citizens, who reviews their cases, and who seeks to resolve their problems and complaints. each one of these ‘microcommunications’ constitutes an opportunity to build trust between citizens and the institutions. in pursuit of this goal, i will continue to promote a constructive dialogue with the institutions and to draw their attention to problems so that they can improve their performance. the way in which a public administration reacts to complaints is a key measure of how citizen-focused it is. while progress has been made in many areas, the year 2006 regrettably saw a rise in the proportion of cases which i had to close with a critical remark. that should be cause for concern for anyone who wants better relations between the eu and its citizens. complaints offer an opportunity to put things right and to demonstrate that the institution concerned is serious about respecting the citizens’ fundamental right to good administration. i am not sure that citizens can easily reconcile the statements often made by institutions concerning their desire to get ‘closer to the citizen’, and for ‘more openness’, with the fact that the very same institutions frequently fail to take up the opportunities offered by the ombudsman to improve relations and increase transparency. i am positively encouraged, however, by a number of indications that, during the present year, 2007, there is a much greater willingness to take up the opportunities offered by my inquiries to resolve complaints. such cooperation is essential, because the ombudsman cannot succeed alone. ensuring a top-class administration is a task that must be tackled in tandem with the eu institutions. delivering on promises, providing proper redress mechanisms, learning from mistakes, working openly and allowing for public scrutiny – these are the all-important ‘means’ towards building trust. equally, the european ombudsman must work concertedly and systematically with national and regional colleagues to ensure that citizens’ rights are fully respected throughout the union. finally, the ombudsman must continue to reach out to citizens so that they can become aware of his services. with parliament’s support and guidance, i will continue to endeavour to build on existing achievements with a view to truly fulfilling my institutional mandate of bringing the union closer to citizens and giving the eu administration a ‘human face’.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the ombudsman for the excellent work he has done, as also reflected in this timely report. i also thank the commission's legal services and all my colleagues in the committee, and in particular the shadow rapporteur and mr mavrommatis, for the cooperation i have had. the culture of service to the citizen, which has as its priority objective a quality, transparent, accessible, prompt and cooperative public administration, has been promoted and nurtured at community level through the joint efforts of the committee on petitions and the ombudsman. its birth certificate can be traced back to the resolution of 6 september 2001, the date on which the european parliament adopted the code of good administrative behaviour proposed by the european ombudsman. on the other hand, since the maastricht treaty, european citizenship has taken a great leap forward, offering every citizen the possibility of submitting a petition to a parliamentary body which remains its sole arbiter, or of having recourse to a more technical body, which, although operating in the extrajudicial sphere, follows a procedure without excluding parliamentary scrutiny, in the event of the reluctance of the community institution responsible for maladministration. i shall not go into statistics, the ombudsman has already spoken about them and they are those confirmed in the report. the cases of maladministration today are based on lack of transparency, denial of information, abuse of power, legal error, failure to fulfil the roles, especially for the commission, as guardian of the treaty. the ombudsman's decisions are not legally binding, but the guarantees he offers through his work help to strengthen powers of persuasion. he has the active support of the committee on petitions, before which he spoke at four meetings in 2006, and the cooperation of the european network of ombudsmen, which should be completed and improved. i would point out the case of italy, which still does not have a national ombudsman. it should be stressed, however, that in order to avoid conflicts of competence between the work of the ombudsman and that of the committee on petitions, files with final effect must be exchanged with each other in real time. the report divides the decisions on investigations concluded in 2006 into several categories: lack of openness of the community institutions and bodies (25% of inquiries); the role of the commission as guarantor of the treaty in relation to the procedure laid down in article 266; the management of contracts, allowances and subsidies; recruitment and staff management in the community institutions. the procedure is often terminated by critical remarks, which are a preventive weapon to prevent future instances of maladministration, when the recommendation is useless. the ombudsman gave several examples which can be read in the report. in this respect, however, the committee on petitions asks the ombudsman to carry out a detailed study of the practical impact of the critical remarks he made in the 2006 inquiries. the fact that the institutions have adopted a code of good administrative behaviour is often not a sufficient guarantee for the establishment of a true culture of service. the report also highlights areas of uncertainty about the commission's abuse of discretionary powers by failing to act in the pre-litigation phase of the infringement procedure, and by entrenching itself behind political considerations. in the area of contractual staff management, some of the inquiries initiated by the ombudsman's own office demonstrate how his powers constitute an effective tool to stimulate the sound principle of self-protection of the administration, which must be used more and more. the committee on petitions believes that the timing and the views of the ombudsman and parliament on the handling of the same cases should be avoided by means of a constant and constructive dialogue. the committee on petitions once again calls on the ombudsman to monitor the epso apparatus in order to protect the rights of candidates, especially young people, in the european parliament's competition procedures, and also in relation to alleged discrimination reported to us at the european school in brussels. this year's report shows, mr president, that the ombudsman is an actor in the democratic life of the union. a privileged intermediary of the citizens in their relations with the public administration. he draws the line between good and bad administration by suggesting remedial measures or satisfactory solutions for the applicants, so as to transform their bad behaviour into virtuous behaviour. to that end, mr ombudsman, it would be appropriate for you to draw up not only a list of good administrative practice covering only the positive examples but also the negative ones. the key principle to be upheld is the democratic equality of all european citizens, without national or linguistic distinctions or discrimination. the ombudsman is called upon to continue his vigilance in the interests of linguistic equality. the committee on petitions is in favour of simplifying the procedure for a more rapid examination of the ombudsman's annual report and is also in favour of adapting the statute, so that the changes merely entail a qualitative extension of the ombudsman's powers and do not affect the nature of his competence or the lack of enforcement of all his decisions.

the agenda includes the commission statement on the application of directive 2004/38/ec on the right of citizens of the union to move and reside freely within the territory of the member states.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, we followed very closely the evolution of the situation in italy. we are worried about the growing street crime and wish to express, first of all, our sympathy to the families of individuals who have been victims of criminal activities. we welcome the bilateral cooperation measures announced last week by the prime ministers of italy and romania. we will ensure that the rights of romanians are respected, as all citizens’ rights should be. under the transitional arrangements to the complete opening of labour markets, romanian nationals must apply for job permits in certain member states. we will make sure that member states observe the principle of non-discrimination in their national legislation and administrative practice. the free movement directive, directive 2004/38/ec, allows for the expulsion of european citizens when an individual represents a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat affecting one of the fundamental interests of society. this is a decision to be made on a case-by-case basis and in the full respect of the guarantees of substance and procedure. in cases of immediate expulsion, the urgency must be duly justified. under the directive, the host member state may expel european citizens also if they no longer fulfil the conditions attached to their right of residence. inactive union citizens may be expelled if they become an unreasonable burden on its social assistance system; in other words, if they do not have legal financial means to guarantee proper daily living conditions. in this case, expulsion shall be based on objective elements and a ban on re-entry cannot be imposed. expelling european citizens is an extreme measure. it is a limitation of one of the basic freedoms of the treaty. measures should be taken to strike the right balance between the right to free movement and the duty of each member state to react in the interests of honest citizens when the legal conditions to stay are not fulfilled. the italian authorities officially notified the commission of the text of the decree on 7 november 2007. the decree must be adopted by the italian parliament within 60 days. as you know, the italian parliament has the power to change the text of the decree. the position of the commission on the italian legislation transposing directive 2004/38/ec will, of course, depend on the final version of the law as it emerges from the italian parliament. the decree entered into force immediately, but the directive is sufficiently precise in its terms to be directly applicable by national courts. this means that if a union citizen considers that the individual expulsion measure taken against him or her does not respect the guarantees laid down in the directive, he or she can appeal before the national courts. in case of doubt on the application of european law, as you know perfectly well, national courts are obliged to refer the issue to the european court of justice. we will continue to monitor the situation, pending the examination of the decree by the italian parliament. we are also worried about some racist and xenophobic demonstrations that have accompanied the introduction of the decree in italy. roma groups are the largest minority in europe. roma communities throughout europe face difficult conditions. there is a long past of persecution. this situation leads to human suffering and social tension. inclusion requires efforts by everyone concerned, including the roma themselves. specific protection must be given to individuals, children and women especially. criminals of whatever nationality very often exploit particularly vulnerable people such as children. roma children face double discrimination. firstly, they are victims of stereotypes and prejudice. but also they may face violations of their fundamental rights, even from within their communities. we see, too often, neglected roma children on our streets or living in poor, often tolerated conditions in modern european favelas. children may be brought into a life of crime or forced to beg. roma schoolchildren tend to leave school early without qualifications for the future or skills to care for themselves and their families. if we only look at a group when we consider how to protect fundamental rights, then we risk missing the protection of individuals within that group and we miss the opportunity to break the circle of wrongdoing and fear. we are ready to assist italy and romania in making the best possible use of all possibilities already existing under european law and under european funds. it should be also stressed that roma communities live in many other member states such as france, ireland, spain, slovakia, the czech republic or hungary. the social inclusion of roma communities can also be further improved in these member states, notably through the structural funds, which can be quite helpful. european funding, specifically targeted at the needs of roma communities, is already available in areas such as social inclusion, the fight against discrimination, regional development and education. in the previous programming period, the structural funds made available more than eur 275 million for roma-related projects. an additional eur 60 million was made available to romania and bulgaria between 2004 and 2006, under the pre-accession instruments. the funding of roma-related projects will continue in the structural fund programming period 2007-2013. the european racial equality directive (2000/43/ec), which covers roma people, provides for protection against discrimination in employment, education, social security, health care, goods and services, and housing. we are actively ensuring that this legislation is applied across the eu. finally, as much as the commission is not prepared to tolerate any form of discrimination or intolerance of its citizens, we equally will support member states who lawfully protect their citizens from criminality, whether they are nationals or citizens of the union in general. after all, freedom, justice and security go hand in hand.
i am pleased that commissioner frattini has presented the report in its entirety and that he has put forward the proposals, ideas, content and values he has defended. the reunification of europe has certainly led to an increasing movement of citizens within the union, which in no case has turned into a real migratory event. this is the case with the presence today in italy of about half a million romanian citizens. the union has taken steps, by means of directive 2004/38/ec, to ensure that the rights of community citizens who migrate from one country to another are respected while member states are entitled to expel community citizens who do not comply with certain rules: i am referring to the ability to provide for oneself and the risks to public security and order. unfortunately, the community directive has been applied in italy in a deficient and delayed manner. the result: the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter, but it is not yet clear whether the commission will take a decision on the matter. unfortunately, there have been crimes that have shocked public opinion, committed by people who had a passport from a european country. this has provoked reactions of unacceptable xenophobic violence. the violence and murders committed in italy must be strongly condemned and all the families of the victims must be in solidarity. the violent and xenophobic reaction must also be condemned, but unfortunately, when the rules are not applied, when the laws are not applied, citizens risk taking justice into their own hands, and this is frankly unacceptable. the states have very clear responsibilities, as do the local authorities. unfortunately, in rome, despite the many complaints, no action has been taken on social realities as such, which really resemble favelas, where roma citizens live, they are realities where action had to be taken in advance and sometimes the interventions made late do not help solve the problems when they have unfortunately exploded. we are not in favour of mass expulsions, and every citizen who commits a crime is personally responsible. it is not a question of nationality or ethnicity. there is certainly a need for further cooperation between romania and italy. it is no coincidence that the ppe text was signed by myself and my colleague mr marinescu. there is also a specific issue concerning the roma population. it is not a matter for the romanian people, and that is why we are calling for the establishment of a special agency for the social integration of the roma communities, in short, a european agency to show that europe is doing its part to solve a problem which otherwise risks arousing ever greater social alarm.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too would like to thank commissioner frattini for his detailed report this evening. in my view, directive 2004/38/ec is a valid reference point, firstly to ensure the full exercise of the right of movement of union citizens, to avoid any form of discrimination, to affirm the principle of full integration. it is a directive which seeks to protect, in accordance with the principle of reciprocity, both the rights of those who establish themselves in a member state and the rights of nationals of the host member state. maximum protection for those who work, for those who study, for those who want to integrate, but also severity for those who do not respect the rules. and we have a duty to give this matter serious thought in this parliament. there are not only rights, but also duties and rules which must be respected. we cannot continue to ignore the fact that there is a percentage - certainly a minority, a very minority - but there is a percentage of people who move to other member states and have no intention of reporting their presence in the host member states, simply because they do not want to be recognised, because they have no intention of respecting the rules and working legally. the problem of those who move and enter a member state determined to put themselves on the margins of social life must be seriously addressed. the instruments can certainly be improved, but some are already available to the member states, starting with directive 38, which must first be implemented in a timely, full, rigorous and practical manner in each member state. it might also be desirable to improve the directive by requiring that the host citizen declare that he is present in the host member state within a certain period of time and also requiring the member states to impose penalties on those who do not comply with the time limits and procedures. in italy, for example, the implementing decree of the directive sets out the procedures and time limits, but there are no penalties and therefore the rule is in fact completely ineffective. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. but i want to make it clear: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european parliament is able to exercise its right to vote and to stand as a candidate in elections. and there must also be rules for those who do not work, for those who live off the grid and can therefore represent an excessive burden on the community of the host member state. i would like to conclude with a nod to roma children and the case of italy. in italy there are about 50,000 children, at least 50,000 exploited children. these are roma children, forced to beg, unvaccinated children, children who do not go to school, children who live in absolutely deplorable sanitary conditions. i would remind everyone that about a week before mrs reggiani was killed in rome, in the same slum, from the slum where mrs reggiani's killer came from, a two-month-old roma girl froze to death in the capital of italy, in a major european capital. so, i really close by saying, is that integration? is this respect for human rights? we have a duty to take the matter seriously, without hypocrisy, and we have a duty to say that the law is the same for everyone.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner dimas, i thank you and i would also like to repeat my thanks to the rapporteur, mrs gutiérrez-cortines, for the work we have done together, and i hope that it has also contributed to the improvement of the text. the directive under discussion today was designed to protect european soil from phenomena such as desertification, erosion and salinization, which are increasingly linked to climate change and specific soil pollution. paradoxically, despite the many regulations on the use and release of pollutants into the environment, there has been no directive to date which provides for any kind of obligation to take responsibility for identifying and certifying severely polluted soils and then proceeding to remediate them. but it is precisely this element that seems to bother some people in this house and elsewhere, who are crying out against the attack on subsidiarity, against the suffocating presence of the european institutions which are planning with proposals such as the soil directive to harm a category of farmers or entrepreneurs by unfair rules, by unfair rules, by new administrative and/or financial burdens. what are we talking about? we are talking about the same directive which provides for a period of 25 years for the member states to identify on their national territory all areas which are presumed to be severely polluted, and therefore compromised for various uses, both public and private, all areas at serious risk of desertification, erosion, salinization, loss of compactness. we are talking about indications to enable systematic clean-up work to be organized, where necessary, in the collective interest. we are talking about protecting human health alongside the environment. we are talking about a framework directive which not only respects the autonomy of the member states but does not even impose such onerous measures. so why is there so much reluctance on the part of some member states and parliament - the usual two or three - to attack, to accept a list of activities and sites to be subjected to mandatory scientific investigation by the national authorities? what's so bad about them? why such a dislike when their governments in the council have already accepted the binding nature of the investigation of all sites proposed by the commission in annex ii, and the principle of transparency which must prevail in land transactions? on the other hand, there is an added value of a european approach to soil monitoring activity which will improve the capacity of member states to know their soil and reports to the commission will also be virtually automatic; i'm referring to the satellite tracking. perhaps it is not known that there is already a work done by the commission, the soil atlas of europe, which is a good example of what can be done together. but there is another consideration for a community approach and soil protection and that is the challenge of climate change, a challenge for all of europe. this challenge is the worsening of extreme events, heavy and more intense rainfall, longer droughts, more rainfall and less snowfall, rising sea levels. this implies a duty for us to do soil maintenance, precisely to prevent these challenges: increase water retention times throughout the territory to prevent flooding and promote groundwater recharge, particularly along the coasts to prevent saltwater infiltration, which is more likely due to sea level rise. maintaining forests to control the fire load, worsening droughts, will mean greater risk of desertification in the event of fire. this maintenance of the site will also allow for the further exploitation of renewable energy, hydraulics and biomass. and we must not forget the appearance of the soil, which is the balance of greenhouse gases. i would ask you to think, when you vote on wednesday, of the need, now more than ever, for a strategy and a directive which can guarantee future generations the use, the use and the enjoyment of the same land we now have, each in its own member state, but all subject to the same environmental threats and risks. soil is a resource, a scarce resource throughout europe and we must make this resource as available as possible.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented. i thank commissioner dimas for his treatment. i say this as a member of a group which is often critical of directives and the commission: that's not the case. this directive is a significant step forward for europe, both in terms of the quality of its policy and its effectiveness. the framework directives on the major natural elements are being supplemented, and soil is being considered as a key element of the biosphere, a fundamental element of environmental and climatic balances. it is no longer a mere platform to be cemented. soil is alive, it absorbs co2, it produces biomass: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is protected. europe understands this. we have had a long and difficult debate in committee, and i thank mrs cristina gutiérrez for her passion. but there is a risk that parliament will make the commission's text worse, and i never like that, i always prefer that parliament should be ahead of the commission. europe must look to the future and the soil is our own soil, the only one we have and which we must protect!

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, climate change is one of the most serious problems we face. if we want to secure our future, we cannot ignore the environmental issue any longer and we must be prepared to change our lifestyles, particularly in terms of mobility. transport is one of the sectors that contributes most to energy consumption and is the one that is most affected by the use of fossil fuels. air transport is increasingly being included in this sector. in 2004, greenhouse gas emissions from aircraft and attributable to the community increased by 87% compared with 1990. europe is responsible for about half of the co2 emissions from aviation. this is no longer sustainable and serious action is therefore needed, for example by abolishing the tax benefits in this sector. i believe that the commission's proposal for a directive on aviation emission allowances is an indispensable tool for tackling the problems of climate change in a consistent way and we very much welcome the envi report which strengthens the original directive. however, it is important to stress that there are some qualifying points which must be retained in the debate and the vote tomorrow, and i think that the community emissions trading system for all flights, both those arriving and those leaving the union, is important among them, and this cannot be postponed beyond 2010. it is also important that a significant proportion of allowances should be auctioned and the proceeds of such sales should be used to subsidize cleaner transport, for example by taxing environmentally friendly transport, so as to create low-cost tourism using less polluting systems such as the train. the second is to focus on the search for more efficient aircraft engines, more effective air traffic management. i hope that tomorrow the house will not dismantle the advanced compromise which will enable europe to become a leader in the fight against climate change.

member of the commission. mr president, firstly i would like to express my thanks to the rapporteur, mr braghetto, and to the committee on fisheries for this report, which raises the issue of the recovery plan for bluefin tuna. the eastern atlantic and mediterranean bluefin tuna is a key stock for the community. as confirmed by scientific advice, this bluefin tuna stock is now at high risk of collapse. all the states involved in this fishery have agreed to the need for urgent measures to ensure the sustainability of the bluefin tuna stock and of the fishery. i am convinced that the recovery plan adopted by the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas in 2006 represents a realistic chance for the gradual recovery of bluefin tuna if it is fully respected. therefore, decisive and effective action is immediately necessary at community level. the speed of the implementation of the iccat recovery plan is an absolute must, both for conservation reasons and to safeguard the common fisheries policy’s credibility and the credibility of the eu fishermen themselves. the objective is to have the proposal agreed at the november council. during discussions held in the context of the council preparations, many changes were introduced to the original proposal, some of which go in the direction of your suggested amendments. i am sure that we are in agreement on the objectives of urgently taking measures to eliminate overfishing and to ensure strict compliance with iccat measures, in order to bring the bluefin tuna stock to sustainable levels. this will, at the same time, improve the profitability of the fishing industry in the long term. apart from the benefits to industry, there is also an international political commitment that we are obliged to fulfil. turning now to the report, i appreciate and share the fisheries committee’s view that the community needs to address the excess fishing effort of its fleet. the commission also considers that the annual fishing plan is an effective instrument to avoid overfishing because of the overcapacity of the community fleet. in this context, the commission can accept amendments 1, 2, 7 and 8 concerning the establishment of annual fishing plans to ensure a balance between the fishing effort of the community fleet and the quotas. a relevant provision on this issue has been introduced in the presidency compromise. in addition, the commission asks the member states concerned to include in their operational plans a reduction of their fishing capacity, either temporary cessation or scrapping, to ensure that their quotas for 2008 and the following years are fully respected. i recognise that we are asking the industry to make considerable sacrifices, but these are necessary to ensure the long-term sustainability of the fisheries, fleets and coastal communities concerned. the choice is between short-term sacrifice and the collapse of the stock. moreover, i totally agree with you that, in order to alleviate the socio-economic impact that will be caused by the reduction in fishing activity, it is necessary to ensure financial compensation for the industry. a provision on the related financing measure in line with amendment 5 has also been introduced in the presidency compromise. i am aware that there are other concerns. i share many of those concerns and know that they too will need to be addressed. with respect to amendment 3, let me state first of all that i am well aware that the number of cages for tuna fattening has increased greatly since 1990 and that their capacity exceeds the total sum of the tac available. iccat has now adopted a strict regulation in order to ensure the sustainable development of farming activities for bluefin tuna. the next step will be to regulate the number of farms. the commission fully supports the adoption of the recommendation made by the iccat working group on capacity in july 2007. this recommendation proposes the implementation of a freeze on boat fishing capacity and farming capacity for bluefin tuna. we need to wait for the final results of the iccat discussion being held in antalya this week. that is the reason why the commission cannot accept, at this stage, the amendment concerning the limitation of farming capacity. on the derogations relating to fishing areas and minimum size, i would like to remind you of the context within which such derogations were accepted by iccat. all contracting parties have agreed these derogations as part of the package on the recovery plan. these derogations were granted for artisanal fleets and for some seasonal fleets because their impact on catches is insignificant. in addition, these derogations include a series of strict conditions, such as a limited number of vessels, limited catches and designated ports. having said that, the recovery plan may be revised in 2008 on the basis of new scientific advice or weaknesses detected in its implementation. at this stage, the community has a responsibility to ensure that the recovery plan is incorporated in community legislation to ensure its full implementation. in this context, i cannot accept parliament’s amendments on the deletion of the derogations, that is amendments 4 and 6, or amendments 12 and 13 on the renaming of the plan, the modification of the ec quotas and the introduction of a new payback system. these amendments are not in line with the recovery plan adopted by iccat and the iccat rules on payback. similarly, i cannot accept amendment 10 regarding traps, since the proposal does not include measures to address this issue. for the first time, the recovery plan regulates trap activity and this will, in future, enable an evaluation of the impact of this fishing activity on the stock. regarding amendments 9 and 11 relating to the harmonisation of sanctions and the possible closure of a national fishery of a member state where it fails to respect its reporting requirements, let me say that, whereas we fully understand and share the spirit behind this proposal, we cannot accept the amendment in this context, as the proposal does not include measures that address the issue. the issue is one of general policy and the commission will examine it in the forthcoming 2008 reform of the control framework of the common fisheries policy. we consider that documentation and transmission of information to the commission at set times is a crucial element for the success of the bluefin tuna recovery plan, and it is also a prerequisite if we are to monitor the uptake of the eu quota in real time. the commission has therefore opened infringement procedures against all seven member states which take part in the bluefin tuna fishery for shortcomings in data transmission. in conclusion, let me state that we are deeply concerned about the overshoot of the quota by some member states, which undermines the credibility of the community at international level and jeopardises the success of the bluefin tuna recovery plan. at the meeting of the compliance committee, which took place in antalya on 8 and 9 november, the contracting parties – notably the united states and canada – criticised the lack of compliance with iccat rules. as expected, the european community was severely criticised for overshooting the tac in 2007. at the same time, the contracting parties acknowledged the difficulties for the european community fleet in adapting to the reality of the recovery plan, which entered into force in 2007, and welcomed the european community proposal on a specific payback regime. the compliance committee has adopted a specific recommendation concerning a payback system for the overshoot of the ec quota in 2007, which comes to 4 440 tonnes, based on an ec proposal. in accordance with this recommendation, the overharvesting of the european community’s quota in 2007 will result in a yearly deduction of 1 480 tonnes from its annual quota for the period 2009-2011. in addition, the compliance committee agreed that the figure for the european community was provisional and may be subject to review and eventual adjustment as a result of ongoing investigations. this recommendation will be adopted by iccat during its plenary session on 18 november. nevertheless, we have to reassure the iccat parties that the european community will do its utmost to ensure that quotas allocated to the vessels of our member states are scrupulously monitored by those member states and by the european commission, in order to ensure respect for the quota set for 2008 and the forthcoming years. following the adoption of this regulation, the commission is resolved to work closely with the member states to ensure and closely monitor the full implementation of the bluefin tuna recovery plan. the community fisheries control agency will also play an active role. the agency has started the preparatory work for the coordination of control and inspection activities by member states, with a view to having everything in place for the 2008 bluefin tuna season.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the european commission's plan for the recovery of bluefin tuna stocks, launched by iccat, aims to respond to the scientific community's concerns about the critical situation of the stocks due to excessive fishing effort. it was a plan that was judged differently because of a different perception among scientific experts and fishermen about the need to protect the resource. however, it is considered to meet the needs identified, in particular where it provides for a progressive reduction of the catch quota up to 20% in 2010 compared to 2006, an increase in the minimum size to 30 kg, the provision of a limitation of the fishing period, the strengthening of measures to control and combat illegal fishing. in particular, the work carried out in the committee was intended to strengthen certain lines of the plan by proposing: to provide for and encourage the submission of fishing plans by member states in the framework of fisheries agreements, even if the stock is in good biological condition, since one of the main problems is the overcapacity of the fleet in relation to the available quotas; to establish in each member state a balance between the capacity of its fattening farms and the quotas at its disposal; to eliminate derogations for both fishing zones and minimum sizes: they are contrary to the indications of all scientific experts and to the opinion expressed by the majority of the member states. the derogations are not biologically justified, since the mediterranean and atlantic stocks are unique, they introduce severe distortions in the competitive mechanism, they lead to increased fishing in those areas even by the fleet not traditionally concerned and they reduce the effectiveness of controls. to encourage member states to comply with their obligations to submit data and information to the commission, by ending national fishing activities when member states do not provide catch data; to develop a plan for the rehabilitation of atlantic bluefin tuna and the recovery of discontinued tuna in the mediterranean in order to preserve a sustainable and highly selective tuna fishery; provide for financial compensation from the european fisheries fund to be paid to seafarers during periods of fishing closure in order to safeguard and protect the socioeconomic balance of fisheries undertakings and workers; harmonise the sanctioning measures in order to avoid differences between the different member states in the implementation of this regulation. finally, the infringement procedures opened in recent months against some member states for failure to respect the quotas allocated in 2007 are certainly a necessary and proper step, but it should also be remembered that the current provisions are due to enter into force this year. the commission is also aware that the management of the resource is particularly complex, particularly in areas where there is strong competition from other non-eu fleets, particularly in the mediterranean, and calls for greater respect for the principle of reciprocity to ensure the loyal pursuit of the objectives set by iccat. these measures will only be effective if their principles and provisions are applied by all eu and non-eu countries. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to thank all my colleagues in particular for the work they have done together.

in writing. the braghetto report contains key ideas for the implementation of the bluefin tuna recovery plan. this plan imposes severe restrictions on fishing, motivated by the need to protect stocks of an endangered species. the initiative is likely to be ineffective, however, if the european union does not take measures to offset its socioeconomic impact. the report has the merit of highlighting this shortcoming by proposing appropriate instruments to implement the recommendations of the commission and iccat effectively. in terms of socioeconomic aspects, tuna fishing is a traditional activity, providing thousands of families with an exclusive source of income: the total closure must be accompanied by financial compensation from the eff for the operators. it is also essential that the member states apply sanctions against illegal fishing, which is the real cause of the depletion of stocks. there's no point in targeting honest fishermen without the tools to stop the predators in the sea. finally, it is essential to require reciprocity from third states: it is not worth sacrificing our operators to protect the species if other countries, and i am referring to libya, turkey, but also china and japan, do not apply equally severe restrictions in their seas. they would have a competitive advantage over european operators, but the problem of depopulation of tuna would not be solved.

platforms that make their repertoire available for online music shops across europe. i refer to the three examples i have just mentioned. the celas joint venture alone is in fact in a position to will carefully consider the issues raised in the lévai report of 5 march 2007. if, between now and 2010, we observe, for example, that monopolistic licensing structures are emerging on the internet, that the repertoire available on the internet does not adequately reflect europe’s cultural diversity and that the marketplace alone is not delivering eu licensing structures that are adapted to the internet era, then the commission will consider adequate alternative means for reaching those objectives.
