member of the commission. mr president, i welcome this opportunity to explain where we are in the economic partnership agreement (epa) negotiations. i am glad to note that the strategy proposed by the commission in its communication of 23 october was endorsed by the council last week. as commissioner mandelson said to parliament’s committee on international trade last week, we have turned a corner in these negotiations. these negotiations are moving very quickly. let me give you a sense of where we stand at this moment. in east africa, a stepping-stone agreement has been initialled with the east african community: kenya, uganda, rwanda, burundi and tanzania. we are very close to an interim deal with the indian ocean countries in the context of the eastern and southern africa grouping. in the southern african development community, we have initialled a stepping-stone agreement with botswana, lesotho, swaziland and mozambique. angola will join as soon as it is able. south africa and namibia will decide on their participation in the next day. regarding the pacific region, we are working in parallel on an umbrella agreement for the region as a whole and specific agreements on market access to safeguard the immediate interests of those countries which account for the region’s trade with the european union. i expect agreement on those to be announced very shortly. in the remaining regions, the picture is less clear. for west africa and central africa, meetings are taking place with so-called ‘subgroups’. it is possible that we will be able to conclude interim agreements on goods with the countries most affected, which could then be enlarged to full epas with the whole region in 2008. that will, of course, depend on the wish of those concerned to take this route and to present wto-compatible market access agreements. in the caribbean region, we have an agreement on nearly everything but, crucially, not on trade in goods, where the region’s proposal falls well short of what can be defended in the wto. negotiations are continuing, but we now need a clear political decision from the region to unlock the negotiations by producing a wto-compatible market access schedule. in all regions, we are taking a pragmatic and flexible approach to achieving what remains our objective for these agreements: full epas with four regions. this will modernise our trade relationship and put it at the service of development, so full agreement with four regions is our objective. we have made significant progress in recent days, but we cannot today guarantee that there will be an agreement including new wto-compatible trade arrangements with all acp countries. wto compatibility is the essential component of all agreements, whether they are full epas, stepping-stone agreements, or even goods-only deals. without this, we can only offer the generalised system of preferences. next week, the general affairs and external relations council will decide on the ec regulation to implement the market access which has been offered to the acp. it is the best ever offer in a bilateral agreement: full duty/quota-free access, with transition periods for only two products – sugar and rice. we will continue to do everything possible to reach agreements. our offer is on the table and the moment any acp state provides a wto-compatible offer to complete a deal, we can move quickly to propose to the council that it should benefit from the epa market access regulation. we have indicated our willingness to work with subregions, if that is what the acp states wish. we have agreed to continue negotiating beyond 1 january 2008 on other issues, like services, investment and other trade-related areas, which are such an important part of the development component of these agreements. we have delivered on our commitment to provide trade arrangements equivalent to or better than cotonou to any country reaching an agreement with us. we have offered to open our markets fully and match the goods trade offer with generous services offers. what we cannot do is extend the cotonou trade regime while we continue negotiations. in the absence of an epa, we have made clear that we cannot and will not propose solutions which are illegal or insecure. our acp partners will need support to implement the agreements and make the necessary adjustments and reforms. this is why the commission is working to ensure that the european development fund will make ‘aid for trade’ in the context of epas a priority. it is why we are working closely with member states so that they bring additional money in the context of the newly-adopted eu aid-for-trade strategy. we know that concluding these negotiations means taking difficult political decisions, but we welcome the leadership shown by those acp regions and countries which have decided to join us in initialling epa agreements. we will continue to support them as they implement the commitments they have made and as we work together to ensure that this is a trade relationship that genuinely contributes to their development.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after the adoption of the first two railway packages in 2001 and 2004, before the adoption of the third railway package, the commission proposed on 13 december 2006 a new set of legislative measures on the cross-validation of rolling stock, in particular locomotives. these measures are intended to support the revitalisation of the railway sector by removing obstacles to train movement on the european rail network. the commission has launched this initiative for two main reasons: firstly, to facilitate the free movement of trains within the union by making the procedure for putting locomotives into service more transparent and efficient; secondly, to simplify the regulatory environment by consolidating and merging the three directives on railway interoperability into one. the package includes a communication, three legislative proposals and their impact assessment: a communication illustrating the current difficulties and proposing solutions to simplify the certification of railway vehicles, a proposal to revise the existing directives on railway interoperability, an amendment to the railway safety directive, a proposal to amend the regulation establishing a european railway agency and, finally, an impact assessment report. what was the common thread of this set of texts? a crucial aspect is to facilitate the free movement of trains and it concerns the approval procedure for locomotives. according to manufacturers and railway undertakings, this type approval procedure is very long and very costly; some requests from the competent authorities appear to be unjustified from a purely technical point of view. the commission shares this analysis and proposes to solve the problem by providing for a change in the legislative framework and by asking the competent authorities in the member states to change their behaviour now. this is why the communication accompanying the legislative proposals is important, as it proposes solutions that can be applied immediately, without waiting for the legislative framework to be changed. this communication did not remain without effect. we have already had a cooperation agreement signed in may for the rotterdam-genoa corridor. this agreement follows exactly the concepts proposed in our communication. the second is the proposal to revise the directives on interoperability and security. the commission had two objectives in presenting these two proposals. firstly, simplify the procedure for the approval of railway vehicles. we have introduced the principle of mutual recognition of authorizations for placing in service already issued by a member state. this principle means that rolling stock already authorised for placing in service in one member state should be subject to additional certification in another member state only in respect of additional national requirements arising, for example, from the characteristics of the local network. secondly, for the sake of clarity, we have brought together in one text the 1996 directive on the interoperability of the trans-european high-speed rail system and the 2001 directive on the interoperability of the conventional rail system. the new regulatory procedure with scrutiny was introduced for certain powers delegated to the commission by the council and the european parliament. the amendments to the interoperability and safety directives have given us the opportunity for two further operations. on the one hand, we have introduced a number of amendments on technical points in the new interoperability directive, in the light of the experience gained during the ten years of work carried out not only by the commission, but also by the member states in the framework of comitology, by industry and the sector and, since 2005, by the railway agency. on the other hand, we wanted to respond to some operators by clarifying the relationship between the railway undertaking and the entity in charge of maintenance in the safety directive. this provision was necessary to reflect the new regulatory framework resulting from the community directives on the opening of the market and the new wagon operating contract established at international level by the cotif convention. finally, i come to the proposal for amending the regulation establishing a european railway agency. this is an extension of the powers of the european railway agency, so that the agency can identify the various national procedures, the technical rules in force for the approval of locomotives and establish, by extending it subsequently, the list of requirements which must be verified only once, either because they are internationally recognized rules or because they can be considered equivalent between member states. this work will be carried out in cooperation with the network of national safety authorities, which the agency is responsible for leading. the agency will be responsible for producing technical opinions at the request of the national safety authorities or the commission. finally, in connection with this amendment, we have clarified certain other points of the regulation on the basis of experience gained, particularly in the context of the implementation of the ertms (european rail traffic management system) and of rolling stock registers. i would like to say, mr president, that while the first and second railway packages, and soon the third, establish the legal and economic framework for the proper functioning of rail services within the single market, the task had to be completed by ensuring the technical decoupling of national markets. this is the purpose of these proposals, which the railway sector has been waiting for for a long time. i am grateful to parliament for the rapid and quality work it has done on these texts.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr vice-president of the commission, although, as the vice-president of the commission said, we are forced to go through the technical debate in quotes, we are making a major political step forward today. since the establishment of the first treaty, at the end of the 1950s, there have been three main lines of european transport policy: the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the information it receives, and to make it more accessible to the public. interoperability is not a technical fact, but it is the precondition for the construction of the european markets which are absolutely necessary and which are the aim of the treaty. great strides have been made in almost everything. we're a little behind in the railroad business. we are still facing the same objectives as in the 1960s. the reasons are different, this is not the time to do it, but this must be said to strengthen our conviction that we are taking a fundamental step and that it is crucial that we achieve these results. interoperability is therefore an essential condition for building, for being able to move on networks without technical barriers, which are raised to prevent the complete full circulation of engines and wagons, and so it is a fundamental step that had to be taken and that has to be done as quickly as possible. the commission has done well in no longer distinguishing between high-speed and traditional network interoperability and in pushing as far as possible in this direction. it was also a good thing that he also raised the issue of security, which is sometimes presented - and here we must be very careful in this statement - as a reason for conditional interoperability. how do you get the same driver across a border who may not understand the language of the country he is driving in? how do you get a locomotive across the border that might not be perfectly suited to the network on the other side? and so on and so forth. so you're right to put the two together. we must absolutely guarantee security but within a system which is interoperable, because if security is put forward as a condition to prevent interoperability, there is something wrong with this. the fact that it has been decided to have a european agency to deal with this and other matters, as we shall see, is certainly a sign that we are serious about this. what has parliament done? parliament approved the commission's proposals in substance, with some recommendations aimed at making the system more interoperable. in the report on interoperability you imagined that there are time limits within which authorizations are reached, of course for rolling stock already in operation, that the burden of proof that something is not interoperable also for safety reasons is shifted to the member states, that is to say it is assumed a priori that once certified everything can go anywhere, unless someone explains to me that there is some serious reason why this can be done, and you also imagined that state aid can be considered for retrofitting everything that exists in this way. that seems to me to be the contribution made in this situation. the same goes for security. here too, we have tried to say that by a certain date - for example, 2010 - we propose that there should be a mandatory certification. this makes it easier for everyone, without exception, to treat everyone the same, and not to continue to regard the monopolies which still operate rail services as being particularly capable of running them automatically and therefore exempt from this situation. the third point is to get the agency to act. i must say that this is the key question for me, which i put to everyone and to the commission in particular. we have rightly imagined that we would distinguish security from the rest by creating 25 european agencies. it was an important decision we made some time ago. i wonder, since they are not yet operational, whether it is not worth imagining having a single european agency working through 25 offices in different countries. this is the key issue which would allow the related problem of interoperability and security to be resolved in a positive way at european level.

number of policies which have a major effect on tourism and its ability to grow or maintain its competitiveness as a world leader as europe is. so, the idea of this report is to point out some possibilities. the list which we have drawn up, and which parliament has drawn up with the help of all, is only an indicative list, and i hope that it can be enriched further. it is a list of possibilities for using the full powers of the european union that exist today for tourism purposes. two examples for everyone: the tourist is a traveller and therefore, by definition, many transport policies can be viewed in terms of and in favour of tourism or be reviewed in terms of and in favour of tourism. the tourist is a consumer, so many of the european union's consumer protection activities can be traced back to the needs of the tourist. but if we want other policies, the tourist, especially the non-european tourist who comes to europe, is a gentleman who crosses borders just as others cross borders for different reasons. a visa policy, an immigration policy of the european union needs to be carefully reviewed, so as to take account of the opportunity to invite as many tourism is one of the industries with the greatest prospects for europe, that it is useful above all for the cohesion objectives it is able to maintain, for the enhancement of resources such as prolonging the system of planting rights until the end of 2013 was based on the clear idea of a two-stage approach to balancing the sector – first grubbing-up to bring down the production, and then liberalisation to give the successful producers the freedom to expand. i have listened to the comments from the sector but one thing is clear – the final date for the planting rights system is indispensable. what that exact date will be, will be part of the final compromise. so overall, i have been listening to arguments from all the different sides, including all the arguments from the european parliament, but one iron fact has not changed: our wine sector still needs reform if we want to keep it at the front of the pack. we have to seize the chance now and agree on a real reform. carrying out reform will mean that we have to invest effort, but i am quite sure that we will get a good return. the cost of inaction is too high for us to accept, and i hope that we can agree on this point.

emergencies: the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. hence the support for a more efficient use of economic resources, for national development programmes and for the implementation of those measures which best meet the specific needs of each producing state. that is why we have considered in the report, commissioner, to extend the list of measures that can be production. the report therefore calls for a harmonised system for the protection of designations of origin and geographical indications, clear labelling, transparent labelling and clearly identified oenological practices. only then will the consumer, whom we put at the centre, be able to have confidence in what he is buying. it is therefore essential, commissioner, that the designations of origin and geographical indications which represent the quality of european wine production be strongly protected. protection which means the obligation to make wine within the demarcated area, but which also means limiting the mention of the vintage on the label to wines with designation of origin and geographical indication only. they are the only ones that are subject to continuous checks and therefore the only ones for which it is possible to ensure the veracity of the information provided, otherwise we are harming the very producers of quality and deceiving the consumers. the report also supports the proposal for a voluntary withdrawal programme with a premium, to enable those who wish to do so to leave the market with dignity. i cannot help but be pleased that the commissioner has already accepted my idea of reducing the period from five to three years, and it seems that the number of hectares to be planted has actually fallen from 200 000 to 175 000. unlike our original proposal, the report also seeks to meet the need for certainty in the future that our wine producers need. so, for the same reason of certainty, we cannot decide to liberalize planting rights right away, before we see whether the new system works and, above all, how it works. the report therefore provides for the rights to be maintained until at least 2013 and calls on the commission to prepare an impact assessment from the first stage of the reform so that we can make informed choices, bearing in mind that in geographical indication areas decisions need to be taken in compliance with and under the control of those who have invested capital and labour in those projects. if it is true that such a system holds back the development of those who are competitive, then we can facilitate community movement and ensure the effective use of reserves where they exist. the commissioner has made a final point. i am not going to go into the details of the commission's proposals. coming from a country like italy where the use of sucrose is banned and even more so from sicily, where must is produced, no one can understand the commissioner's disappointment on this subject better than i can. however, we are talking about the need to give european wines a new impetus and competitiveness, to enable them to compete on the markets. that is our aim, and to achieve this aim we have worked by trying to look beyond national differences. i thank you, commissioner, for your work and especially for the contribution you have made to the appreciation of the work of the european parliament. we the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european vocation of the balkan countries is now a given, as the thessaloniki european council stated in 2003 and as we have repeatedly stated in this parliament, and it is no longer a subject for discussion. montenegro is certainly in a pool position on the road to eu membership, as the facts show: following independence from the union with serbia in 2006, which was democratically declared by a regular referendum and agreed with the serbian government, negotiations for the country-specific stabilisation and association agreement were reopened and concluded in just over two months. the agreement was signed on 15 march, but unfortunately there were some technical problems which slowed down the process, but we are now on the way to the finish line. the commissioner has just announced that they have already opened a branch in podgorica - we congratulate them on this - everything is now ready for the ratification of the agreement. the progress made by the country over the past year, the commitments it has made to the european community, the relentless reform work also in recent days, all these things lead us to approve without hesitation the opinion in favour of the conclusion of the agreement. it is clear that this is not the final goal, on the contrary, it is only a starting point. montenegro should now apply to take all necessary measures to complete the reform process already initiated in order to fulfil the commitments undertaken under the stabilisation and association agreement. in this respect we note the good atmosphere of cooperation between the european parliament and the parliament of montenegro, which we have already met on a number of occasions and where we will be guests next week in podgorica. montenegro has all the numbers to complete this process in a short time, starting with candidate status. montenegro has been experiencing steady economic growth for some years now, which has attracted considerable foreign investment, partly thanks to its business-friendly tax policies. the result is a rapid fall in unemployment from 33 to 12%. the new constitutional charter was adopted a few months ago, a clear sign of how the country is strengthening its democratic prerogatives within the balkan area. the montenegrin authorities are working hard to bring themselves up to european standards. the most recent developments have led us to table five amendments to take account of the updates. a cooperation agreement was signed just these days with the criminal tribunal for the former yugoslavia to regulate technical assistance with the latter. we recall that unconditional cooperation with the ad hoc tribunal in the hague is of crucial importance for all the states which have emerged from the break-up of yugoslavia. we also recall that montenegro has never shied away from its international obligations, and has always been commended for its effective cooperation with foreign and judicial authorities. the council also called on the commission to take all necessary measures to ensure that the eu's financial instruments are used effectively. another requirement raised by the european parliament concerned the fight against corruption in the public administration and the judiciary: the country is responding positively to european demands, as is shown by the new constitution which introduces mechanisms to protect the autonomy and independence of the judiciary. the capacity of the management class will then be developed by participation in community twinning and exchange programmes with the member states. some of these programmes will be conducive to the growth of younger people and scholars. the free movement of persons, in particular students and researchers, is also being facilitated by the simplification of the procedure for issuing short-stay visas, the subject of specific agreements with the european union signed last september. the final objective is to achieve full visa liberalisation in order to make effective the freedom of movement, another sensitive point of the stabilisation and association agreement, and to facilitate a dialogue that is an opportunity for growth and training. we believe that cultural issues should be given a wide scope, for example by promoting associations and protecting representatives of civil society. the free expression of thought must be guaranteed, as must the right to information. particular mention should be made of the environmental question: the previous constitution defined montenegro as an ecological republic, the first in the world to have given itself this label. the country has been blessed with nature, from the picturesque coastal landscape to the natural bay of bocche di cattaro, to the durmitor mountain range, inscribed on the unesco world heritage list. these riches must be protected by specific legislation, legislation which in many cases exists on paper but is not strictly enforced, often because of a lack of economic resources. the country receives a large income from tourism, but unfortunately tourism itself is at risk of backfiring on the environment, as the accommodation facilities are not equipped with systems suitable to manage, from an ecological point of view, the large influx of tourists. that is why we asked commissioner rehn at another time to direct the commission's attention to promoting environmental policies, particularly with regard to renewable energy sources, waste and water management and coastal protection. montenegro is not indifferent to the problem and is continuing to work on the proper management of natural resources. the spatial plan was recently approved to regulate building activity so as not to distort the coastal landscape.
i am a doctor who has been working on aids for 20 years and i have to say that, frankly, i would have expected the commission to come up with much more precise and pragmatic proposals. in the european union, transmission is primarily by sexual transmission. so, to be very specific: does the commission encourage all member states to organise sex education courses in schools? does it encourage states to reduce the cost of contraceptives, which are currently the only means of stopping sexual transmission? in europe, the second level of transmission is intravenous, mainly for those who use drugs. so what is the commission doing to encourage states to implement harm reduction strategies, which are the only ones that can reduce intravenous transmission for those who are unable, unwilling or unwilling to stop taking substances? as for the rest of the world, i would have expected the commission to come here and say: after eight months of wrangling with parliament, we note that parliament voted to amend article 6 of the trips agreement, even though it stated that it would not lead to any change, but to a commitment by the commission to fight for changes in the wto rules. currently, the trips rules grant patents to multinational companies for 20 years, with the result that drugs do not reach africa. i have heard absolutely nothing of this! if these rules are not changed, then talking about africa is just talking! and lastly, but perhaps not least, while everyone is talking about the fight against aids, you have a commissioner mandelson writing letters to the thai government saying not to make laws allowing the distribution of generic drugs and going to sponsor in his letters companies, with names and surnames, like sanofi-avensis! but i think the commission should have something to say about that!
mr president, commissioner, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the committee on transport and tourism, i should like to state the reasons for the motion for a resolution on the shipwrecks in the kerch strait in the black sea. our solidarity goes to the victims of this catastrophe! we call on the council and the commission to follow the situation in the black sea closely and to take concrete action to help reduce the ecological impact of the disaster. europe is not yet ready to prevent the recurrence of very serious accidents such as that which occurred in the black sea, with the full range of necessary rules, which must include, among other things, the responsibility of the states for the safety of the ships they fly in prosecuting those responsible for these environmental disasters in civil proceedings. the european parliament voted on the third maritime safety package at first reading in april 2007, but it has not yet been adopted in its entirety and is inexplicably stalled in the council, despite the commitment on this issue by the portuguese presidency in the committee on transport and in parliament itself. the package, which consists of seven reports, is directed in one direction: it increases maritime safety standards, protects passengers and reduces environmental damage in the event of accidents, and provides for obligations and liability for states, carriers and shipowners. by fragmenting the debate and favouring some issues over others, the council shows that it does not want to take the security issue seriously and is putting the brakes on the whole package. maritime safety is too serious a subject to be the subject of tactics, too serious for the experiences we have already had: erika, prestige, most recently segesta jet in the straits of messina and sea diamond in santorini! the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of ships is not compromised. this is why the european parliament believes that all seven proposals must be put forward positively and as soon as possible, before another environmental disaster with human losses takes place: the commission has also proposed that the member states should be required to provide for the establishment of a common system of classification, to require states to control the ships they flag, to carry out inspections of ships in ports and to monitor their movements, to provide for procedures for responding to accidents and to verify and manage liability both to third parties and to passengers. we therefore urge the council not to be insensitive to this tragic warning from the black sea.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the aim of this report is to remove most of the obstacles to the recovery of maintenance payments within europe by creating a legal framework which is suited to the legitimate aspirations of maintenance creditors. the most important starting point is that in the vast majority of cases the maintenance creditor is the weak party and must therefore be protected with particular energy. it is clear that the greatest difficulty is the de facto situation of the debtor. however, it is at least necessary to do what is possible, that is to say, to eliminate any bureaucratic obstacles and thus make certain the applicable law, to give preference to the law of the place of residence of the creditor, to give immediate effect to the judicial decision imposing the obligation to pay maintenance, even in countries other than the one in which it was pronounced. the legal affairs committee, which was called upon to deliver an opinion under the enhanced cooperation procedure on the regulation on jurisdiction and the enforcement of decisions in matters of maintenance obligations, played an important role in producing the text, achieving an important compromise agreement between the main political groups, for which i publicly thank mrs wallis. the main objectives of the amendments tabled by the committee on legal affairs were to define clearly the maintenance obligation, to extend its scope, to protect the most vulnerable parties involved and to simplify the proposed text. it was necessary to define the maintenance obligation unequivocally and to include all injunctions relating to lump sum payments within the scope of the regulation. the commission has also proposed that the directive be amended to include a new provision on the protection of workers from the risks of exposure to carcinogens. in conclusion, since the time for speaking has expired, i can assure you that the people's party will support this decision with conviction.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as the memorandum of understanding between the european union and china is about to expire, the questions put seem to me to clearly reflect the legitimate concerns of industry and industry in the light of the impact that imports - or rather the widespread invasion of chinese products in european countries - has had and still has. i have had occasion to stress on several occasions - and i have not been the only one to say so - that genuine competition and the competitiveness of our products on the internal market, even more so than on the external market, is ensured not only and not so much by the quota system, but essentially by defending the sector against unfair competition. unfair, because it is based on immensely lower cost and production conditions. the added value of chinese products at this cost is disproportionate because of the known inconsistencies in production factors compared with those in force on our civilized continent. how can we expect to compete with products produced at infinitely lower costs and which, even in terms of comparative quality, are now almost on a par with many european products? i believe that there is essentially one, the only way to restore some of what i would call fair trade and sustainable competition: i think that a system of surveillance of chinese imports must be based on the ascertainment of production conditions not too far removed from those which support our industries. can't we expect the labor costs to be the same? the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. a different policy should also be applied to european industries which relocate and compete unfairly with industries which continue to be produced by our states, perhaps through tax measures which balance the advantage with those which do not relocate. i conclude: the distribution conditions in europe should also be monitored more closely, as is certainly the case in italy, where retail distribution is masked as wholesale.
member of the commission. mr president, i find myself in broad agreement with most of the sentiments that have been expressed during this debate. however, i would at the outset reject mr belder’s view that we do not have a common trade policy in the eu, and that the member states are so divided that we cannot pursue a policy on, for example, textiles. our experience in textiles demonstrates only too clearly that we do, in fact, have a common trade policy, through which we have been able to bring together member states with different emphases and different orientations, to weld together their views and to produce a common trade policy in textiles that has been consistently pursued. there may be differences on the use of trade defence instruments, but through the review and anticipated reform i want to build fresh consensus and solidarity amongst member states on the use of those trade defence instruments, and notably on their greater use by smes, for which i want to bring forward proposals. some specific points have been made, for example about the double-checking surveillance which will be in operation in 2008. the commission will monitor textile imports from china in as close to real time as possible. this includes double-checking surveillance and any other monitoring means at the commission’s disposal, such as the taxud surveillance, which provides trade data on the basis of actual trade. in the face of a sudden surge of chinese textiles, the commission stands ready to use all the instruments at its disposal, should the situation so require. however, i would stress that the 2005 deal was a once-and-for-all deal, and the commission does not intend to make proposals for the extension of the levels agreed. as such, it is not opposed to more trade, and an increase could be expected. should the upsurge, however, take such dimensions that action is justified, this will be based on existing requirements and criteria. we do rely on the co-responsibility of china for this smooth transition. china is well aware that it is not in its interests to repeat what happened in 2005. we also rely on the economic operators’ self-interest to avoid a recurrence of 2005. textiles are now moving into the same category as any other product, so the usual instruments – including trade defence instruments – apply, with the usual standards. the issue of eu assistance for the textiles industry has been raised. let me make two last points on this. at the eu level, the commission has committed over eur 70 million, for research and development under the sixth framework programme, to textile and clothing projects, while two innovation project proposals have acquired funding within the europe innova framework. as far as the globalisation fund is concerned, it is as open to the textile sector as to other sectors. there have, so far, been eight formal applications for a contribution from the european globalisation fund, of which four concern textiles. none of these textile cases have yet been approved by the budgetary authority. they are all still being assessed by the commission services. lastly, i turn to the issue of the euro-mediterranean, raised by mr sturdy. the commission has set up a formal euro-mediterranean dialogue on the future of the textile and clothing industry, in order to define common strategies towards achieving better competitiveness of the industry in the euro-mediterranean zone. the objective of the dialogue is to bring euro-mediterranean countries and candidate countries together, in order to find common solutions for improving their competitiveness. i look forward to receiving proposals emerging from that dialogue.
